This is the only red in the whole suite, so it is the first of the open-bug milestones.</p> <h2 id="the-defects"><a class="header" href="#the-defects">The defects</a></h2> <ul> <li><strong>host-reference CI is red</strong> (<a href="https://github.com/connollydavid/host-reference/issues/2">connollydavid/host-reference#2</a>): the <code>lint</code> and <code>features</code> jobs fail because the pinned <code>1.95.0</code> toolchain is installed without the <code>rustfmt</code>/<code>clippy</code> components (<code>'cargo-fmt' is not installed</code>). The <code>release</code> job, gated on them, is skipped, so a tagged release publishes no binaries. <code>test</code>, <code>allium</code>, and every <code>build</code> job pass, so the code is sound and this is a CI-config defect. It predates plan/0057 (v0.1.3 failed the same way).</li> <li><strong>host-reference-ocr and host-reference-openscad carry no CI workflow.</strong> Their reproducibility is anchored by agentic-host's <code>software --verify-build</code>, yet neither has a per-repo test or build lane, so a regression in a helper is caught only downstream.</li> </ul> <h2 id="decided-direction"><a class="header" href="#decided-direction">Decided direction</a></h2> <ul> <li>Install the components on the pinned toolchain (<code>components = ["rustfmt", "clippy"]</code> in <code>rust-toolchain.toml</code>, or <code>rustup component add rustfmt clippy</code> before the lint and features steps), so <code>lint</code>, <code>features</code>, and <code>release</code> go green and the release binaries publish.</li> <li>Add a CI workflow to each helper that covers its test and build lanes, in the host-reference shape scaled to a single-crate helper.</li> </ul> <h2 id="verification-26"><a class="header" href="#verification-26">Verification</a></h2> <p>All three repos' CI green on a fresh push, host-reference's release job publishing its artifacts, and agentic-host's whole-suite verify still green. A host-reference CI-only change carries no binary change, so it re-pins by the artifact-preserving pin-advance reserved for a pure CI fix (no version bump); a helper that gains a workflow does the same.</p> <h2 id="as-built-complete"><a class="header" href="#as-built-complete">As-built (complete)</a></h2> <p>host-reference's toolchain now declares the rustfmt and clippy components, which turned <code>lint</code> and <code>features</code> green and un-masked three advisories cargo-deny had never reached under the earlier fmt failure:</p> <ul> <li><strong>quick-xml RUSTSEC-2026-0194 and 0195</strong> (real DoS advisories) are accepted as a scoped, tracked ignore in <code>deny.toml</code>. They reach the workspace only through the opt-in office and geometry readers (<code>undoc</code>, <code>threemf</code>), never the deployed default-features binary, and the upgrade is blocked upstream (<code>threemf</code> 0.8.0 is unpatched; bumping <code>undoc</code> drags in a still-vulnerable 0.40.1; forcing 0.41 breaks the API). Tracked in <a href="https://github.com/connollydavid/host-reference/issues/3">connollydavid/host-reference#3</a> until upstream lands quick-xml >= 0.41.0 (operator ruling: scoped ignore over a breaking dependency surgery).</li> <li><strong>ttf-parser RUSTSEC-2026-0192</strong> (unmaintained only, no vulnerability, under the opt-in pdf reader) is accepted on the same footing as the existing unmaintained advisories.</li> </ul> <p>ocr and openscad each gained a test, lint, and build workflow plus a pinned toolchain; openscad's new fmt lane fixed one pre-existing formatting diff. All three re-pinned artifact-preserving (openscad's fmt re-derives byte-identically, verified). The three repos' CI and <code>software --check</code> are green.</p> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><h1 id="plan0059-remap-and-allowlist-hardening-the-migration-tooling-withstands-the-process-it-prescribes"><a class="header" href="#plan0059-remap-and-allowlist-hardening-the-migration-tooling-withstands-the-process-it-prescribes">plan/0059 remap-and-allowlist-hardening: the migration tooling withstands the process it prescribes</a></h1> <p>This milestone continues the plan/0056 recipe-and-materialisation-hardening lineage. Where plan/0056 hardened the recipe parser and the bare-store layout, this one hardens the migration tooling: <code>remap</code> and the allowlist surface both mishandle states the methodology's own documented process produces. All four issues were surfaced by the pgs-release adopter exercising a real migration.</p> <h2 id="the-defects-1"><a class="header" href="#the-defects-1">The defects</a></h2> <ul> <li><strong><a href="https://github.com/connollydavid/host-lifecycle/issues/11">#11</a></strong> <code>remap --check</code> (run inside <code>software --check</code>) errors on the retired or absent <code>.host-remap</code> that the host process itself prescribes: the documented remap phase ends by committing the substitutions and removing <code>.host-remap</code>, and the recheck then fails on exactly that end state. The tool contradicts its own flow. (Sibling of plan/0056's #7, which fixed the empty-dictionary case; this is the absent case.)</li> <li><strong><a href="https://github.com/connollydavid/host-lifecycle/issues/12">#12</a></strong> <code>remap --apply</code> rewrites inside <code>host-lint:ignore</code> fenced blocks, corrupting the boxed durable records whose whole purpose is to preserve old names verbatim. In pgs-release it rewrote the rename dictionary inside a migration decision's boxed block and had to be restored from an archive commit.</li> <li><strong><a href="https://github.com/connollydavid/host-lifecycle/issues/13">#13</a></strong> the sanctioned-token allowlist is split: the hooks and <code>host-lint --all</code> read <code>LEXICON</code>, while <code>remap --check</code> reads a different surface, so a token declared in one is unknown to the other. One concept, two disagreeing sources.</li> <li><strong><a href="https://github.com/connollydavid/host-lifecycle/issues/14">#14</a></strong> <code>software --materialize</code> always does a full-history bare clone, with no shallow or filtered option, so a large-history component pays the full cost on every CI leg. An enhancement folded in here (operator ruling: bugs plus the coverage gaps).</li> </ul> <h2 id="decided-direction-1"><a class="header" href="#decided-direction-1">Decided direction</a></h2> <ul> <li><code>remap --check</code> treats the retired or absent <code>.host-remap</code> as a fail-safe no-op the same way #7 made the empty dictionary one, so the documented end state reads clean rather than error.</li> <li><code>remap --apply</code> honours the <code>host-lint:ignore</code> fence, skipping substitution inside a boxed block the way the naming scan already skips it, so a durable record is never corrupted.</li> <li>The allowlist reads one source, so every code path honours the same declared tokens.</li> <li><code>--materialize</code> gains a filtered or shallow option (or a documented cache contract) that still lands the pinned commit's tree, so the pin stays the reproducibility anchor.</li> </ul> <p>The cast's Fen (the real <code>qwen3.5-4b</code>) is the acceptance test for the tool-carried behaviours.</p> <h2 id="verification-27"><a class="header" href="#verification-27">Verification</a></h2> <p>Each defect carries a regression test; #12 and #13 additionally assert the anti-corruption and single-source properties. Ships as one host-lifecycle release, re-vendored and propagated, with the whole-suite verify gate green and the Fen probe passing.</p> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><h1 id="plan0059-implementation-audit-of-record"><a class="header" href="#plan0059-implementation-audit-of-record">plan/0059 implementation (audit of record)</a></h1> <p>The per-bug audit against host-lifecycle v0.37.0 source, with the code paths located, so the fix work starts grounded.</p> <h2 id="issue-11-remap---check-on-an-absent-or-comment-only-host-remap-resolved"><a class="header" href="#issue-11-remap---check-on-an-absent-or-comment-only-host-remap-resolved">Issue 11: remap --check on an absent or comment-only .host-remap (resolved)</a></h2> <p><code>load_remap</code> (src/main.rs:750) is already fail-safe: an absent file (NotFound) returns an empty rule set, and a comment-only file skips every line to the same empty set, with no error. Verified against v0.37.0: <code>remap --check</code> reports clean at exit 0 on both states, and the manifest recheck is exactly <code>host-lifecycle remap --check .</code>, so the recheck and the standalone agree. Neither error string from the report (<code>cannot read .host-remap</code>, <code>no usable entries</code>) exists in the current source; the report was against a pre-fail-safe build. Closed on the tracker; no code change owed.</p> <h2 id="issue-12-remap---apply-rewrites-inside-host-lintignore-fenced-blocks"><a class="header" href="#issue-12-remap---apply-rewrites-inside-host-lintignore-fenced-blocks">Issue 12: remap --apply rewrites inside host-lint:ignore fenced blocks</a></h2> <p><code>apply_text</code> (src/main.rs:850) substitutes line by line with no fence awareness, so <code>remap --apply</code> corrupts a <code>host-lint:ignore</code> boxed block, the very record the box preserves verbatim. The scan side is already correct: <code>remap --check</code> calls <code>host_lint::scan_text_with_allow</code>, which skips the fence. The fix teaches <code>apply_text</code> the same rule: track a <code>host-lint:ignore</code> fenced region and emit its lines untouched, while a regular code block stays substituted (the spine skips only the tagged fence). A small self-contained fence tracker in host-lifecycle keeps M2 independent of a host-lint change.</p> <h2 id="issue-13-the-sanctioned-token-allowlist-is-split"><a class="header" href="#issue-13-the-sanctioned-token-allowlist-is-split">Issue 13: the sanctioned-token allowlist is split</a></h2> <p><code>load_allow</code> (src/main.rs:787) reads <code>.host-lint-allow</code>; host-lint and the hooks read <code>LEXICON</code>. <code>remap --check</code> uses <code>load_allow</code>, so a token declared in <code>LEXICON</code> is unknown to remap, and one in <code>.host-lint-allow</code> is unknown to host-lint. Operator ruling: full unification on <code>LEXICON</code>, which needs no host-lint change. <code>host_lint::load_lexicon</code> is already public and returns <code>Lexicon { phrases_lc, .. }</code> (the lowercased masking phrases the <code>--all</code> and <code>--docs</code> lanes use), and its doc names an embedder as a caller. So <code>remap --check</code> calls <code>host_lint::load_lexicon(root).phrases_lc</code> and passes it to <code>scan_text_with_allow</code> in place of <code>load_allow(.host-lint-allow)</code>, honouring the phrases host-lint honours. <code>.host-lint-allow</code> is read as a legacy alias merged into the phrase list, with a deprecation note, so an existing adopter file keeps working while <code>LEXICON</code> becomes canonical.</p> <h2 id="coupling-correction"><a class="header" href="#coupling-correction">Coupling correction</a></h2> <p>An earlier draft assumed issue 13 needed a new host-lint LEXICON-scan API, which would have coupled M2 to a host-lint release. That was wrong: <code>load_lexicon</code> is already public. So M2 (issues 12, 13, 14) is host-lifecycle-only, and M3 (issue 18, the hook script in host-lint's <code>main.rs</code>) is host-lint-only. The two milestones are independent, as originally cut.</p> <h2 id="issue-14-software---materialize-clones-full-history-every-time"><a class="header" href="#issue-14-software---materialize-clones-full-history-every-time">Issue 14: software --materialize clones full history every time</a></h2> <p><code>software --materialize</code> does a full-history bare clone, paid on every CI leg for a large-history component. Fix: a <code>--filter=blob:none</code> partial-clone option (or a documented cache contract) that still lands the pinned commit's tree, so the pin stays the reproducibility anchor. An enhancement folded in by operator ruling (bugs plus the coverage gaps).</p> <h2 id="cascade"><a class="header" href="#cascade">Cascade</a></h2> <p>The spec (<code>host-lifecycle.allium</code>) and obligations are updated for any new behaviour, with a Rust regression test per bug (issue 12 asserts the fence is preserved, issue 13 the single-source property). Ships as one host-lifecycle release, re-vendored and propagated to consumers, with the whole-suite verify gate green and the Fen probe passing on the tool-carried behaviours.</p> <h2 id="as-built"><a class="header" href="#as-built">As-built</a></h2> <p>All three landed in host-lifecycle's source, each with a regression test. <code>apply_text</code> gained a self-contained <code>host-lint:ignore</code> fence tracker that replicates host-lint's <code>fence_info</code> (a regular code fence stays substituted, matching the scan side, so a tell cannot be laundered by inline-quoting). <code>remap_allow</code> unifies host-lint's LEXICON as the canonical vocabulary with the legacy <code>.host-lint-allow</code> merged in as a deprecated alias, noted when present. <code>software --materialize</code> gained an opt-in <code>--partial</code> flag that clones with <code>--filter=blob:none</code>, so the pin still round-trips while the whole-history blob download defers to worktree checkout. The full inline suite passes and clippy is clean. No allium or obligations change is owed: the manifest records that the remap and materialize git mechanics are out of the spec's scope, so the regression tests carry the specification. The code ships with the host-lifecycle release for this batch.</p> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><h1 id="plan0060-host-lint-pre-commit-hook-the-hook-skips-a-gitlink-instead-of-failing-closed-on-it"><a class="header" href="#plan0060-host-lint-pre-commit-hook-the-hook-skips-a-gitlink-instead-of-failing-closed-on-it">plan/0060 host-lint-pre-commit-hook: the hook skips a gitlink instead of failing closed on it</a></h1> <p>The host-lint pre-commit hook blocks any commit that stages a submodule pointer. Found while bumping the host-template pointer during the plan/0057 release, and worked around there with a gitlink-only <code>--no-verify</code> commit.</p> <h2 id="the-defect"><a class="header" href="#the-defect">The defect</a></h2> <p><a href="https://github.com/connollydavid/host-lint/issues/18">connollydavid/host-lint#18</a>: the hook lints each staged path via <code>git show ":$file" | host-lint --stdin-as "$file"</code> under <code>set -o pipefail</code> (the pipefail was added by the fail-open hardening). For a submodule gitlink, <code>git show ":<submodule>"</code> exits 128 (a gitlink is not a blob), and pipefail propagates that 128 to the hook's <code>rc</code>, which the default case treats as fail-closed:</p> <pre><code>host-lint: error linting <submodule> (exit 128); failing closed </code></pre> <p>So the pipefail hardening, correct in itself, regressed submodule-pointer commits: every commit that stages a gitlink is now blocked. A gitlink carries no text to lint, so failing on it is wrong.</p> <h2 id="decided-direction-2"><a class="header" href="#decided-direction-2">Decided direction</a></h2> <p>Skip the gitlink rather than fail on it: drop mode-160000 entries from the staged path list (read the mode with <code>git diff --cached --raw</code> and skip <code>160000</code>), or treat a <code>git show</code> exit 128 on a gitlink as clean. Preserve the fail-closed behaviour for every real failure (a usage error, a panic, a genuine <code>git show</code> failure on a blob), so the hardening the pipefail bought is not lost.</p> <h2 id="verification-28"><a class="header" href="#verification-28">Verification</a></h2> <p>A regression test that stages a submodule pointer and confirms the hook exits clean rather than fail closed, plus the existing fail-closed tests still passing on a real error. Ships as a host-lint release with the hook asset rebuilt, re-vendored and propagated to the consumers, whole-suite verify green.</p> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><h1 id="plan0061-adopt-elsewhere-and-elicit-adopt-from-an-arbitrary-folder-by-creating-the-host-elsewhere-and-eliciting-its-name"><a class="header" href="#plan0061-adopt-elsewhere-and-elicit-adopt-from-an-arbitrary-folder-by-creating-the-host-elsewhere-and-eliciting-its-name">plan/0061 adopt-elsewhere-and-elicit: adopt from an arbitrary folder by creating the host elsewhere and eliciting its name</a></h1> <p>This milestone extends adoption so an agent can start an agentic project in whatever folder it is already working in. Today <code>adopt</code> takes a directory and a revision and scaffolds in place, and the arbitrary-folder case is only half-served by the <code>refuse-adopt-in-place</code> message, which tells the operator to make a separate host by hand. The feature builds the active path: elicit the project name, create the host in a fresh <code>agentic-<name></code> folder, scaffold it, and request that the operator switch to it. The source folder is never written to.</p> <p>The cast's Fen (the real <code>qwen3.5-4b</code>) is the acceptance test.</p> <h2 id="where-it-came-from-3"><a class="header" href="#where-it-came-from-3">Where it came from</a></h2> <p>A feature request from the operator: an agent should start an agentic project from an arbitrary folder, create the host elsewhere on the machine, and ask the operator to switch to it. Two refinements landed in the same conversation. The source folder may be a large aggregate directory or the home directory, so the tool must be defensive and touch nothing within it. And a folder that already matches <code>agentic-<name></code> exactly is a carve-out that adopts in place. The operator flagged the question of how an authentic name Q&A works across Claude Code, opencode, and codex, as a major concern and a skill-related item.</p> <h2 id="the-three-routes"><a class="header" href="#the-three-routes">The three routes</a></h2> <p>Adoption becomes a decision on the current directory:</p> <ol> <li>A software repository (a manifest at its root) keeps the existing refuse-and-embed path: become the Where room of a separate host. Unchanged.</li> <li>A folder already named <code>agentic-<name></code> and empty adopts in place; the name is the <code><name></code> the operator already chose, so there is no Q&A and no handoff. The carve-out.</li> <li>Any other folder is arbitrary. The tool elicits the name, creates the host at <code>../agentic-<name></code> (override with <code>--at</code>), scaffolds it, seeds a one-line purpose, and requests the operator switch. The source folder is untouched.</li> </ol> <h2 id="the-name-qa-across-claude-code-opencode-and-codex-the-operators-major-concern"><a class="header" href="#the-name-qa-across-claude-code-opencode-and-codex-the-operators-major-concern">The name Q&A across Claude Code, opencode, and codex (the operator's major concern)</a></h2> <p>The name carries operator intent, so it is elicited rather than read off the folder; a folder named <code>pdf-notes</code> never becomes a project named <code>pdf</code>. The elicitation must read authentically in whatever host drives the agent. The mechanism is layered.</p> <ul> <li>MCP elicitation (Form mode) where the client supports it. The June 2025 MCP specification added an <code>elicitation/create</code> request: the server names the fields it needs (here <code>name</code>, plus a one-line <code>purpose</code> for the seed), the client renders the prompt in its own native surface, the operator answers or declines, and the tool resumes. A URL mode covers sensitive input. The reference memory records the specification link.</li> <li>A stdout contract as the universal backstop. Where a client does not implement elicitation, <code>adopt</code> exits with a distinct code and names the missing field, so the agent asks the operator through its own native surface and re-runs with <code>--name</code>. This is the path validated on the real 4B.</li> </ul> <p>The Q&A belongs to the tool, and the skill only points at it. Each host has its own skill format, so an elicitation authored into skill markdown would not travel; the tool's protocol and stdout contract keep it portable.</p> <h2 id="the-casts-throughline-2"><a class="header" href="#the-casts-throughline-2">The cast's throughline</a></h2> <ul> <li><strong>Mara</strong> (operator, final say): the name and the switch are hers. No agent, in any host, can relocate her session, so the switch is a request she performs. The tool proposes a name and a path and never invents them. She added the load-bearing constraint: assume the source may be the home directory, and touch nothing in it.</li> <li><strong>Wren</strong> (amnesiac executor): the agent that creates the host and the agent that continues in it are separate sessions with total amnesia between them. The handoff must be written into the new host's files, because the creating session's context does not survive the switch. Hence the seeded purpose note.</li> <li><strong>Orin</strong> (maintainer): express the behaviour once and make it fail safe when followed literally. If the operator never switches, nothing is left half-built, because the source stays pristine and only the new host exists.</li> <li><strong>Bly</strong> (writes now, reads cold): the new host self-describes to a memoryless read through the stamp and the adopt checklist, which re-list the next steps and so over-report. The source carries no ambiguous breadcrumb that a later cold read could mistake for a half-adopted host.</li> <li><strong>Fen</strong> (acceptance test, driven not simulated): the real <code>qwen3.5-4b</code> routed all three decision points correctly on the corrected scenario, six of six each. It asks the operator for the name rather than reading it off the folder, it requests the operator switch rather than relocating itself, and it adopts in place in the carve-out. The condition is that the tool output carries the routed next move, which the design is built to do.</li> </ul> <h2 id="locked-decisions-operator"><a class="header" href="#locked-decisions-operator">Locked decisions (operator)</a></h2> <ul> <li>The name Q&A is carried by MCP elicitation with the stdout contract as the universal backstop.</li> <li>An arbitrary folder relocates in one command: elicit, create <code>../agentic-<name></code> (<code>--at</code> to override), scaffold, request the switch.</li> <li>The source folder is touched by nothing, even when it is the home directory.</li> <li>The new host is seeded with a one-line purpose so the amnesiac next session is not cold.</li> </ul> <h2 id="open-questions-2"><a class="header" href="#open-questions-2">Open questions</a></h2> <ul> <li>How host-lifecycle speaks MCP. It is a CLI today, and Form-mode elicitation needs it to answer an MCP client. Whether that is a <code>host-lifecycle</code> server mode, a separate thin MCP surface, or the adopt verb made MCP-callable is unsettled, and it is the largest piece of work here.</li> <li>Where the behaviour lives. The active relocate-and-handoff extends an existing methodology rule (adopt into a separate host) rather than adding a new one, so it reads as host-lifecycle software. Whether any part is spine doctrine that needs a host-template ledger entry is for the milestone to settle, gated by the anti-ouroboros scope rule.</li> <li>The seed's shape. A seeded purpose is a <code>plan/</code> entry or a MEMORY line; the milestone picks one and defines what a declined purpose does (the seed is optional, the name is not).</li> </ul> <h2 id="verification-29"><a class="header" href="#verification-29">Verification</a></h2> <p>Ships as one host-lifecycle release, then re-vendor and propagate to consumers, with the whole-suite verify gate green and the Fen probe passing on all three routes. The cheap-verification bar: a run in an arbitrary folder writes nothing there and creates a well-formed <code>agentic-<name></code> host elsewhere; a run in a pattern folder adopts in place; a run in a software repository still refuses.</p> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><h1 id="plan0062-plan-index-coverage-gate-that-planmd-indexes-every-milestone-directory"><a class="header" href="#plan0062-plan-index-coverage-gate-that-planmd-indexes-every-milestone-directory">plan/0062 plan-index-coverage: gate that PLAN.md indexes every milestone directory</a></h1> <p>The audited-plan rule says every milestone gets a row in PLAN.md's index. CLAUDE.md asserts it, and nothing checks it, so the milestone directories plan/0056 through plan/0060 sat unindexed for five milestones before the gap was noticed by eye. This is the self-blindness class plan/0036 and plan/0038 already named: a rule with a home but no gate.</p> <h2 id="the-defect-1"><a class="header" href="#the-defect-1">The defect</a></h2> <p>PLAN.md is the human-readable index of the plan/ room, and its rows are authored by hand on each milestone. No check compares the rows against the directories on disk, so a milestone can ship its directory and README, be committed and pushed, and never appear in the index, with no complaint from any gate. The work itself is tracked truthfully by the receipts and <code>software --check</code>; what drifts is only the index a reader navigates by, which is the artifact a cold reader trusts to find the milestones.</p> <h2 id="decided-direction-3"><a class="header" href="#decided-direction-3">Decided direction</a></h2> <p>A coverage check, in the shape reconcile already uses for <code>.host-software</code>: derive the owed set from repo state each run. List the <code>plan/NNNN-slug</code> directories, list the rows PLAN.md links, and HAZARD any directory with no row. The check reads the repo, holds no stored state, and re-lists on the next run, so a partial fix never buries the remainder. This is a coverage invariant rather than a receipt: no action is being attested, only a correspondence between the directories and their index.</p> <h2 id="the-casts-throughline-3"><a class="header" href="#the-casts-throughline-3">The cast's throughline</a></h2> <ul> <li><strong>Bly</strong> (writes now, reads cold): the index is what a memoryless read navigates by, so an unindexed milestone must surface as owed, over-reporting, never silently absent.</li> <li><strong>Orin</strong> (maintainer): express the rule once and gate it where it lives; an asserted rule with no gate is the recurring defect.</li> <li><strong>Fen</strong> (acceptance test): one check names the gap and the directory that owes a row, so the weak agent fixes it in one move rather than auditing the index by hand.</li> </ul> <h2 id="open-questions-3"><a class="header" href="#open-questions-3">Open questions</a></h2> <ul> <li>Whether the check lives in <code>validate</code> (which already owns plan/ naming) or <code>reconcile</code> (which owns the repo-level coverage pattern).</li> <li>Whether it is spine doctrine. PLAN.md and the plan/ room are methodology structure that every adopter carries, so a plan-index coverage check reads as spine, which would need a host-template ledger entry, gated by the anti-ouroboros scope rule. The milestone settles this.</li> <li>Whether the reverse direction is checked too (a PLAN.md plan-row that points at no directory), the same coverage read from the other side.</li> </ul> <h2 id="verification-30"><a class="header" href="#verification-30">Verification</a></h2> <p>Ships as one host-lifecycle release, then re-vendor and propagate to consumers, with the whole-suite verify gate green. The check HAZARDs a synthetic unindexed milestone directory and passes once the row is added. A real qwen3.5-4b probe confirms the weak agent reads the HAZARD and adds the missing row.</p> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><h1 id="plan0063-software-check-walk-safe-the-software---check-tree-walk-must-not-follow-a-symlink-into-a-cycle"><a class="header" href="#plan0063-software-check-walk-safe-the-software---check-tree-walk-must-not-follow-a-symlink-into-a-cycle">plan/0063 software-check-walk-safe: the software --check tree walk must not follow a symlink into a cycle</a></h1> <p><code>host-lifecycle software --check</code> recursively walks each component worktree, and three of its lanes did so unsafely: they followed symlinks and had no cycle guard. A gitignored directory whose symlinks form a cycle (a Wine prefix, <code>node_modules</code>, a virtualenv) made the walk never terminate. On a WSL2 <code>/mnt/c</code> 9P mount, which is exactly this development host, each <code>openat</code> blocked in <code>p9_client_rpc</code>, so the process wedged in uninterruptible sleep that even a kill signal could not reap, and repeated invocations piled up wedged walkers. The gate that verifies pins, spec lanes, obligations, and build reproducibility became unrunnable.</p> <p>Reported as <a href="https://github.com/connollydavid/host-lifecycle/issues/15">connollydavid/host-lifecycle#15</a>.</p> <h2 id="the-defect-2"><a class="header" href="#the-defect-2">The defect</a></h2> <p>Three recursive walks, <code>read_obligations_text</code>, <code>find_specs</code>, and <code>read_dir_recursive</code>, tested each entry with <code>p.is_dir()</code>, which dereferences a symlink, so a link pointing at an ancestor produced unbounded recursion. They also descended into gitignored, untracked scratch, which is where a Wine prefix or a <code>node_modules</code> places the arbitrary symlink structures that trigger the cycle. The sibling <code>collect_files</code> walk was already safe: it reads the type from the <code>DirEntry</code> (an <code>lstat</code>, which does not follow the link) and treats a symlink as a leaf.</p> <h2 id="decided-direction-4"><a class="header" href="#decided-direction-4">Decided direction</a></h2> <p>One shared symlink-safe, depth-bounded walker, <code>walk_files_safe</code>, that the three lanes route through, so no lane can re-introduce the unguarded walk. A symlink is always a leaf and is never followed, which breaks the cycle by construction; a depth cap is defence-in-depth against a non-symlink cycle such as a bind mount; an unreadable directory is skipped rather than fatal. <code>read_dir_recursive</code> keeps an empty skip list so the file set its input digest is taken over is unchanged.</p> <h2 id="as-built-1"><a class="header" href="#as-built-1">As-built</a></h2> <p><code>walk_files_safe</code> is added and the three lanes call it. A <code>#[cfg(unix)]</code> regression test builds a directory whose child symlinks back to an ancestor, walks it, and asserts the walk terminates, still reaches the real files under the cycle, and never descends the link. Under the old <code>is_dir</code> walk the test would not terminate. clippy is clean and the full inline suite passes. The obligations manifest is unchanged (the lanes keep their names and <code>exercises=</code> links), so no discharge re-derivation is owed.</p> <h2 id="verification-31"><a class="header" href="#verification-31">Verification</a></h2> <p>Ships in the host-lifecycle release with the lifecycle batch, then re-vendor and propagate to consumers, with the whole-suite verify gate green. The cheap-verification bar: a worktree carrying a gitignored symlink cycle passes <code>software --check</code> in bounded time rather than hanging.</p> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><h1 id="plan0064-prose-audits-the-repo---prose-with-no-files-and---all-audit-the-tracked-doc-set"><a class="header" href="#plan0064-prose-audits-the-repo---prose-with-no-files-and---all-audit-the-tracked-doc-set">plan/0064 prose-audits-the-repo: --prose with no files and --all audit the tracked doc set</a></h1> <p><code>host-lint --prose</code> with no file arguments did not audit the repository. It once reported clean at exit 0 with no output, a fail-open for a script that trusts the exit code, and after the plan/0055 hardening it exited with an error instead. Either way there was no <code>host-lint</code> CLI invocation that prose-audited a whole repository, and <code>--all</code> ran only the naming lane, so no single command matched the authoritative <code>host-lifecycle prose</code> gate. An author who ran <code>host-lint --prose</code> as a local pre-flight saw a result that disagreed with the CI gate on the same tracked docs.</p> <p>Reported as <a href="https://github.com/connollydavid/host-lint/issues/20">connollydavid/host-lint#20</a>.</p> <h2 id="the-defect-3"><a class="header" href="#the-defect-3">The defect</a></h2> <p>The prose audit ran only when explicit file paths were passed. <code>--prose</code> with no files had no repo-wide behaviour, and <code>--all</code> covered the naming lane alone. The repo-wide prose audit existed as <code>--docs</code>, but nothing tied it to <code>--prose</code> or <code>--all</code>, so the obvious pre-flight commands missed the tropes the gate catches.</p> <h2 id="decided-direction-5"><a class="header" href="#decided-direction-5">Decided direction</a></h2> <p>One shared <code>audit_tracked_docs</code> helper runs the tracked-doc prose audit, and <code>--all</code>, <code>--docs</code>, and no-file <code>--prose</code> all route through it. <code>--all</code> becomes the comprehensive repository audit: the naming lane over tracked files plus the prose lane over tracked authored docs, so one command matches the host-lifecycle naming and prose gate. <code>--prose</code> with no files audits the tracked docs rather than erroring; <code>--prose <files></code> still scans exactly those files.</p> <h2 id="as-built-2"><a class="header" href="#as-built-2">As-built</a></h2> <p>The dispatch is reordered so <code>--all</code> is handled before <code>--prose</code>, which lets <code>--all --prose</code> fold into the comprehensive audit rather than erroring. Integration tests assert that <code>--prose</code> with no arguments, <code>--all</code>, and <code>--all --prose</code> each flag a tracked-doc trope; the existing <code>--all</code> symlink and termination tests stay green, and <code>--docs</code> behaviour is unchanged. The README records that <code>--all</code> now runs both lanes. clippy is clean and the unit and integration suites pass.</p> <h2 id="verification-32"><a class="header" href="#verification-32">Verification</a></h2> <p>Ships in the host-lint release that carries the pre-commit-hook gitlink fix (plan/0060, host-lint#18 and host-lint#19), then re-vendor and propagate to consumers, with the whole-suite verify gate green. The cheap-verification bar: <code>host-lint --prose</code> and <code>host-lint --all</code> in a repository with a tracked-doc trope both report it, matching <code>host-lifecycle prose</code>.</p> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><h1 id="plan0065-onboarding-and-mcp-layer-one-engine-two-human-shims-a-spawned-mcp-surface-one-dual-mode-entrance"><a class="header" href="#plan0065-onboarding-and-mcp-layer-one-engine-two-human-shims-a-spawned-mcp-surface-one-dual-mode-entrance">plan/0065 onboarding-and-mcp-layer: one engine, two human shims, a spawned MCP surface, one dual-mode entrance</a></h1> <p>This milestone records how a human and an agent start and connect an agentic project. It absorbs the earlier adopt-elsewhere design (<code>plan/0061</code>) as the <code>host-adopt</code> shim described below.</p> <h2 id="build-status-2026-07-07"><a class="header" href="#build-status-2026-07-07">Build status (2026-07-07)</a></h2> <p>The onboarding and MCP surface is <strong>built and shipped</strong> as host-lifecycle v0.39.0: the <code>init</code> and <code>adopt</code> verbs, the renamed <code>scaffold</code> primitive, the <code>host-init</code> and <code>host-adopt</code> shims, the spawned <code>mcp</code> stdio server with elicitation, and the oneshot git-and-optional-GitHub finalize. The decisions were grounded in data first (<code>gather-data.md</code>: a Fen acceptance run and an installer survey), the migration was flagged (call/0041 adopt-to-scaffold, call/0042 the MCP-on-tokio decision), and the surface passed a five-dimension adversarial review whose twelve confirmed findings are all fixed (<code>code-review.md</code>). The release re-vendored a self-owned bundle (call/0043, since tokio diverged host-lifecycle from host-lint's shared superset). The spine doctrine (the onboarding narrative, the source-read-only and refuse-existing invariants, the adopt phase running <code>scaffold</code>) shipped in host-template with an adopt-to-scaffold UPGRADING ledger entry, adopted here through the ledger. <strong>Remaining: the <code>host</code> install mode (the reproducible-build-anchored installer and its receipt) and its spine install contract, plus the Fen acceptance run on the built oneshot and agent-driven-resolve paths.</strong></p> <p>This design was reviewed by the cast and a Fable 5 advisor, and their required changes are folded in here. The real <code>qwen3.5-4b</code> routed the three-route decision twenty of twenty across five scenarios, so the two-verb split is legible to a weak agent. The cast's Fen remains the acceptance test for the paths that are built.</p> <h2 id="where-it-came-from-4"><a class="header" href="#where-it-came-from-4">Where it came from</a></h2> <p>A run of operator refinements in one working conversation. Adoption should start from an arbitrary folder and elicit the project name. A human should also start a project greenfield from a given name and have the GitHub repository created. The name Q&A should read authentically across Claude Code, opencode, and codex, which is one concern across the three clients rather than three separate ones. A single MCP surface should serve the components rather than each speaking the protocol alone. The human on-ramp should install as simply as the agent on-ramp reads. The whole human path is aimed at one-command execution.</p> <p>The design that answers these keeps one implementation and adds thin, well-named faces over it.</p> <h2 id="the-one-engine-and-its-two-shims"><a class="header" href="#the-one-engine-and-its-two-shims">The one engine and its two shims</a></h2> <p><code>host-lifecycle</code> is already the generator. Scaffolding a project, stamping it, and generating its book are its work today, so the create-and-adopt logic lives there rather than in a new library. It grows two human-facing verbs, <code>init</code> and <code>adopt</code>, each carrying the name Q&A and the optional GitHub creation. Because <code>host-lifecycle</code> is a single static binary, installing it is one download, so a human front door does not need a separate lightweight tool underneath.</p> <p><code>host-init</code> and <code>host-adopt</code> are tiny shims over those verbs, the same binary invoked under two names. They give a human a clean, purpose-named command instead of the internal engine name, and they carry no logic of their own. On a platform without cheap symlinks the shim is a copy or a small wrapper that forwards to the engine, so the two names cannot skew from one build.</p> <p>Adoption keeps the full three-route decision <code>plan/0061</code> locked, restated here so absorption drops nothing.</p> <ol> <li>A software repository (a build manifest at its root) keeps the refuse-and-embed path: an agentic host is created separately and this repository becomes its subject. <code>host-adopt</code> refuses in place.</li> <li>A folder already named <code>agentic-<name></code> and empty adopts in place. The name is the one the operator already chose, so there is no Q&A and no handoff. This is the carve-out.</li> <li>Any other folder is arbitrary. <code>host-adopt</code> elicits the name, creates the host at <code>../agentic-<name></code> (override with <code>--at</code>), scaffolds it, seeds a one-line purpose, and requests the operator switch. The source folder is untouched.</li> </ol> <p><code>host-init <name></code> is the fresh-folder path: it takes a given name, creates <code>agentic-<name></code> as a new directory, and refuses a target that exists. This is the <code>cargo new</code> shape against <code>host-adopt</code>'s <code>cargo init</code> shape.</p> <p>The bare <code>adopt</code> command name retires in favour of <code>host-adopt</code>. That rename is a migration, not only a naming choice: the live <code>adopt</code> skill and the <code>classify</code>, <code>upgrade</code>, <code>remap</code>, and <code>embed</code> skills invoke the command by name. The rename ships with a deprecate-then-retire shim, parallel to the front-door-to-entrance rename in <code>call/0027</code>, and its ledger accounting is in the spine-boundary section.</p> <h2 id="the-mcp-surface-spawned-not-resident"><a class="header" href="#the-mcp-surface-spawned-not-resident">The MCP surface: spawned, not resident</a></h2> <p>The single-surface goal is honoured by a spawned MCP server, not a persistent daemon. The cast and the Fable advisor converged that a resident service with per-platform units buys a service lifecycle, an endpoint surface, and a registration protocol to deliver an optional form prompt, when the backstop already covers every path. So the locked shape is the lighter one: <code>host-lifecycle</code> exposes <code>init</code> and <code>adopt</code> as MCP tools over stdio, and the client spawns and manages that process for the length of a session. There is no daemon, no port, no per-platform service, and no runtime registration surface to secure.</p> <p>A resident hub that components and plugins register with stays a future option, and it must earn itself. Before it is built it owes a named list of at least three concrete capabilities that need runtime registration beyond the name Q&A, a transport choice, and a registration-trust design, because a runtime registry that any local process can write to would inject tool descriptions into every agent session. Until then, registration is a declared manifest read at spawn, which also self-describes to a cold read.</p> <p>The elicitation path is explicit. MCP elicitation is a server-to-client request inside a session, so it exists only when <code>init</code> or <code>adopt</code> run as MCP tools on the spawned server, not when they run as a shell command. A client that invokes the shell verb gets the backstop; a client that invokes the MCP tool and declares the capability gets the Form-mode prompt. That the agent must choose the shell verb or the MCP tool is a new weak-agent decision, and it joins the Fen acceptance set.</p> <p>The client research grounds the layering. Claude Code implements elicitation in its interactive command-line surface at a recent version. Codex implements it in its interactive surface behind a config gate. opencode does not implement it and advertises no capability. Every client lacks it in a headless or print run. So elicitation is the enhanced path and the backstop is load-bearing. The reference memory records the per-client detail and the specification link.</p> <h2 id="the-backstop-belongs-to-the-verb"><a class="header" href="#the-backstop-belongs-to-the-verb">The backstop belongs to the verb</a></h2> <p>The name backstop is a per-invocation contract on <code>host-lifecycle init</code> and <code>host-lifecycle adopt</code>, and it holds whenever no MCP client answers, which is every headless run, every client without the capability, and every plain shell call. The verb accepts the name by flag or environment, else prompts on a controlling terminal, else exits with a distinct code and a machine-parseable message naming the missing field so the caller re-invokes with the name supplied. The exit-code set and the message shape are the load-bearing contract for every scripted and agent caller, so they are specified with the verb rather than left as an implementation detail. The real 4B is driven through this path.</p> <h2 id="the-dual-mode-entrance"><a class="header" href="#the-dual-mode-entrance">The dual-mode entrance</a></h2> <p><code>host</code> is the single canonical front door in two modes. Read-and-follow is the existing methodology entrance an agent consumes. Install is the new parallel mode a human or a machine runs to place the pinned host binaries on the path. The entrance is a repository and a URL, and its install mode is a script served beside the read document; no executable named <code>host</code> is placed on the path, so it does not collide with the system <code>host</code> lookup tool. The install script installs the named tools, <code>host-lifecycle</code> with its <code>host-init</code> and <code>host-adopt</code> shims, and it does not install a resident service.</p> <p>Install preserves provenance or it is a hollow install, and the trust chain is anchored at the root, not only at the leaves.</p> <ul> <li>The install manifest records each binary's version and canonical hash, and the installer verifies every download against the recorded hash before it lands on the path.</li> <li>The manifest and the install script are themselves authenticated before they run, so a corrupted or substituted manifest cannot present a self-consistent set that the leaf hash-check would pass. The trust root, a signing key or an equivalent anchor, is named in the design and its material travels into the local install receipt so a later verification does not depend on refetching a moving remote.</li> <li>The manifest's hashes are single-sourced from the public per-component release receipts, <code>host-lint</code>, <code>host-lifecycle</code>, <code>host-prove</code>, and the rest, never from agentic-host's <code>.host-software</code>. The dev environment is neither referenced nor leaked, and the two records cannot drift.</li> <li>The manifest is keyed to the template revision, because <code>host</code> install is also the upgrade route. An adopter on a given revision receives the binaries that revision pins, so the spine and the binaries cannot drift out of step.</li> </ul> <p>The install writes a durable machine-side receipt: each installed binary, its version, its verified hash, and the trust anchor used, persisted locally and re-verifiable offline. A memoryless later read learns what is installed and at what verified hash from this receipt, which is the machine analog of the dev host's release receipts. The per-project <code>.host</code> stamp describes a project, not the machine's binaries, so the receipt carries this record, not the stamp.</p> <p>Install is all-or-nothing on the path. A partial install, where some binaries verify and one fails, records the missing binaries as absent or pending in the receipt and never leaves a silently-missing tool untraceable. A self-update rewrites the receipt to the new version and hash in the same step it swaps the binary, so a later read never reports an old hash for a new binary.</p> <h2 id="the-oneshot-human-run"><a class="header" href="#the-oneshot-human-run">The oneshot human run</a></h2> <p>The human path is one command that ends with a ready, pushed project or a clean error, never a half-made state. The initializer survey across cargo, the create generators, the template scaffolders, and the GitHub command-line tool converges on a small set of rules.</p> <ul> <li>Prompt only for the name. The name carries operator intent that the folder cannot supply, so it is the one field elicited when it is absent. Every other choice is a flag with a sensible default, and a name-given call runs with no prompt at all.</li> <li>Refuse an existing target. A non-empty or already-stamped destination aborts with an actionable message, and overwrite lives behind an explicit force flag.</li> <li>Scaffold locally, wire the remote last. The order is resolve, then preflight before any write, then scaffold, then commit, then create and push the remote. A remote failure after the commit leaves a valid local project and prints the exact manual remote command, and it never discards good local work.</li> <li>Treat GitHub as optional and fully flagged. The tool probes for the command-line tool and a live token, drives it with explicit flags, and degrades to a local-only success when either is absent.</li> <li>Hand off explicitly and machine-readably. The final block names the created path, the remote if any, and the next command, and the same output serves a scripted or agent caller. That output is the stdout backstop doing double duty, so its shape is part of the specified contract.</li> </ul> <p><code>host-adopt</code> adds one invariant: the source folder is read-only. Every write goes to the target host elsewhere, the source is never touched even when it is the home directory, and the run ends by requesting the switch rather than working in place. The declined-name case aborts clean and writes nothing; the name is required, the seeded purpose is optional.</p> <p>Install and create are two failure domains, so the one-command form does not fold them into one atomic step. A first-run install that then bootstraps a project runs the install to completion, verifies the whole toolset landed, and only then runs create, so a bootstrap never runs against a partial toolchain. A first-run install does not drive a token-bearing GitHub creation inside the install channel; the create step, with its own remote handling, is the place the live token is used.</p> <h2 id="the-spine-boundary-drawn-now"><a class="header" href="#the-spine-boundary-drawn-now">The spine boundary, drawn now</a></h2> <p>The boundary is what fans out to adopters, so it is drawn here rather than deferred to each build. Each element is diff-visible spine prose (which owes no ledger entry), a structural migration (which owes a revision-keyed ledger entry), or pure software (no spine change).</p> <ul> <li>Spine prose: the onboarding narrative, the refuse-existing-target and source-read-only invariants, and the provenance-verified install contract. These ship as template doctrine and are read by adopters; they owe no ledger entry on their own.</li> <li>Structural migration, ledger entry owed: the <code>adopt</code>-to-<code>host-adopt</code> rename, carrying a deprecate-then-retire shim and a <code>requires</code> host-lifecycle version, keyed to the doctrine commit, with an independent flag so a late adopter can take it alone. Whether an adopter must place the spawned MCP tools is a second possible entry, and it is decided by the mandatory-or-optional question below.</li> <li>Software, no spine change: the shim binaries, the install receipt format, the manifest verification, and the engine's <code>init</code> and <code>adopt</code> internals.</li> </ul> <p>The entrance ships its install mode through the entrance's own release authority, because <code>host</code> is the <code>[entrance]</code> member set apart from the components, so the phrase about each piece shipping through its own lifecycle release does not apply literally to it.</p> <h2 id="the-casts-throughline-4"><a class="header" href="#the-casts-throughline-4">The cast's throughline</a></h2> <ul> <li><strong>Mara</strong> (operator, final say): the name, the visibility, and the switch are hers, and the tool proposes and never invents. Her standing constraint holds: the source folder is touched by nothing. Her review cut the daemon back to the spawned surface and restored the three routes.</li> <li><strong>Wren</strong> (amnesiac executor): the creating session and the continuing session share no memory, so the handoff is written into the new host's files. The seeded one-line purpose is the one artifact crossing the boundary, so its shape is settled in the open questions before build, not left implicit.</li> <li><strong>Orin</strong> (maintainer): the onboarding doctrine that ships in the template fails safe when followed literally. An install that skips root authentication, a manifest that drifts from the release receipts, or a rename with no shim is the failure-unsafe shape he rejects, and each is closed above.</li> <li><strong>Bly</strong> (writes now, reads cold): the installed binaries self-describe to a memoryless read through the local install receipt, and a partial install over-reports the missing tool rather than hiding it. The receipt, not the per-project stamp, is the machine-side record.</li> <li><strong>Fen</strong> (acceptance test, driven not simulated): the real <code>qwen3.5-4b</code> routed the three-route decision twenty of twenty. The one-command run, the shell-verb-against-MCP-tool choice, and the agent-driven resolve owe their own runs at build.</li> </ul> <h2 id="locked-decisions"><a class="header" href="#locked-decisions">Locked decisions</a></h2> <ul> <li><code>host-lifecycle</code> is the one engine. <code>host-init</code> and <code>host-adopt</code> are tiny shims over its <code>init</code> and <code>adopt</code> verbs, and there is no separate scaffolding library.</li> <li>The bare <code>adopt</code> command retires in favour of <code>host-adopt</code> through a deprecate-then-retire shim, and the skills that call it migrate.</li> <li>The full three-route adoption decision from <code>plan/0061</code> stands, with the <code>--at</code> override.</li> <li>The MCP surface is a stdio-spawned server exposing <code>init</code> and <code>adopt</code> as tools, not a resident daemon. A hub must earn itself with named capabilities and a trust design.</li> <li>The name backstop is a per-invocation contract on the engine verb, and it holds when no MCP client answers.</li> <li><code>host</code> gains a parallel install mode with a root-anchored, revision-keyed, receipt-recording, all-or-nothing install; no executable named <code>host</code> lands on the path.</li> <li>The human run defaults are private visibility, name-only prompting, an <code>agentic-<name></code> target that refuses an existing folder, and local-first remote-last with no rollback of good local work.</li> </ul> <h2 id="decisions-ruled-2026-07-07-operator"><a class="header" href="#decisions-ruled-2026-07-07-operator">Decisions ruled (2026-07-07, operator)</a></h2> <p>The four questions the design left open are ruled, so the build proceeds against fixed contracts.</p> <ul> <li><strong>Trust anchor: the reproducible build (revised 2026-07-07; the earlier cosign-bootstrapped-by-<code>gh attestation verify</code> lever was removed as the wrong layer).</strong> Every host-* binary is reproducibly built from pinned source plus a recorded toolchain, so <code>software --verify_build</code> re-derives its recorded hash anywhere; the installer treats that hash as the root. The manifest single-sources each binary's canonical hash from the public release receipts, and the installer verifies every download against it before anything lands on the path. An adopter can rebuild any binary against the pinned source and toolchain to confirm the hash independently. This is the project's own trust mechanism: no external signer, no bootstrap problem, offline by construction. Sigstore keyless (cosign) is an optional identity layer for release attribution, not the load-bearing root.</li> <li><strong>MCP is optional, backstop-covered.</strong> The spawned MCP tools are the enhanced path, never mandatory: the per-invocation verb backstop covers every client without elicitation (opencode, every headless run) and every plain shell call. No second UPGRADING ledger entry is owed, so the only migration is the <code>adopt</code> rename.</li> <li><strong>Seed shape: a MEMORY.md purpose line.</strong> The seeded one-line purpose is written as a MEMORY.md project line, the cross-session handoff a cold continuing session reads first. A declined purpose leaves the default MEMORY untouched. The name is required; the seed is optional.</li> <li><strong>Exit codes and handoff: line-based <code>key: value</code>.</strong> Success prints a final stdout block of <code>key: value</code> lines (<code>host-path</code>, <code>remote</code>, <code>next</code>); the codes are <code>0</code> success, <code>2</code> usage error, <code>3</code> name-required with no controlling terminal (a machine-parseable stderr line names the missing field), <code>4</code> target-exists or refuse, <code>5</code> remote-failed-after-local-commit (the local project is intact and the manual remote command is printed). The line-based shape is chosen over JSON for weak-agent legibility.</li> </ul> <p>These rulings are grounded, not asserted, in <code>gather-data.md</code>: a Fen acceptance run on the qwen3.5-4b (twelve of twelve, position-bias controlled, genuinely reasoned) shows the exit-code and shell-verb-vs-MCP contracts are legible to a weak agent, and a survey of nine established installers grounds the hash-check pattern (a published checksums list, then verify each download against it) as a shipping majority, which the reproducible-build root generalizes: an adopter can always rebuild rather than trust an external signer.</p> <h2 id="open-questions-4"><a class="header" href="#open-questions-4">Open questions</a></h2> <p>The operator-gated questions are ruled above. What remains is installer implementation detail, pinned during the build rather than owed to the operator: the per-platform path setup and binary placement, the self-update mechanics, and the survey of the established installer family that grounds them.</p> <h2 id="verification-33"><a class="header" href="#verification-33">Verification</a></h2> <p>Each software piece ships through its own lifecycle release with the whole-suite verify gate green; the entrance ships through its own release authority. The Fen probe runs on the one-command run, the shell-verb-against-MCP-tool choice, and the agent-driven resolve. The cheap-verification bar for the human run restates all three routes: a fully-flagged <code>host-init</code> creates a well-formed, committed, pushed host and prints a machine-readable handoff; a name-absent call at a terminal prompts only for the name; a <code>host-adopt</code> in a pattern folder adopts in place; a <code>host-adopt</code> in a software repository refuses; a <code>host-adopt</code> in an arbitrary folder writes nothing there and creates the host elsewhere. The bar for the install mode: a download whose hash does not match the manifest is rejected before it lands on the path, a manifest that fails root authentication is rejected before any download, and an interrupted install leaves a receipt that re-lists the missing binaries rather than hiding them.</p> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><h1 id="plan0065-code-review-adversarial-review-of-the-onboarding-surface-before-release"><a class="header" href="#plan0065-code-review-adversarial-review-of-the-onboarding-surface-before-release">plan/0065 code-review: adversarial review of the onboarding surface before release</a></h1> <p>Before releasing the onboarding surface (the init/adopt/scaffold verbs, the host-init/host-adopt shims, the MCP stdio server, and the oneshot git and GitHub finalize), a multi-agent adversarial review swept the new code across five dimensions (correctness, the MCP protocol, the gh oneshot, security and invariants, and reproducibility), and each raised finding was independently verified against the real code. Twelve findings survived verification as confirmed defects; three were rejected. All twelve are fixed here, per the doctrine that a review finding is a requirement, not a descope.</p> <h2 id="confirmed-findings-all-fixed"><a class="header" href="#confirmed-findings-all-fixed">Confirmed findings, all fixed</a></h2> <ul> <li><strong>High, the deprecate shim mutated the source.</strong> <code>adopt</code> treated any two positional arguments as the retired <code>adopt <dir> <revision></code> primitive and forwarded to <code>scaffold</code>, so a mistaken <code>host-adopt <source> <name></code> wrote the rooms and stamp into the source folder and broke the flagship source-read-only invariant. Fixed: the two-positional form is now a hard error that names <code>scaffold</code>, never a silent forward (call/0041 corrected).</li> <li><strong>High, the MCP elicitation assumed the next line was the response.</strong> An interleaved notification between <code>elicitation/create</code> and the answer was mistaken for the answer. Fixed: read until the response whose JSON-RPC id matches, and skip any interleaved message.</li> <li><strong>High, a clean commit read as a fatal error.</strong> <code>git_init_commit</code> checked stderr for "nothing to commit", but git writes that to stdout. Fixed: check both streams.</li> <li><strong>High, MCP argument injection through the adopt source.</strong> The <code>source</code> argument was emitted as a bare positional, so a value beginning with a dash was read as a flag by the subprocess. Fixed: the source follows an end-of-options <code>--</code>, and the adopt parser honours it.</li> <li><strong>Medium, the software-repo refusal returned the wrong exit code.</strong> Route one exited 2 (a usage error) rather than the ruled contract's 4 for a refuse. Fixed: route one exits 4.</li> <li><strong>Medium, the in-place emptiness test counted <code>.git</code>.</strong> A freshly <code>git init</code>ed or cloned empty <code>agentic-<name></code> folder failed the route-two carve-out and could dead-end. Fixed: emptiness ignores the artifacts a fresh repo carries (<code>.git</code>, <code>.gitignore</code>, a README, a LICENSE).</li> <li><strong>Medium, one bad line killed the MCP server.</strong> <code>read_message</code> returned the same sentinel for a parse failure and a closed pipe. Fixed: a non-JSON line is skipped, not treated as end-of-input.</li> <li><strong>Medium, the conflicting-flags check ran after scaffolding.</strong> The <code>--no-git</code> with <code>--github</code> conflict was caught inside the finalize, after the directory was already created. Fixed: it is preflighted before any write.</li> <li><strong>Medium, in-place adopt ignored the git and GitHub flags.</strong> Route two never committed or wired a remote. Fixed: route two runs the same finalize as the create-elsewhere route and init.</li> <li><strong>Medium, <code>--force</code> on a populated repo committed unrelated files.</strong> <code>git add -A</code> swept the whole working tree. Fixed: only the scaffold artifacts are staged.</li> <li><strong>Medium, route three could target inside the source.</strong> An <code>--at</code> pointing into the source would create the host within it, breaking source-read-only. Fixed: the resolved target is checked to lie outside the source, else refused.</li> <li><strong>Medium, the release must re-vendor.</strong> Adding tokio and serde_json grew the lockfile past the vendored deps-bundle, so the offline locked musl reproducible build fails until re-vendored. Resolved as the release step: a fresh deps-bundle is vendored and pinned with the release.</li> </ul> <h2 id="verification-34"><a class="header" href="#verification-34">Verification</a></h2> <p>The verbs' unit tests cover the routing, the name backstop, <code>dir_effectively_empty</code>, and <code>git_init_commit</code>; the MCP tests cover the elicitation round trip, the interleaved-notification skip, and the <code>--</code>-guarded argv. The behavioural fixes were smoke-verified on the built binary: the two-positional form errors without touching the source, a software repo refuses with exit 4, a <code>.git</code>-only <code>agentic-<name></code> adopts in place, and an <code>--at</code> inside the source is refused. The whole suite is green and clippy is clean.</p> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><h1 id="plan0065-gather-data-grounding-the-onboarding-and-mcp-build-in-measured-data"><a class="header" href="#plan0065-gather-data-grounding-the-onboarding-and-mcp-build-in-measured-data">plan/0065 gather-data: grounding the onboarding-and-MCP build in measured data</a></h1> <p>The ruled decisions and the install-mode design are grounded here in two measured streams before any code: a Fen acceptance run on the new weak-agent contracts, and a survey of the established single-binary installer family. This answers the standing requirement that a decision rest on data, not assertion.</p> <h2 id="fen-acceptance-qwen35-4b-the-new-weak-agent-contracts-are-legible"><a class="header" href="#fen-acceptance-qwen35-4b-the-new-weak-agent-contracts-are-legible">Fen acceptance (qwen3.5-4b): the new weak-agent contracts are legible</a></h2> <p>The design names decisions the weak agent must make that the prior three-route run (twenty of twenty) did not cover. Each was probed on the real qwen3.5-4b (rope API, the qwen sampler with <code>top_k</code>, serial on the single GPU, parsed after the thinking block), three runs each, with the correct option placed at a different letter per probe so a first-option bias cannot pass spuriously.</p> <div class="table-wrapper"><table><thead><tr><th>Probe</th><th>Contract tested</th><th>Correct letter</th><th>Result</th></tr></thead><tbody> <tr><td>exit-code re-invoke</td><td>on exit <code>3</code> name-required with no controlling terminal, re-invoke with <code>--name</code></td><td>C</td><td>3/3</td></tr> <tr><td>shell-verb vs MCP tool</td><td>inside an elicitation-capable client with no name, use the MCP tool</td><td>B</td><td>3/3</td></tr> <tr><td>adopt route one (software repo)</td><td>a <code>Cargo.toml</code>-rooted folder is refused in place</td><td>D</td><td>3/3</td></tr> <tr><td>adopt route three (arbitrary)</td><td>an arbitrary folder elicits a name and creates the host elsewhere, source untouched</td><td>A</td><td>3/3</td></tr> </tbody></table> </div> <p>Twelve of twelve, the correct letters spread across C, B, D, and A, every run genuinely reasoned: the traces reject the wrong options by name rather than blurting a letter. The exit-code and surface-choice shapes stand as specified. The one-command run and the agent-driven resolve owe their own runs once the verbs exist.</p> <h2 id="installer-family-survey-what-the-field-actually-does"><a class="header" href="#installer-family-survey-what-the-field-actually-does">Installer-family survey: what the field actually does</a></h2> <p>Nine established installers were read at their real install scripts and self-update source (rustup, cargo-binstall, uv and cargo-dist, deno, starship, ollama, cosign, Homebrew, and the registry-driven aqua). The load-bearing findings, each tied to a fetched artifact:</p> <ul> <li><strong>In-script verification is rare.</strong> Only uv and cargo-dist check integrity in-script (an embedded SHA256); the mainstream pipe-to-shell installers trust the transport to the host only, and rustup removed its GPG path as buggy. Real in-installer signature verification is on the frontier (basecamp, HALO, aqua), so a provenance-verified host install sits ahead of the mainstream, alongside that cohort.</li> <li><strong>The majority cosign pattern</strong> verifies a signed <code>checksums.txt</code> with a keyless bundle, then <code>sha256sum -c</code> checks each binary against it, so one signature covers the whole release.</li> <li><strong>Keyless cosign needs an identity and an issuer.</strong> Since cosign version 2.0, <code>cosign verify-blob</code> requires <code>--certificate-identity</code> (or a regexp) and <code>--certificate-oidc-issuer</code>; the identity is the signing workflow's ref, pinned to the tag for the tightest guarantee. A <code>.*</code> identity is a degenerate anti-pattern that proves signed-by-someone, not by-whom.</li> <li><strong>Bootstrapping cosign is a chicken-and-egg</strong>, and nobody verifies cosign with cosign. The honest paths are <code>gh attestation verify</code> as the primary (GitHub is the trust root, needing no cosign binary) with cosign as a fallback, or a pinned SHA256 of the cosign binary checked before it runs.</li> <li><strong>The receipt model</strong> (cargo-dist writes an <code><app>-receipt.json</code>, Homebrew an <code>INSTALL_RECEIPT.json</code>) records the installed binaries, versions, and hashes. For offline re-verification the receipt also stores the verified identity and issuer, the Rekor log pointer (log index, entry UUID, integrated time), and the trusted-root snapshot used.</li> <li><strong>Path, platform, and self-update majorities:</strong> the binary lands in <code>~/.local/bin</code> with no root, and an env script sourced from the shell rc keeps uninstall clean and is skipped under CI or with no controlling terminal. A <code>uname</code> map selects the target triple, a static musl build is preferred on Linux, and an unknown target hard-errors against an allowlist rather than a silent fallback. Self-update uses a temp directory, a sanity run, and an atomic rename that first moves a running Windows executable aside.</li> </ul> <h3 id="the-verification-shape-the-host-install-adopts"><a class="header" href="#the-verification-shape-the-host-install-adopts">The verification shape the host install adopts</a></h3> <p>The signed-checksums majority pattern, pinned to the tag-templated workflow identity (basecamp/HALO):</p> <pre><code class="language-bash">cosign verify-blob checksums.txt \ --bundle checksums.txt.bundle \ --certificate-identity "https://github.com/connollydavid/host-lifecycle/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/tags/vX.Y.Z" \ --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com sha256sum -c --ignore-missing checksums.txt </code></pre> <p>Cosign is bootstrapped by <code>gh attestation verify</code> as the primary path with a pinned-SHA256 cosign binary as the fallback, never by cosign itself. Offline re-verification from the receipt runs <code>cosign verify-blob --offline</code> against the stored bundle and the recorded identity and issuer.</p> <h3 id="concrete-grounding-for-the-ruled-decisions"><a class="header" href="#concrete-grounding-for-the-ruled-decisions">Concrete grounding for the ruled decisions</a></h3> <ul> <li>The <strong>cosign keyless</strong> trust anchor is confirmed implementable in a shell installer, with a shipping majority pattern to copy and a real offline re-verification mode from a receipt-borne inclusion proof.</li> <li>The <strong>install receipt</strong> shape is grounded in two production receipts, extended with the Rekor pointer.</li> <li>The <strong>all-or-nothing landing</strong> is grounded against ollama's fail-open partial state as the anti-pattern.</li> <li>host-lint already ships the canonical static-musl binary and <code>.host-software</code> already records the canonical hashes, so the musl-first build and the pinned-hash cosign bootstrap fit the existing anchors.</li> </ul> <h2 id="the-mcp-surface-hand-rolled-on-tokio-grounded-against-the-sdk-and-the-spec"><a class="header" href="#the-mcp-surface-hand-rolled-on-tokio-grounded-against-the-sdk-and-the-spec">The MCP surface: hand-rolled on tokio, grounded against the SDK and the spec</a></h2> <p>The spawned MCP server is built on tokio (operator directive: async is required for the server-initiated elicitation request). The implementation choice, the official rmcp SDK against a hand-rolled protocol, was grounded in the SDK's manifest and the <code>2025-06-18</code> spec (call/0042 records the decision).</p> <ul> <li><strong>rmcp 2.1.0</strong> is the official Rust SDK, Apache-2.0, tokio-native, and it does support a server sending <code>elicitation/create</code> (<code>create_elicitation</code>, the typed <code>elicit<T></code>, the <code>elicit_safe!</code> guard, and client capability negotiation). A stdio-only server needs the <code>server</code>, <code>macros</code>, <code>transport-io</code>, and <code>elicitation</code> features, which exclude the HTTP and TLS stacks but still pull schemars, tokio-util, url, pastey, and a support set, on the order of dozens of transitive crates, from a crate that shipped a major version bump on a one-to-two-week cadence.</li> <li><strong>The wire surface is small and static.</strong> stdio transport is newline-delimited JSON, one compact object per line, no content-length framing. The methods are <code>initialize</code> (echo the protocol version, advertise a <code>tools</code> capability), the <code>notifications/initialized</code> follow-up, <code>tools/list</code>, <code>tools/call</code> (a <code>content</code> array result, tool errors in-band as <code>isError</code>), and one server-initiated <code>elicitation/create</code> (a flat object schema of primitives; the client answers accept with content, or decline, or cancel). The client must declare the <code>elicitation</code> capability in <code>initialize</code>, and the server elicits only when it did.</li> <li><strong>The one fiddly part</strong> is correlating the server-initiated elicitation response by JSON-RPC id while a <code>tools/call</code> is in flight on the same pipe, a bounded problem that is the piece to test hardest.</li> </ul> <p>Decision (call/0042): hand-roll the protocol on tokio and serde_json. The surface is two fixed tools plus one elicitation Form, so the SDK's macro ergonomics buy little, while its vendored, hash-pinned, musl reproducible-build tax (dozens of crates to pin and re-derive on every fast-moving bump) is the dominant cost in this repository. The hand-roll adds only tokio to the vendored set; serde_json is already present.</p> <h2 id="sources"><a class="header" href="#sources">Sources</a></h2> <ul> <li>rustup-init.sh and self_update.rs (rust-lang/rustup); cargo-binstall SIGNING.md (cargo-bins).</li> <li>uv-installer.sh (releases.astral.sh); axoupdater receipt.rs and lib.rs (axodotdev).</li> <li>deno install.sh and upgrade.rs (denoland); starship install.sh; ollama scripts/install.sh.</li> <li>cosign verify docs and cosign_initialize.md (sigstore/cosign); Homebrew Bottles docs and the Trail of Bits build-provenance writeup.</li> <li>Shipping <code>cosign verify-blob</code> installers: basecamp/basecamp-cli, context-labs/HALO, guidewire-oss/fern-platform, opengrep/opengrep, automagik-dev/genie; the aquaproj/aqua verify path.</li> <li>Kubernetes verify-signed-artifacts and the Argo release verification recipes.</li> </ul> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><h1 id="plan0066-task-band-and-ordinal-detection-a-sanctioned-task-group-and-the-gate-that-catches-its-ordinal-workaround"><a class="header" href="#plan0066-task-band-and-ordinal-detection-a-sanctioned-task-group-and-the-gate-that-catches-its-ordinal-workaround">plan/0066 task-band-and-ordinal-detection: a sanctioned task group, and the gate that catches its ordinal workaround</a></h1> <p>This milestone answers host-lifecycle#4 in two halves. A plan author who wants to group tasks has no sanctioned construct, so an author reaches for an ordinal band name, the position-naming the milestone-naming rule forbids. The fix is a content-named band over the anchored tasks (the construct), and a detection rule so the gate catches the ordinal workaround the band replaces (the enforcement).</p> <h2 id="the-detection-half-shipped-as-host-lint-v0140"><a class="header" href="#the-detection-half-shipped-as-host-lint-v0140">The detection half (shipped as host-lint v0.14.0)</a></h2> <p>host-lint already blocks a phase-synonym noun followed by an arabic numeral. The gap was the spelled form: a phase-synonym noun followed by a spelled-out ordinal read clean, which is exactly how the band workaround in plan/0049 slipped every gate. host-lint now recognises a closed spelled set (the cardinals and ordinals no higher than twenty) after a phase-synonym noun and blocks it the same way the arabic form blocks, and the gather lane surfaces a novel such noun as an emergent-tell candidate.</p> <p>The disposition is corpus-grounded, not asserted, per the plan/0055 doctrine. Spelled blocking applies to the phase-synonym work-unit nouns only. It is excluded from the checklist nouns and from the domain-heavy warn nouns, because their spelled forms are ordinary descriptive prose. The repo's own <code>cast/applying-personas.md</code> carries the deciding data point, a legitimate spelled use of a checklist noun that a blanket rule would have flagged and broken the zero-warning doc gate on.</p> <p>Released as host-lint v0.14.0 (change class adds-flag, the tool flags a superset), reproducibly built, re-pinned in <code>.host-software</code>, receipt recorded, and the host-template <code>tools/host-lint</code> pin bumped (call/0038). The whole-suite <code>software --check</code> is green. VOCABULARY.md carries the new shape, and the lib source stays flag-free so a real tell in it is still caught.</p> <h2 id="the-construct-half-shipped"><a class="header" href="#the-construct-half-shipped">The construct half (shipped)</a></h2> <p>The band is a content-named grouping over the anchored tasks, with execution order still carried by the <code>depends</code> edges rather than by the band's name or position. The authoring surface is settled on data: the real <code>qwen3.5-4b</code> authored both a heading-marked band and a per-task-field band correctly, and it read group membership correctly in both, so the choice rests on the engineering factors. The heading form wins on backward-compatibility (an existing plan with no marker parses unchanged), on rendering (a visible divider in the book), and on referenceability (the band carries its own anchor). One implementation note the Fen scoring surfaced: the parser must attribute a band marker only to its own immediately-preceding heading, with no look-ahead, or it mis-reads a task as a band.</p> <p>The construct is doctrine, now shipped: a band paragraph in the template task-graph section (host-template <code>67d63e9</code>) plus a <code>parse_tasks</code> recognition in host-lifecycle v0.38.0 (tool-local, released with the coded remap and materialise fixes, plan/0062, and the book-mount tool side, and re-vendoring the host-lint above). The UPGRADING ledger entry keyed to <code>67d63e9</code> (requiring v0.38.0) carries it to adopters, and agentic-host adopted it through the ledger (baseline advanced to <code>962630c</code>).</p> <h2 id="verification-35"><a class="header" href="#verification-35">Verification</a></h2> <p>Detection: host-lint unit and integration tests cover the block on a phase-synonym plus spelled ordinal, the clean pass on a checklist or warn noun plus spelled ordinal, and the gather surfacing; the released binary reproduces its recorded hash. Construct: a band-bearing plan fixture validates, a unit test asserts the linear <code>depends</code> default still chains across a band heading, and the weak-agent authoring run passes at the plan/0042 bar. Both halves land with the whole-suite verify gate green.</p> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><h1 id="plan0067-book-mount-sub-path-publish-the-development-book-under-a-sub-path-of-an-existing-site"><a class="header" href="#plan0067-book-mount-sub-path-publish-the-development-book-under-a-sub-path-of-an-existing-site">plan/0067 book-mount-sub-path: publish the development book under a sub-path of an existing site</a></h1> <p>This milestone answers host#17. Some adopters already serve a content-full product site from their Pages root, so the reference Site workflow, which publishes the generated book as the whole site, would overwrite it.
