And the dependency licences must stay clear of the strongest copyleft.</p> <p>A single comprehensive Office reader was evaluated, to avoid the per-format work. <code>litchi</code> reads the whole Office and OpenDocument family in pure Rust, which is attractive. It was deferred for two reasons. Its embedded objects and images are still in progress, so it cannot extract the images a slide deck carries, the capability this work needs. And it sits at version 0.0.1, with an API that by its own note may change without notice. It is worth revisiting once it stabilises and gains embedded-media extraction.</p> <h2 id="decision-19"><a class="header" href="#decision-19">Decision</a></h2> <ul> <li>Pluggable by feature. Each format or family is a normaliser crate, gated by a Cargo feature in the consumer. Only the enabled formats compile and register, so a project stands up the readers its corpus needs and pays for no others. A heavy reader is an opt-in cost.</li> <li>Pure-Rust, with no C dependency. Every reader builds in pure Rust, so the offline reproducible build and the no-reach-out rule of <code>call/0031</code> hold without a foreign toolchain. The C-linking readers are out.</li> <li>The best maintained pure-Rust reader per format, chosen on merit rather than weight, since the weight is opt-in. The current picks: <ul> <li><code>calamine</code> for spreadsheets, both xlsx and the legacy xls.</li> <li><code>htmd</code> for HTML.</li> <li><code>mail-parser</code> for internet mail, with <code>msg_parser</code> over <code>cfb</code> for Outlook <code>.msg</code>.</li> <li>the <code>zip</code> and <code>quick-xml</code> and <code>image</code> crates for the Office documents and their embedded media.</li> <li><code>lopdf</code> with <code>pdf-extract</code> for born-digital PDF.</li> <li><code>ocrs</code> over <code>rten</code> for optical character recognition.</li> </ul> </li> <li>Recognition stays in the overlay. A pure-Rust optical-character reader does exist, <code>ocrs</code> over the <code>rten</code> runtime, so recognition need not link C. It is a machine-learning reader, though: it carries model weights, vendored for the offline build, and its inference can vary across hosts at the float level. So the recognised content (the text inside an image, a description of it) lives in the overlay through the provider-agnostic adapter, recorded with its provenance, while the attested layer holds only what re-derives deterministically: the image metadata and its alt-text and the structure. A pinned model that proves cross-host deterministic could later promote the text into the attested layer. This refines the deterministic-recognition note of <code>call/0030</code>.</li> <li>The in-scope format set is the adopter's judgement, not ours. The methodology carries the superset of readers and the open plugin interface; the adopting project enables the subset its corpus needs and may author further readers on the interface. We build the menu and the interface and leave the scope to the project.</li> <li>Licences are per plugin, and copyleft is bounded. Each plugin's licence is the one its libraries carry, so a project reads a plugin's licence before it enables it. AGPL is never allowed, a hard rule. GPL is avoided where a permissive reader exists, and any GPL reader is expressly noted, so enabling its plugin is a knowing choice. A <code>cargo-deny</code> lane enforces the rules: it denies AGPL and surfaces GPL. The current readers are all permissive (MIT, Apache-2.0, or Unlicense), so the build carries no GPL and no AGPL today; <code>mail-parser</code> is Apache-2.0 or MIT, the parser crate rather than the AGPL Stalwart server.</li> <li>A GPL reader, were one ever the only option for a format, runs out-of-process behind an arms-length boundary (a pipe or a socket or a command line, the FSF aggregation position), so our plugin and the build stay permissive rather than taking on the copyleft. The boundary stays arms-length, not a shared-memory or tightly-coupled call that the FSF reads as equivalent to linking. Such a plugin is flagged GPL and is opt-in, and it carries a dependency on the external binary, which leaves the in-process pure-Rust model. LGPL may link directly; AGPL has no such escape and stays banned.</li> </ul> <h2 id="considered-options-12"><a class="header" href="#considered-options-12">Considered Options</a></h2> <ol> <li><strong>Pluggable, pure-Rust, the best reader per format, permissive licences (chosen).</strong> A project pays only for what it stands up, the build stays offline and reproducible, a reader is chosen on merit, and the licence stays clear of copyleft.</li> <li><strong>One comprehensive Office reader, litchi.</strong> Rejected for now: it extracts no embedded media and carries a 0.0.1 unstable API. A revisit candidate once it matures.</li> <li><strong>A fixed, always-compiled reader set.</strong> Rejected: every project would pay the weight of every reader, the heavy ones included.</li> <li><strong>Allow a C-linking reader where it is best (libtesseract, PDFium).</strong> Rejected: it breaks the pure-Rust offline reproducible build and the no-reach-out rule.</li> <li><strong>Allow AGPL or GPL where convenient.</strong> Rejected: AGPL is banned outright, and GPL is avoided and flagged, so a plugin's copyleft is never a surprise to the project that enables it.</li> </ol> <h2 id="consequences-17"><a class="header" href="#consequences-17">Consequences</a></h2> <ul> <li>Good: a project pays only for the formats it enables; the build stays pure-Rust and reproducible; a reader is chosen on merit; recognition stays out of the attested layer; and the licence of each plugin is legible and copyleft-bounded.</li> <li>Costs: the feature matrix adds build-configuration surface; pptx image extraction is a scoped in-house walk (<code>zip</code> with the <code>image</code> crate), since no pure-Rust library extracts slide media today; optical character recognition is machine-learning, so its text is overlay-only until a pinned model proves deterministic; and a <code>cargo-deny</code> lane has to be carried and kept current.</li> </ul> <h2 id="confirmation-11"><a class="header" href="#confirmation-11">Confirmation</a></h2> <p>The normalisers already built (prose, structured data, HTML, vector, netlist) are retrofitted behind feature gates, the Office and mail and fixed-layout readers each land behind a feature, and a <code>cargo-deny</code> lane denies AGPL and surfaces GPL. The conformance fixtures and <code>software --check</code> stay green. The operator set the direction this session: pluggable, pure-Rust, the best reader per format, the adopter's judgement on the in-scope set, and copyleft bounded with AGPL banned.</p> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><h1 id="ocr-ships-now-as-the-first-out-of-process-plugin-attested-behind-an-arms-length-boundary"><a class="header" href="#ocr-ships-now-as-the-first-out-of-process-plugin-attested-behind-an-arms-length-boundary">OCR ships now as the first out-of-process plugin, attested behind an arms-length boundary</a></h1> <ul> <li>Status: accepted</li> <li>Date: 2026-06-28</li> <li>Scope: the OCR reader of <code>host-reference</code> (<code>plan/0049</code>, <code>call/0030</code>, <code>call/0033</code>). Instance software, binds no adopter, no spine change. Refines the recognition-stays-in-overlay clause of <code>call/0033</code> and the recognition split of <code>call/0030</code>.</li> <li>Relates: <code>call/0030</code> (the immutable-against-overlay split and "a deterministic engine for the attested layer"); <code>call/0033</code> (pluggable pure-Rust readers, the out-of-process rule, the recognition-in-overlay clause, and the pinned-model promotion path); <code>call/0031</code> (untrusted input and the no-reach-out rule).</li> </ul> <h2 id="context-and-problem-statement-18"><a class="header" href="#context-and-problem-statement-18">Context and Problem Statement</a></h2> <p>The recognition-and-engineering wave was directed to deliver image and OCR together. <code>call/0033</code> had parked the recognised text of an image in the overlay until a pinned model proved cross-host deterministic, and it named the GPL OpenSCAD helper as the first use of the out-of-process rule. Two facts reshaped the choice for OCR.</p> <p>The only pure-Rust OCR engine, <code>ocrs</code> over the <code>rten</code> runtime, carries its model weights as a pair of <code>.rten</code> files licensed CC-BY-SA-4.0. That is a copyleft content licence. The <code>host-reference</code> component is otherwise permissive (Unlicense code, permissive dependencies), and it must not absorb a ShareAlike obligation into its own distribution as a derivative of the weights.</p> <p>The engine is also run-to-run deterministic on a host: the helper run twice over the same image with the same pinned models returns byte-identical text. So the recognised text of a fixed engine over fixed bytes behaves as a parse, not as the open-ended inference the overlay was built for.</p> <p>The out-of-process rule of <code>call/0033</code>, designed to keep the GPL OpenSCAD code out of the permissive build, fits the CC-BY-SA models exactly. A separate helper program carries the licence-encumbered engine and weights, and the permissive plugin runs it at arm's length.</p> <h2 id="decision-20"><a class="header" href="#decision-20">Decision</a></h2> <ul> <li>OCR ships now as an attested reader, rather than deferring to the overlay. The recognised text of a fixed engine over fixed bytes is the deterministic parse that <code>call/0030</code> placed in the attested layer, and the vendored pinned models are the pinned model that <code>call/0033</code> named as the promotion path.</li> <li>It is the first out-of-process plugin, ahead of OpenSCAD. The <code>host-reference-ocr-helper</code> binary embeds <code>ocrs</code>, <code>rten</code>, and the CC-BY-SA-4.0 ocrs models, and it is its own component, the public <code>host-reference-ocr</code> repo embedded in <code>.host-software</code>. So the <code>host-reference</code> repo and workspace carry neither the engine nor the copyleft models. The permissive <code>host-reference-ocr</code> plugin writes the image to a temporary file, runs the helper as a separate process, and reads the recognised text from its stdout. The two are an aggregation, not a linkage, so the plugin and its dependents stay permissive and the copyleft weights never enter their distribution as a derivative. This is the same arms-length boundary <code>call/0033</code> specified for GPL, applied to a content licence, taken one step further by giving the helper its own repository.</li> <li>The plugin implements the same <code>Normalizer</code> interface as every in-process reader, which proves the interface drives an out-of-process helper with no special case. That is the interface test <code>call/0033</code> wanted from the OpenSCAD route.</li> <li>The helper must be installed. The plugin finds it through <code>HOST_REFERENCE_OCR_HELPER</code> or the binary name on <code>PATH</code>, and returns a recorded refusal when it is absent, which is the cost the <code>call/0033</code> out-of-process consequence already named.</li> <li>Conformance is a byte-for-byte golden over a synthetic text image, the same contract the in-process readers carry. Cross-host bit-determinism is not yet proven, so the reproducible-build attestation of the recognised text is the open edge, carried by the verification ladder when the spec-and-release task lands.</li> </ul> <h2 id="consequences-18"><a class="header" href="#consequences-18">Consequences</a></h2> <ul> <li>The CC-BY-SA-4.0 models are confined to the separate <code>host-reference-ocr</code> repo and attributed in its <code>NOTICE.md</code>, with the licence split (Unlicense code, CC-BY-SA-4.0 models) and the citations stated upfront in its <code>README.md</code>. The licence watch-list in <code>readers.md</code> records the first content-copyleft dependency and its confinement behind the boundary.</li> <li>A consumer that enables the <code>ocr</code> feature must install the helper binary. The default text build pays nothing for OCR.</li> <li>OpenSCAD remains the planned GPL out-of-process plugin. OCR is the first instance of the pattern and validates it before OpenSCAD arrives.</li> </ul> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><h1 id="host-lifecycles-discharge-check-verifies-an-exercises-link-and-verify-build-reports-only-what-it-checked"><a class="header" href="#host-lifecycles-discharge-check-verifies-an-exercises-link-and-verify-build-reports-only-what-it-checked">host-lifecycle's discharge check verifies an <code>exercises=</code> link, and verify-build reports only what it checked</a></h1> <ul> <li>Status: accepted</li> <li>Date: 2026-06-30</li> <li>Scope: the <code>host-lifecycle</code> component (its obligation-discharge check and <code>software --verify-build</code>). Instance software. The methodology doctrine this realises ("a verification lane that cannot perform its check must not report clean") is a separate <code>host-template</code> spine change recorded under <code>plan/0052</code> with an <code>UPGRADING</code> entry; this decision binds no adopter except through the tool they already run.</li> <li>Relates: <code>plan/0051</code> (the host-lifecycle review that found the gap), <code>plan/0052</code> (the no-hollow-green doctrine and this realisation), <code>call/0018</code> (discharge is re-derivation in a pinned toolchain, the pattern reused here), <code>call/0042</code> (the receipted task graph the gate guards).</li> </ul> <h2 id="context-and-problem-statement-19"><a class="header" href="#context-and-problem-statement-19">Context and Problem Statement</a></h2> <p>The plan/0051 review found, and the plan/0050 review of <code>host-reference</code> had found independently, that a verification lane can report clean without performing its check. The <code>obligations</code> check confirmed only that a <code>test:<name></code> disposition named a test that exists (a substring match), never that the named test exercised the rule it discharges. Seven hazarded-verdict obligations in host-lifecycle's own manifest were dispositioned to <code>host_root_escape_is_detected</code>, a pure helper test that never called the gate, and the ladder stayed green. Separately, <code>software --verify-build</code> printed "every non-exempt build reproduces its recorded artifact" and exited 0 even when no container runtime was present, attesting a guarantee it never checked. The same two findings share one shape: a lane may report clean only after it performs its check.</p> <p>The deep rungs (<code>kani</code>, <code>apalache</code>, <code>tlaps</code>) already discharge correctly through <code>--rederive</code>, which re-runs the verifier via host-prove and requires a PASS, and which returns <code>UNPROVEN</code> when the re-deriver cannot run. So the fix finishes an uneven application of a pattern the codebase already trusts rather than inventing one.</p> <h2 id="decision-21"><a class="header" href="#decision-21">Decision</a></h2> <p>The obligation-discharge check and the reproducible-build lane are strengthened in host-lifecycle:</p> <ul> <li>A <code>test:</code> disposition gains an optional <code>exercises=<symbol></code> link. The check resolves the named test to exactly one <code>fn <name></code> definition (<code>AMBIGUOUS</code> otherwise, not a loose substring) and confirms the declared symbol appears in that test's body (<code>HOLLOW</code> otherwise). A <code>test:</code> with no link is <code>UNLINKED</code>, and an <code>#[ignore]</code>'d discharging test is flagged. These are advisory by default and HAZARD under <code>--strict-discharge</code>, so tightening a shared gate reaches adopters warn-then-retire rather than reddening a green ladder on a tool bump (the cast's propagation rule).</li> <li>The two relabel escapes are closed in the same change: a behavioural obligation dispositioned <code>structural</code> is <code>RELABEL</code> (the analyse lane does not discharge it), and a <code>waived:</code> with no reason is <code>UNWAIVED</code>. Hardening <code>test:</code> without these would only move the hole.</li> <li><code>software --verify-build</code> becomes three-state: VERIFIED (rebuilt and matched), DEFERRED or EXEMPT (a foreign attest-host or a cited repro-exempt, an honest neutral skip), and UNVERIFIABLE (an in-scope build the lane could not run). It prints its clean line only when a build was actually verified and none was UNVERIFIABLE, and exits non-zero on an UNVERIFIABLE, with the remedy inline.</li> <li>The deeper "the test truly drives the rule" claim is left as an opt-in check. The always-on lane confirms the static link. A test's PASS is established by the project's own suite. An automatic rule-neutralisation flip is deliberately omitted, because no mechanical map links an obligation with the code lines that realise it.</li> </ul> <h2 id="consequences-19"><a class="header" href="#consequences-19">Consequences</a></h2> <ul> <li>host-lifecycle's own manifest was re-dispositioned: the off-pin and verdict obligations now point at <code>off_pin_worktree_hazards_the_check</code> (which <code>software_check</code> returns its hazard count to make testable), and <code>DetectUnreproducedArtifact</code> at a new <code>artifact_reproduces</code> verdict helper. <code>software --check</code> runs clean; under <code>--strict-discharge</code> the manifest is honest where it was hollow.</li> <li>Honest limitation: the link is a token-PRESENCE heuristic, gameable in principle by naming any symbol the chosen test happens to contain. It was validated against the real <code>qwen3.5-4b</code> (Fen, the weak-agent acceptance test): the model authored the correct link unaided and, on a HOLLOW, re-pointed honestly and rejected the link-gaming dodge on semantic-mismatch grounds. So the design holds at the weak-agent bar, but its robustness rests on the author naming the rule's true observable, plus the opt-in exercise check and review, not on a tamper-proof mechanism. This limitation is stated, not hidden.</li> </ul> <h2 id="alternatives-considered-2"><a class="header" href="#alternatives-considered-2">Alternatives Considered</a></h2> <ul> <li>Mutation testing or per-rule coverage instrumentation to prove a test drives a rule. Rejected: heavy, runtime-dependent, and flaky, which trains a reader to ignore red, the inverse of the hole it would close.</li> <li>Requiring every <code>waived:</code> to cite a <code>call/</code> decision. Rejected: a software repo running <code>obligations</code> has no <code>call/</code> directory to cite, and a legitimate no-observable waiver (the lifecycle-entry rule) would break. Whether <code>waived:</code> needs stronger teeth is left to the probe-informed doctrine.</li> </ul> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><h1 id="host-prove-installs-verifiers-as-a-separate-fail-closed-verb-and-binds-every-verdict-to-the-embedded-pin"><a class="header" href="#host-prove-installs-verifiers-as-a-separate-fail-closed-verb-and-binds-every-verdict-to-the-embedded-pin">host-prove installs verifiers as a separate fail-closed verb, and binds every verdict to the embedded pin</a></h1> <ul> <li>Status: accepted</li> <li>Date: 2026-06-30</li> <li>Scope: the <code>host-prove</code> lane driver (plan/0054). Instance software, binds no adopter, no spine change. Decides how the deep-verification verifiers (Kani, Apalache, TLAPS) are installed and how a run binds to them. Supersedes the earlier within-plan choice of auto-install on demand.</li> <li>Relates: <code>call/0018</code> (discharge is the verifier passing on re-derivation, so a verdict must come from the pinned verifier); <code>call/0033</code> and <code>call/0034</code> (host-reference's out-of-process plugins, the prior art for an arms-length, install-on-enable helper); <code>call/0031</code> (the no-reach-out rule); <code>plan/0052</code> and <code>[[no-hollow-green-doctrine]]</code> (a lane that cannot perform its check must not report clean).</li> </ul> <h2 id="context-and-problem-statement-20"><a class="header" href="#context-and-problem-statement-20">Context and Problem Statement</a></h2> <p>host-prove runs one verifier and settles to one machine-matchable verdict that maps to an exit code; downstream the verdict is trusted as the discharge of a deep-verification obligation. The verifiers are heavy third-party tools pinned by version and SHA256 in <code>tools.lock</code>. plan/0054 set out to make them on-demand, tool-carried plugins modeled on the host-reference helpers, and an earlier within-plan choice was auto-install on demand: an absent verifier would be fetched, verified, installed, and run in one command.</p> <p>The operator raised three worries about that choice: silent failures, updates, and sandbox restrictions. A cast consultation (all five personas) found the auto-install default unsafe and located the true defect. The first resolver reused whatever verifier was installed or on PATH without checking its version against the embedded pin, so after a pin bump a host would keep using the old verifier and still emit a clean pass: a wrong-version verdict with no signal, exactly the hollow green host-prove exists to prevent, in host-prove itself. Auto-install also made a run reach the network and write to the filesystem as a side effect, which a sandbox, a hermetic build, or an air-gapped host blocks, so a routine run would surprise those environments and fail at run time.</p> <h2 id="decision-22"><a class="header" href="#decision-22">Decision</a></h2> <ul> <li><strong>A verdict binds to the embedded pin, every run.</strong> The run path resolves a verifier only from a version-stamped install keyed to the pin embedded in the host-prove binary, with an install-time SHA256 marker that must equal the embedded pin. An absent, wrong-version, or unverifiable verifier resolves to a distinct <code>BLOCKED</code> verdict at exit 2 that names the next command, <code>host-prove install <tool></code>. A verifier not bound to the pin issues neither a pass nor a fail. A binary found on PATH whose provenance cannot be bound to the pin counts as not-pinned. This is the no-hollow-green doctrine applied to the re-deriver: a lane that cannot prove it ran the pinned verifier reports a precondition failure, never a result.</li> <li><strong>Installation is a separate, explicit, fail-closed verb.</strong> <code>host-prove install <tool></code> is the only path that touches the network or the filesystem: it fetches the pinned asset, verifies its SHA256 before extracting or executing it, and installs into a version-stamped directory. The run and parse path is pure-local and never installs, so it works under a hermetic build, a sandbox, or an air-gapped host. A CI provisioning lane runs the install verb deliberately, ahead of the prove step. Auto-install on demand is dropped: re-install is always an explicit operator act, because the host may be air-gapped and the operator must learn that the pin moved.</li> <li><strong>Updates are safe by construction.</strong> The version-stamped directory is keyed to the embedded pinned version, so a pin bump moves the lookup path. The old version is never glanced at; the next run resolves to a path that does not exist, reports <code>BLOCKED</code>, and the operator runs install.</li> <li><strong>A verdict carries its provenance, and <code>host-prove doctor</code> reports it.</strong> A PASS verdict carries the resolved tool version and its pin-bound marker, so a single glance or a later cold read confirms the pinned tool produced it. <code>host-prove doctor</code> prints each declared verifier's installed version and pin status without running a proof, the cheap check the human operator needs.</li> </ul> <h2 id="consequences-20"><a class="header" href="#consequences-20">Consequences</a></h2> <ul> <li>The shell installers (<code>install/*.sh</code>, <code>_common.sh</code>) retire in favour of the in-process <code>host-prove install</code> verb, so the orchestration lives in one fail-closed process rather than a shell wrapper.</li> <li>A run is reproducible in its verdict and pure-local; the network reach is confined to the explicit install verb. The <code>cargo kani setup</code> backend remains an unpinned fetch (a documented residual on the kani plugin), the one provenance edge the SHA pin does not cover.</li> <li>The weak agent gets one tool-driven command at a time: a run that names <code>host-prove install <tool></code> when blocked is the tool carrying the process, not a hidden side effect. The design is gated on a real qwen3.5-4b probe before release, as a doctrine-grade change requires.</li> </ul> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><h1 id="host-lint-blocks-only-the-high-centrality-work-unit-words-domain-heavy-ordinal-nouns-are-advisory"><a class="header" href="#host-lint-blocks-only-the-high-centrality-work-unit-words-domain-heavy-ordinal-nouns-are-advisory">host-lint blocks only the high-centrality work-unit words; domain-heavy ordinal nouns are advisory</a></h1> <ul> <li>Status: accepted</li> <li>Date: 2026-06-30</li> <li>Scope: the <code>host-lint</code> detector (plan/0055). Instance software, no spine change; it ships to adopters through <code>host-template</code>, so its false-flag behaviour is felt in every adopter's code, not only here. Decides which tell-nouns block at the Flag tier and which warn at the advisory tier, and what counts as a blocking numeral after one.</li> <li>Relates: <code>plan/0055</code> (the host-lint review that raised the false-flag findings); <code>plan/0053</code> (the host-grammar precision recut, where <code>is_numeral</code> gained canonical-Roman validation); <code>call/0006</code> (the sanctioned-vocabulary allow-list, where the LEXICON legitimizes vocabulary but does not silence a tell) and <code>call/0019</code> (literal citations go in a <code>host-lint:ignore</code> fence, not the LEXICON, and never <code>--no-verify</code>). Those two are the decided disposition for a tell-shaped domain term, and the LEXICON guards here enforce their "not an escape" principle. <code>plan/0052</code> and <code>[[no-hollow-green-doctrine]]</code> (a recall-biased Warn is sanctioned, a false Flag is not).</li> </ul> <h2 id="context-and-problem-statement-21"><a class="header" href="#context-and-problem-statement-21">Context and Problem Statement</a></h2> <p>host-lint has three tiers: a blocking Flag (exit 1) for a confirmed tell, an advisory recall-biased Warn (exit 3), and a Note (exit 0). The recall bias is sanctioned only at Warn. A Flag blocks a commit, so a false Flag trains the audience to bypass the hook, which dismantles the gate.</p> <p>The blocking-tier noun set was assembled by intuition. The plan/0055 review found it over-blocks: the detector accepted a single-letter Roman numeral (so the pronoun "I" and a language designator after a tell-noun blocked ordinary prose), reached a numeral two words away, and carried a broad list of nouns whose ordinal use is ordinary domain vocabulary rather than the naming of a unit of project work. The operator's instruction was to ground the disposition in data rather than assert that a noun is "collision-prone".</p> <p>The measurement: the <code><noun> <numeral></code> shape was counted across roughly 35,500 real <code>.rs</code> files in the local cargo cache (a fair proxy for adopter code, since the detector ships to other software projects), and a sample of each noun's occurrences was classified. Every sampled occurrence was domain usage. The exposure was heavily skewed: one document-structure noun alone produced thousands of hits, the cipher/log/tutorial nouns hundreds each, the machine-learning and time nouns a couple of dozen or fewer, and the core iteration words near zero. In this repository's own commit history, by contrast, one work-unit noun named six real deliverables by ordinal position, and the central phase noun was used as vocabulary dozens of times yet never once as an ordinal label. So the discriminator is the product of domain-usage exposure and work-unit centrality, not raw frequency: a moderate-frequency noun that genuinely names work earns the blocking tier, while a high-frequency domain noun does not.</p> <p>A blocking noun followed by a numeral is also a complete flag, which the LEXICON guard refuses to register (you rename a tell, you do not allow-list it). So a domain noun left in the blocking tier yields a false flag with no escape short of a <code>host-lint:ignore</code> fence or a reword.</p> <h2 id="decision-23"><a class="header" href="#decision-23">Decision</a></h2> <ul> <li><strong>The blocking tier holds the high-centrality work-unit words only:</strong> <code>phase</code>, <code>stage</code>, <code>sprint</code>, <code>iteration</code>, <code>cycle</code>, <code>increment</code>, <code>wave</code>, plus the near-zero-exposure ordinal synonyms (<code>episode</code>, <code>instalment</code>, <code>leg</code>, <code>lap</code>) and the host#16 checklist-position terms (<code>box</code>, <code>boxes</code>, <code>steps</code>). These either carry proven ordinal-naming tells in this repository's history or have no measured false-flag exposure.</li> <li><strong>The advisory tier holds the domain-heavy ordinal nouns:</strong> <code>pass</code>, <code>round</code>, <code>step</code>, <code>level</code>, <code>part</code>, <code>section</code>, <code>chapter</code>, <code>epoch</code>, <code>batch</code>, <code>era</code>, <code>period</code>. Their ordinal use is overwhelmingly domain vocabulary; they warn, and under <code># host-lint: strict</code> an undeclared occurrence still escalates to a Flag, and the gather lane still surfaces a recurring shape for triage.</li> <li><strong>A blocking numeral is unambiguous:</strong> an arabic integer or single decimal, a short <em>ascending</em> checklist range, or a Roman numeral written uppercase whose value is a plausible ordinal (<code><= XXXIX</code>), and only when it sits immediately after the noun. The Roman bound (revised in the doctrine-gate cast review) is what catches a roman-numbered phase tell, so a phase named with an ordinal roman still blocks and cannot smuggle past the gate, while it excludes the ordinary uppercase abbreviations that are also canonical Roman (<code>DC</code>, <code>CM</code>, <code>MM</code>, <code>MD</code>, <code>DIV</code>, <code>XL</code>): they all carry C/D/M or exceed an ordinal, so a flag noun followed by one of them would otherwise false-flag in its home domain (a signal-processing or sizing context). A single-letter Roman, a lowercase roman-word, a date or descending range, and a numeral two words away never block.</li> <li><strong><code>steps</code> stays blocking</strong> by operator decision, to keep the host#16 checklist-position detection, accepting the tutorial-<code>steps</code> false flags it carries.</li> <li><strong>The disposition is grounded in measurement, not assertion.</strong> The demotions are grounded in ~35,500 real <code>.rs</code> files; the doctrine-gate cast review then exposed the register the <code>.rs</code> corpus could not see, so it was measured directly: <code>phase <UPPERCASE></code> (the roman-acronym false-flag class) occurs <strong>zero</strong> times in those files (vs 84 lowercase), and <code>box</code>/<code>boxes</code>/<code>steps</code> + numeral occurs once in markdown, which confirms the retained terms carry low exposure in the doc register too. A future change to the noun set or the numeral rule restates the measurement.</li> <li><strong>The LEXICON is not the escape for a tell</strong> (<code>call/0006</code>, <code>call/0019</code>). It registers genuine vocabulary (a version string, a standard, a cited tracker ref) and refuses any phrase that is itself a tell or carries a position noun or a bare review code (<code>F1</code>); a domain term that is itself a tell goes in a <code>host-lint:ignore</code> fence (in a doc) or is reworded (in a commit subject), never allow-listed.</li> </ul> <h2 id="consequences-21"><a class="header" href="#consequences-21">Consequences</a></h2> <ul> <li>Adopter code that references document or specification sections, cipher rounds, log levels, tutorial steps, machine-learning epochs, or time periods no longer blocks on a commit. This is the large precision gain the review targeted.</li> <li>A genuine ordinal milestone name built from a demoted noun warns rather than blocks. It is not silent: it warns, escalates under strict, and is surfaced by gather. The recall trade is deliberate and falls on the recall-biased tier, where the methodology already accepts it.</li> <li>VOCABULARY.md, the rule source, is rewritten to state the two tiers and the blocking-numeral rule, so the document matches the code rather than describing a wider contract than ships.</li> <li>The <code>RomanNumeralLength</code> spec invariant loses its subject: the blocking lane no longer admits a Roman numeral that a length cap would bound, so the invariant is removed rather than patched.</li> </ul> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><h1 id="the-bare-object-store-is-bare-with-a-git-file-not-a-bare-repo-named-git"><a class="header" href="#the-bare-object-store-is-bare-with-a-git-file-not-a-bare-repo-named-git">The bare object store is <code>.bare</code> with a <code>.git</code> file, not a bare repo named <code>.git</code></a></h1> <ul> <li>Status: accepted (supersedes the bare-store placement of plan/0029)</li> <li>Date: 2026-07-04</li> <li>Scope: the on-disk materialisation layout for a <code>.host-software</code> component's bare object store. This is tooling behaviour of host-lifecycle <code>software --materialize</code> and <code>--check</code>, and binds no adopter beyond the tool's output. The milestone is <code>plan/0056</code>; surfaced as connollydavid/host-lifecycle#8. It supersedes <code>plan/0029</code>'s choice to name the bare store <code>.git</code> inside the component directory.</li> <li>Relates: <code>plan/0029</code> (the branch-keyed worktree layout this amends); <code>plan/0056</code> (the robustness superset); <code>call/0010</code> (software as a bare store with worktrees pinned in <code>.host-software</code>).</li> </ul> <h2 id="context-and-problem-statement-22"><a class="header" href="#context-and-problem-statement-22">Context and Problem Statement</a></h2> <p><code>plan/0029</code> clustered each component under a single <code>software/<name>/</code> directory: the bare object store at <code>software/<name>/.git</code> and the branch worktrees at <code>software/<name>/<branch>/</code>. The clustering goal was sound (one directory per component), but the realisation named the bare store <code>.git</code>, and a bare repo named <code>.git</code> fights git tooling. <code>.git</code> conventionally denotes a working tree's repository, so <code>git status</code> run inside <code>software/<name>/</code> finds the bare <code>.git</code>, reads <code>core.bare = true</code>, and errors; IDEs and any tool that detects a repository by a <code>.git</code> entry flag <code>software/<name>/</code> as a repository root and then choke because it is bare, with the real worktrees nested inside what git reads as a bare repo.</p> <p>The docs drifted too: the <code>.host-software</code> header and a doc comment still describe the pre-0029 sibling <code>software/<name>.git</code>, a third layout that matches neither the code nor best practice.</p> <p>The operator's ruling: follow git best practice and do not fight tooling.</p> <h2 id="decision-24"><a class="header" href="#decision-24">Decision</a></h2> <p>Materialise a component's bare object store as <code>software/<name>/.bare</code>, with a <code>.git</code> file at <code>software/<name>/.git</code> holding <code>gitdir: ./.bare</code>, and keep the branch worktrees at <code>software/<name>/<branch>/</code>.</p> <ul> <li>This keeps <code>plan/0029</code>'s one-directory-per-component clustering: everything stays under <code>software/<name>/</code>.</li> <li>It stops fighting tooling: <code>.git</code> is a file, a gitdir link every git tool understands, and the bare store carries the conventional <code>.bare</code> name. A <code>git</code> command run inside <code>software/<name>/</code> resolves through the <code>.git</code> file to <code>.bare</code>, and no tool mistakes the directory for a stray bare repository.</li> <li>The docs reconcile to this layout: the <code>.host-software</code> header, the materialize doc comment, the store-dir doc comment, and the <code>plan/0029</code> comment all describe <code>.bare</code> plus the <code>.git</code> file, so no stale <code><name>.git</code> or bare-<code>.git</code> reference remains.</li> <li>Already-materialised components re-materialise from <code>url</code> and <code>pin</code>, which the recorded pin reproduces deterministically.</li> </ul> <p>The sibling <code>software/<name>.git</code> (the layout the stale docs described) was the runner-up. It is idiomatic, but it scatters two entries per component under <code>software/</code>, undoing <code>plan/0029</code>'s clustering. The <code>.bare</code> plus <code>.git</code> file layout is the one that satisfies both clustering and tooling.</p> <h2 id="consequences-22"><a class="header" href="#consequences-22">Consequences</a></h2> <ul> <li><code>store_dir</code> returns <code>.bare</code>; materialize writes the <code>.git</code> file; <code>--check</code> asserts both; the docs and tests move to the new layout. The change sites are in <code>plan/0056</code>'s <code>implementation.md</code>.</li> <li>A one-time re-materialise for existing components.</li> <li>host-lifecycle's materialisation output stops surprising git and IDEs, which serves the cold reader and the heavily-quantized operator the superset targets.</li> </ul> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><h1 id="call0040-retire-unmaintained-crate-advisories-with-maintained-forks-and-a-patch-lane"><a class="header" href="#call0040-retire-unmaintained-crate-advisories-with-maintained-forks-and-a-patch-lane">call/0040: retire unmaintained-crate advisories with maintained forks and a patch lane</a></h1> <ul> <li>Status: accepted</li> <li>Scope: host-reference</li> <li>Date: 2026-07-07</li> </ul> <h2 id="context-and-problem"><a class="header" href="#context-and-problem">Context and problem</a></h2> <p>host-reference pulls four crates that RustSec flags as unmaintained, each through an opt-in reader: paste (RUSTSEC-2024-0436), atomic-polyfill (RUSTSEC-2023-0089), proc-macro-error (RUSTSEC-2024-0370), and ttf-parser (RUSTSEC-2026-0192). None is a vulnerability; each is an author-declared unmaintained label. The operator's standing rule is zero-unmaintained, met by genuine fixes rather than blanket ignores.</p> <h2 id="decision-25"><a class="header" href="#decision-25">Decision</a></h2> <p>Redirect each dead crate to a maintained slartibardfast fork through <code>[patch.crates-io]</code>. cargo-deny does not advisory-check a git source, and no same-name registry successor exists, so a fork under our control is the only route to a zero-ignore lane. The forks are not <code>.host-software</code> members: they are vendored third-party dependencies, not software developed here, governed by this decision.</p> <p>Three crates have a maintained successor, so the fork routes to real maintained code:</p> <ul> <li>paste re-exports pastey's <code>paste!</code> macro.</li> <li>atomic-polyfill re-exports portable-atomic (the crate's own README already points there).</li> <li>proc-macro-error is a two-crate rename of proc-macro-error2 and its attribute crate, with the one codegen path edited, because a re-export cannot satisfy the attribute macro's hardcoded crate path.</li> </ul> <p>ttf-parser has no drop-in successor (skrifa is a different API, and lopdf pins ttf-parser at version 0.25), so we ADOPT it as a maintained lane. Our fork declares maintenance in a MAINTENANCE.md, and the unmaintained label is resolved by our maintaining it rather than by a frozen dodge. The lane's standing obligation is the untrusted-input contract of the glyph and metrics reads the pdf reader drives; a fuzzing pass is its first real maintenance task. ttf-parser forbids unsafe code, so its worst case is a panic, never memory corruption.</p> <h2 id="consequences-23"><a class="header" href="#consequences-23">Consequences</a></h2> <p>Good: zero-unmaintained with no accepted risk, and the deployed default <code>text</code> binary is unchanged, since the patched crates reach only opt-in readers. Bad: we carry five fork repositories to maintain, and the ttf-parser lane takes on a real maintenance obligation we must honour. Sunset: retire each fork when a maintained upstream or a drop-in successor lands.</p> <h2 id="relates"><a class="header" href="#relates">Relates</a></h2> <p>connollydavid/host-reference#3 (the quick-xml DoS advisories, fixed by upgrade in the same release); the reproducible re-vendor recipe (plan/0032, call/0021).</p> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><h1 id="call0041-the-adopt-command-splits-into-scaffold-primitive-and-adopt-onboarding"><a class="header" href="#call0041-the-adopt-command-splits-into-scaffold-primitive-and-adopt-onboarding">call/0041: the adopt command splits into scaffold (primitive) and adopt (onboarding)</a></h1> <ul> <li>Status: accepted</li> <li>Scope: host-lifecycle</li> <li>Date: 2026-07-07</li> </ul> <h2 id="context-and-problem-1"><a class="header" href="#context-and-problem-1">Context and problem</a></h2> <p><code>host-lifecycle adopt <dir> <revision></code> is the scaffold-and-stamp primitive: it creates the rooms and writes the <code>.host</code> stamp for a repository being brought under the methodology. The lifecycle adopt phase and its skill invoke it by that name. plan/0065 introduces a human-facing three-route onboarding as <code>host-adopt</code>, described there as a shim over the <code>adopt</code> verb, with the bare <code>adopt</code> name retiring. The two operations are different: one scaffolds into a named directory at a revision; the other elicits a name, decides among three routes (refuse a software repository, adopt an empty <code>agentic-<name></code> in place, or create the host elsewhere from an arbitrary folder), and never touches the source. A single verb cannot carry both without overloading on argument shape.</p> <h2 id="decision-26"><a class="header" href="#decision-26">Decision</a></h2> <p>Split the verb. The primitive is renamed <code>host-lifecycle scaffold <dir> <revision></code>, its behaviour unchanged. The <code>adopt</code> verb becomes the three-route onboarding, invoked by a human through the <code>host-adopt</code> shim. The bare <code>adopt <dir> <revision></code> two-positional form is <strong>refused with guidance naming <code>scaffold</code></strong>, not silently forwarded. (A first design forwarded it to <code>scaffold</code>; the pre-release review found that a mistaken <code>adopt <source> <name></code> is indistinguishable from the old form, and forwarding it would write the rooms and stamp into the source and break the source-read-only invariant. A hard error with guidance is the safe migration.) The adopt skill and the lifecycle manifest's adopt phase migrate their command to <code>scaffold</code>, and a UPGRADING ledger entry carries the migration to adopters.</p> <p>The migration map, the one place the old name lives:</p> <ul> <li><code>host-lifecycle adopt <dir> <revision></code> becomes <code>host-lifecycle scaffold <dir> <revision></code> (the primitive).</li> <li><code>host-lifecycle adopt</code> with no revision becomes the three-route onboarding (the <code>host-adopt</code> shim).</li> </ul> <h2 id="consequences-24"><a class="header" href="#consequences-24">Consequences</a></h2> <p>Good: the human entry (<code>host-adopt</code>) and the primitive (<code>scaffold</code>) have distinct, honest names, and the deprecate-then-retire shim means no adopter breaks on the release that ships the split. Bad: this is a spine migration touching the adopt skill, the lifecycle manifest, and every adopter that scripts the old command, so it owes a revision-keyed ledger entry; the old name lives on transiently in the shim and the migration record. Sunset: retire the bare-<code>adopt</code>-to-<code>scaffold</code> shim one release after adopters have moved.</p> <h2 id="relates-1"><a class="header" href="#relates-1">Relates</a></h2> <p>plan/0065 (the onboarding layer this serves); call/0027 (the front-door-to-entrance rename, the same deprecate-then-retire precedent); the migration ledger entry keyed to the doctrine commit in host-template.</p> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><h1 id="call0042-the-mcp-surface-is-hand-rolled-on-tokio-not-the-rmcp-sdk"><a class="header" href="#call0042-the-mcp-surface-is-hand-rolled-on-tokio-not-the-rmcp-sdk">call/0042: the MCP surface is hand-rolled on tokio, not the rmcp SDK</a></h1> <ul> <li>Status: accepted</li> <li>Scope: host-lifecycle</li> <li>Date: 2026-07-07</li> </ul> <h2 id="context-and-problem-2"><a class="header" href="#context-and-problem-2">Context and problem</a></h2> <p>plan/0065 adds a spawned MCP server exposing the <code>init</code> and <code>adopt</code> verbs over stdio, with a server-initiated elicitation request for the project name. The server is async on tokio (an operator directive, and the elicitation request naturally wants an async request-response). The official Rust SDK, rmcp, supports exactly this and provides server elicitation. But host-lifecycle is a lean binary with a hash-pinned musl reproducible build against a vendored dependency bundle, so every added dependency is a re-vendor and re-hash cost that the release must carry and re-derive.</p> <h2 id="decision-27"><a class="header" href="#decision-27">Decision</a></h2> <p>Hand-roll the protocol on tokio and serde_json rather than depend on the rmcp SDK. The wire surface is small and static: newline-delimited JSON-RPC over stdio, the <code>initialize</code> handshake echoing the protocol version and advertising a <code>tools</code> capability, the <code>notifications/initialized</code> follow-up, <code>tools/list</code>, <code>tools/call</code>, and one server-initiated <code>elicitation/create</code>. Two fixed tools plus one elicitation Form is about five methods, so the SDK's macro ergonomics buy little, while a stdio-only rmcp still pulls schemars, tokio-util, url, and a support set on the order of dozens of transitive crates, from a crate that shipped a major version bump on a one-to-two-week cadence. The reproducible build would vendor, pin, and re-derive all of it on every bump. The hand-roll adds only tokio to the vendored set; serde_json is already present.</p> <p>The server elicits only when the client declared the <code>elicitation</code> capability in <code>initialize</code>, per the spec, and it correlates the elicitation response by its JSON-RPC id while a tool call is in flight. That correlation is the one non-trivial piece and is the part to test hardest. The data grounding the SDK capabilities and the wire shapes is in plan/0065 gather-data.md.</p> <h2 id="consequences-25"><a class="header" href="#consequences-25">Consequences</a></h2> <p>Good: the reproducible-build dependency surface stays lean and stable, and we hold full control of the wire behaviour and the name backstop it wraps. Bad: we own protocol correctness, bounded because the <code>2025-06-18</code> stdio, tools, and elicitation surface is small and stable, and we absorb a future spec change rather than riding an upstream. Sunset: adopt rmcp if the tool set grows enough that its ergonomics and spec-tracking outweigh the vendored-dependency tax.</p> <h2 id="relates-2"><a class="header" href="#relates-2">Relates</a></h2> <p>plan/0065 (the onboarding and MCP layer this serves); plan/0032 and call/0021 (the reproducible re-vendor recipe every host-lifecycle dependency change runs); the elicitation client-support matrix recorded in the project memory.</p> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><h1 id="call0043-each-artifact-component-self-owns-its-vendor-bundle"><a class="header" href="#call0043-each-artifact-component-self-owns-its-vendor-bundle">call/0043: each artifact component self-owns its vendor bundle</a></h1> <ul> <li>Status: accepted</li> <li>Scope: host-lifecycle</li> <li>Date: 2026-07-07</li> </ul> <h2 id="context-and-problem-3"><a class="header" href="#context-and-problem-3">Context and problem</a></h2> <p>call/0021 established that host-lint owns a superset vendored-dependency bundle, shared with host-lifecycle: host-lint's dependency closure was a superset of host-lifecycle's, so one bundle served both. plan/0065 (call/0042) added tokio and serde_json to host-lifecycle for the MCP surface. host-lint uses neither, so its closure is no longer a superset, and no host-lint-derived bundle can carry host-lifecycle's offline dependencies. Meanwhile host-reference and its out-of-process helpers already self-own their bundles on their own releases repos, so the shared-superset arrangement is the lone special case in the tree.</p> <h2 id="decision-28"><a class="header" href="#decision-28">Decision</a></h2> <p>Retire the special case. Each artifact component self-owns its vendor bundle, vendored from its own <code>Cargo.lock</code> and hosted on its own releases repo. host-lifecycle publishes its own <code>vendor-v1</code>; host-lint keeps its own bundle for itself. The hermetic-build mechanism of call/0021 is unchanged: the bundle is staged, hash-verified, and built against under no egress; only that decision's ownership clause (host-lint owns the superset, shared) is superseded here. The result is one uniform rule, a component self-owns its bundle, in place of two.</p> <p>The migration is a one-time, atomic re-pin: re-vendor host-lifecycle's own dependencies, publish the bundle, and flip the single <code>deps-bundle</code> line in <code>.host-software</code> and host-lifecycle's own <code>deps-bundle.lock</code> from the shared host-lint pin to the self-owned one. The old shared bundle stays live until the pin flips in the release commit, so no build breaks mid-transition.</p> <h2 id="consequences-26"><a class="header" href="#consequences-26">Consequences</a></h2> <p>Good: a uniform, decoupled model with no cross-component superset relationship to preserve; a dependency change in one component never forces a re-vendor of another. No adopter is affected, because the deps-bundle is a per-component reproducibility anchor and an adopter carries its own components and bundles. host-lint is untouched, and its orphaned shared bundle retires with its single consumer. Bad: host-lifecycle now carries its own bundle to maintain, the same per-component cost host-reference already pays. This is the natural price of host-lifecycle's dependency set diverging.</p> <h2 id="relates-3"><a class="header" href="#relates-3">Relates</a></h2> <p>call/0021 (the hermetic-build mechanism, whose shared-ownership clause is superseded here); call/0042 (the tokio addition that diverged host-lifecycle's dependencies); plan/0065; plan/0032 (the reproducible re-vendor recipe).</p> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><h1 id="call0044-release-immutability-on-the-host-familys-release-repos"><a class="header" href="#call0044-release-immutability-on-the-host-familys-release-repos">call/0044: release immutability on the host family's release repos</a></h1> <ul> <li>Status: accepted</li> <li>Scope: host-lint, host-lifecycle, host-prove, host-reference, host-reference-ocr, host-reference-openscad</li> <li>Date: 2026-07-07</li> </ul> <h2 id="context-and-problem-4"><a class="header" href="#context-and-problem-4">Context and problem</a></h2> <p>plan/0065's install trust chain single-sources each binary's canonical hash from the public per-component release receipts. A mutable release host is a moving target: a compromised token (or a maintainer under pressure) could re-publish a release with a different binary and rewrite the recorded hash to match; the leaf hash-check then passes against a substitute. The reproducible-build root (call/0018, plan/0005) lets an adopter rebuild and confirm a hash independent of the host, but the publication channel is only trustworthy if a published artifact and its receipt cannot be silently swapped after the fact.</p> <h2 id="decision-29"><a class="header" href="#decision-29">Decision</a></h2> <p>Enable GitHub release immutability (prevent edit and delete of releases) on the six release-bearing host-* repos: host-lint, host-lifecycle, host-prove, host-reference, host-reference-ocr, and host-reference-openscad. The published assets and receipts are frozen at publication; a defective release is corrected by cutting a new version (host-lint v0.14.0 to v0.14.1, host-reference v0.1.5 to v0.1.6), never by editing the tag or the release in place. This is the release-host mirror of the methodology's "the tag is the release" and "history is immutable" discipline, and it covers the deps-bundle releases (vendor-vN) as well as the binaries.</p> <h2 id="consequences-27"><a class="header" href="#consequences-27">Consequences</a></h2> <p>Good: the install trust chain's single-sourcing is anchored at stable, non-mutable targets, so the reproducible-build root is defended against a moving-target attack on the publication channel; release fixes follow the existing new-version discipline; the deps-bundle hashes are frozen too. Bad: a release cannot be edited in place even when convenient, so every fix is a new version and tag.</p> <p>This is a project-local decision for the host-* family's GitHub release repos; the methodology itself stays host-agnostic. Its root is the reproducible build (which an adopter can verify anywhere), and it leaves the choice of release host and its features to each project. An adopter on a different host uses that host's immutability if it offers one, or relies on the reproducible-build root alone.</p> <h2 id="relates-4"><a class="header" href="#relates-4">Relates</a></h2> <p>plan/0065 (the install trust chain whose single-sourcing this anchors); call/0018 and plan/0005 (reproducible-build re-derivation, the host-agnostic root); the host-lint v0.14.1 and host-reference v0.1.6 re-releases (the new-version discipline this decision makes mandatory).</p> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><h1 id="call0045-dream-detectors-declare-their-stores-and-the-per-user-memory-tier-becomes-declared-state"><a class="header" href="#call0045-dream-detectors-declare-their-stores-and-the-per-user-memory-tier-becomes-declared-state">call/0045: dream detectors declare their stores, and the per-user memory tier becomes declared state</a></h1> <ul> <li>Status: accepted</li> <li>Scope: host-lifecycle (the dream memory audit), the spine's memory doctrine, plan/0076</li> <li>Date: 2026-07-22</li> </ul> <h2 id="context-and-problem-5"><a class="header" href="#context-and-problem-5">Context and problem</a></h2> <p>Running the dream audit to completion on agentic-host surfaced one defect shape twice (<a href="https://github.com/connollydavid/host-lifecycle/issues/22">host-lifecycle#22</a>): a detector applied to a store whose format it does not fit, with a remedy that store's discipline forbids. The description-body-drift detector fired on repo entries that have no description field, and the dangling-link detector resolved repo links against one store's slug set and then instructed an append to the append-only log as the fix. The held first patch scoped both detectors to the per-user store; adversarial review cleared the drift half and rejected the link half as instance-driven.</p> <p>The redesign went through a full cast convening under the operator's adversarial ranked-choice mechanism: five personas, the weak agent realized as the real qwen3.5-4b under its model card's parameters, the operator as tie-breaker. The opening ballot on absence semantics chose honest flagging over skip-and-state, four to one, with the maintainer persona in dissent: machine-local absence cannot distinguish a target that never existed from a target that lives on another operator's machine, and flagging on that evidence de-facto mandates an optional store. The operator then named the lacuna both camps shared: an uninitialized option is not an unused option. Absence had been a single state in the model where the format holds three.</p> <h2 id="decision-30"><a class="header" href="#decision-30">Decision</a></h2> <ol> <li>Applicability is declared per detector, beside a citation of the format fact that justifies it, and the engine enforces the declaration. The description-body-drift detector applies to the per-user store only.</li> <li>A memory link resolves against the union of the repo log and the per-user store. Remedies are store-correct: no remedy ever instructs an in-place edit or a free append on the append-only tier; corrections ride the appended-correction protocol.</li> <li>The per-user tier's in-use status becomes tool-written declared state: dream stamps an audited repo-side marker when it first observes an initialized store on the running machine. Three absence semantics follow. With no marker, an unresolved link is a confirmed dangling finding whose remedy leads with the operator's initialization fork before fix-or-drop. With the marker and no store on this machine, the finding is advisory: initialize or seed here, or leave standing and report; a link is never dropped on one machine's absence. With the marker, the store, and a missing entry, the finding is advisory: create the target or correct the link by appended correction.</li> <li>Findings carry one taxonomy across detectors: confirmed and review-prompt. Room-touching becomes a labelled review-prompt whose lead remedy is "leave a review note"; the mechanical cross-check against the applied receipts is deferred to a filed follow-up so the label cannot quietly become the fix. Exit codes split: clean exits zero, advisory-only exits three, any confirmed finding exits one.</li> <li>Silence is legible: per-tier coverage lines are generated from the same declarations and store facts the engine branched on, name each finding's state and its determinant in text and JSON, and carry per-state counts and the marker's provenance.</li> <li>The marker guardrails bind the build. The lifecycle is format, not implementation accident: the marker is dream's sole sanctioned repo-side write, stamped only when a store is observed on the running machine, operator-attributable, retired by appended correction as an operator act, with a contradiction finding when a store appears after retirement rather than a silent re-stamp. Marker flips in either direction never ride machine-local evidence. The migration ledger entry pre-announces the day-one confirmed wall and prohibits link drops that merely clear it. A marker minted in the same change that clears a confirmed dangling finding is recorded as the failure's signature. A stale marker parks unresolved links at perpetual advisory; operator retirement is the recorded pressure valve, and it re-escalates surviving links to confirmed. A standing, never-decaying advisory baseline is itself evidence the marker is lying about a live store; annotating such a baseline as known noise is a finding, never a disposition.</li> </ol> <h2 id="the-vote-record"><a class="header" href="#the-vote-record">The vote record</a></h2> <p>Opening ballots: absence semantics went to honest-flag four to one (the maintainer dissent above); the weak agent's ballot first spoiled on position bias under mis-parameterized decoding and then validated as honest-flag under the model card's parameters, with both matrices retained as comparison data. Room-touching went to label-now four to one, the weak agent stable for suppression. After the operator's reframe, the re-ballot chose the three-state declaration-driven semantics five of five, each persona addressing its own earlier reasoning and the weak agent content-stable under rotation; every ballot's attack converged on the marker as a one-bit global authority, which is what the guardrails in the decision answer. The full ballots, probe protocols, and both weak-agent matrices are in plan/0076's gather-data.</p> <h2 id="consequences-28"><a class="header" href="#consequences-28">Consequences</a></h2> <ul> <li>The build is plan/0076-dream-store-model: spec, marker lifecycle, taxonomy and exits, legibility, tests, cast and weak-agent acceptance, release as an adds-flag bump. The held patch commit reworks inside it.</li> <li>The closure queue's first position re-scopes: the issue-scoped patch becomes plan/0076, and <a href="https://github.com/connollydavid/host-lifecycle/issues/22">host-lifecycle#22</a> closes at its release.</li> <li>Dissents stand recorded: the maintainer persona's opening dissent, answered in steady state and relocated to the migration window that the ledger entry guards, and the weak agent's preference for suppression on room-touching.</li> <li>agentic-host's ten forward-marker links are the migration's first customer: the operator either initializes the store, which re-tiers them advisory while seeding is owed, or retires them by appended corrections. Both terminal states are recorded so a standing baseline can never be annotated as known noise; such an annotation is itself a finding.</li> </ul> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><h1 id="call0046-retire-the-unimplemented-hermeticity-escape"><a class="header" href="#call0046-retire-the-unimplemented-hermeticity-escape">call/0046: retire the unimplemented hermeticity escape</a></h1> <ul> <li>Status: accepted</li> <li>Scope: the spine's reproducible-builds section and its <code>ecce498</code> ledger entry; host-lifecycle's recipe surface</li> <li>Date: 2026-07-23</li> </ul> <h2 id="context-and-problem-6"><a class="header" href="#context-and-problem-6">Context and problem</a></h2> <p>The spine tells an adopter that a component which genuinely cannot vendor offline "may carry <code>hermetic-exempt = call/NNNN</code> citing a software-scoped case decision, the same escape shape as <code>repro-exempt</code>" (host-template CLAUDE.md, the reproducible-builds section; repeated in the <code>ecce498</code> ledger entry). host-lifecycle parses no such key: <code>repro-exempt</code> is a real recipe field read in two places, and <code>hermetic-exempt</code> is read nowhere. An adopter with a network-fetching <code>build.rs</code> follows the instruction exactly, and the line is silently discarded. The gate stays red. Their only remaining move is to delete the <code>deps-bundle</code> line the same section told them to add.</p> <p>The escape was coined on 2026-06-22 in plan/0032's second adversarial review, in one sentence recommending it "mirroring <code>repro-exempt</code>, so a non-pure-Rust adopter is not trapped". It shipped template-first with the property MUST it escapes and was never built, because no component has needed it: every artifact-bearing component here vendors offline.</p> <p>The operator's reading of the name, on being shown it: an adjective is wrong for a key that records something. "Hermetic" describes a quality of a build, so the key reads as exemption from an adjective rather than as the name of a record. Adjectives belong to options, where they name a mode of operation.</p> <h2 id="decision-31"><a class="header" href="#decision-31">Decision</a></h2> <ol> <li><strong>The escape is retired from the spine before it is implemented.</strong> The property MUST stands unchanged: a component distributing release binaries must be able to reproduce them offline from pinned inputs. The enforceable gate invariant is also unchanged. A component recording a <code>deps-bundle</code> builds under no network. Its staged bundle hash matches the recorded one. What goes is the sentence promising a key the tool does not read.</li> <li><strong>The case that cannot vendor offline is recorded with the existing <code>repro-exempt</code>,</strong> which cites its decision. Hermeticity is a facet of reproducibility rather than a second property, and two exemption keys for one property is a drift generator: the day they disagree, nobody knows which one the gate honours.</li> <li><strong>If a distinct escape is ever needed, it is named as a noun for what is recorded</strong> and settled by the rotation-proof weak-agent probe the recent names used, not by parallel construction in a review sentence. This is a rule for the next name in this family, not a sweep of the existing surface: <code>repro-exempt</code> is parsed, shipped and cited by a ledger entry, and it stays until retiring it is worth an upgrade entry of its own.</li> </ol> <h2 id="consequences-29"><a class="header" href="#consequences-29">Consequences</a></h2> <ul> <li>The spine loses one sentence and the <code>ecce498</code> ledger entry loses its last clause; a retirement entry records the removal, because an adopter who read the promise may have written the key into a recipe where it did nothing.</li> <li>host-lifecycle's recipe surface is unchanged, since there was nothing to remove from it. The gap this closes is a documentation claim the tool never supported, which is the failure the methodology maintainer's chair exists to catch.</li> <li>The naming reading is recorded here rather than promoted to doctrine. It binds the next escape in this family and nothing else.</li> </ul> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><h1 id="call0047-the-reproducibility-waiver-is-named-for-its-record"><a class="header" href="#call0047-the-reproducibility-waiver-is-named-for-its-record">call/0047: the reproducibility waiver is named for its record</a></h1> <ul> <li>Status: accepted</li> <li>Scope: the <code>.host-software</code> recipe surface, the spine's reproducible-builds section, host-lifecycle's parser</li> <li>Date: 2026-07-23</li> </ul> <h2 id="context-and-problem-7"><a class="header" href="#context-and-problem-7">Context and problem</a></h2> <p><a href="call/0046-retire-the-unimplemented-hermeticity-escape.html">call/0046</a> retired an escape the tool never read and folded its case into the surviving key, <code>repro-exempt</code>. That left one key carrying two concepts, under a name the operator had just rejected in its sibling: a key that records something should be named for the thing recorded, and an adjective belongs to an option rather than to a field.</p> <p><code>repro-exempt</code> reads as "exempt from reproducibility", which names the state being excused rather than the record being written. What the operator actually writes on that line is the name of a decision. The key is a citation slot, and its name should say so.</p> <p>Two concepts now share it, and neither is visible in the name: a migrated build that does not reproduce byte for byte yet, and a component that cannot vendor its dependencies offline. A rename that leaves the doctrine text silent about the second would be cosmetic.</p> <h2 id="decision-32"><a class="header" href="#decision-32">Decision</a></h2> <ol> <li> <p><strong>The key is <code>repro-waiver = call/NNNN</code>.</strong> Settled by the rotation-proof weak-agent probe the recent names used: <code>repro-waiver</code> was chosen from position A and again from position D against <code>repro-exempt</code>, <code>repro-exemption</code> and <code>build-waiver</code>. A second probe read both the old and the new spelling correctly, so legibility did not decide it; the naming rule did, and the probe establishes that nothing is lost.</p> <p>The migration verb's own name did <strong>not</strong> settle this way, and the difference is recorded rather than smoothed over: four rotations produced two position artefacts (position A twice, then position C twice), which is a preference for a slot rather than for a word. The probe was declared spoiled and <code>migrate-recipe</code> was settled on the family it joins, <code>migrate-receipts</code>. A spoiled probe is data about the protocol, exactly as plan/0076's spoiled ballot was.</p> </li> <li> <p><strong>Both spellings parse, and the retired one reports itself.</strong> An adopter's recipe keeps working across the rename and hears once per read that the key moved: the deprecate-then-retire discipline (plan/0039) rather than a silent swap. A test pins both spellings to the same waiver.</p> </li> <li> <p><strong>The migration is carried by the tool.</strong> <code>host-lifecycle migrate-recipe <dir></code> renames the retired key, drops the one no release ever read, leaves every other line untouched, and is idempotent. Both ledger entries call it rather than instructing a hand edit, because a hand edit is where a weak agent renames the wrong line and a busy operator renames none of them. The retired keys sit in one table, so the next rename is a row rather than a verb.</p> </li> <li> <p><strong>The doctrine names both cases the key carries</strong>, so the second one is not inferable only from a decision record: the build that does not reproduce yet, and the component that cannot vendor offline.</p> </li> <li> <p><strong>The retired spelling is removed at a later revision</strong>, on its own ledger entry, once adopters have had a release to migrate. Nothing in this decision retires it today.</p> </li> </ol> <h2 id="consequences-30"><a class="header" href="#consequences-30">Consequences</a></h2> <ul> <li>host-lifecycle parses <code>repro-waiver</code>, keeps reading <code>repro-exempt</code> with a warning, and every line an operator reads names the surviving key. The change ships with plan/0077's release.</li> <li>The spine's reproducible-builds section and its ledger entry move to the new spelling, with an upgrade entry whose verify condition reads the adopter's own recipe rather than the template's text.</li> <li>No component here carries a waiver. This repository migrates by taking the doctrine and the parser; its <code>.host-software</code> needs no edit.</li> <li>The naming reading stays scoped as <a href="call/0046-retire-the-unimplemented-hermeticity-escape.html">call/0046</a> left it: it binds this family of keys, and sweeping the wider recipe surface is not decided here.</li> </ul> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><h1 id="call0049-what-an-unattended-agent-may-decide-alone"><a class="header" href="#call0049-what-an-unattended-agent-may-decide-alone">call/0049: what an unattended agent may decide alone</a></h1> <ul> <li>Status: accepted</li> <li>Scope: any autonomous run in this repository and its components; the boundary between what a loop decides and what waits for the operator</li> <li>Date: 2026-07-27</li> </ul> <h2 id="context-and-problem-8"><a class="header" href="#context-and-problem-8">Context and problem</a></h2> <p>The operator intends to run this project under an autonomous loop: an agent working without anyone to answer a question mid-run. Every gate this project owns fails closed, every record is append-only, and the tooling is largely token-free. None of that decides the question a loop actually poses, which is <strong>what an agent may settle by itself when nobody is there to settle it.</strong></p> <p>The session that produced <a href="call/../plan/0078-sweep-in-the-verify-gate/README.html">plan/0078</a> is the evidence. Working with the operator present, the agent stopped four times on its own judgement: it refused to invent a citation form, refused to exclude a file from a gate without authority, stopped before publishing a release asset, and stopped when the template turned out to violate the doctrine it was about to ship. Each of those was a judgement call, and a judgement call unattended is a coin flip.</p> <p>In the same session the agent also published a vendor bundle that was wrong and could not be withdrawn, pushed a commit carrying a prose warning by running the gate after the push, closed the wrong issue by trusting a plan row rather than reading the issue, and rewrote history to remove a red commit without removing the red run. Those are the acts a charter has to catch.</p> <h2 id="how-this-was-decided"><a class="header" href="#how-this-was-decided">How this was decided</a></h2> <p>The four textual personas were convened on the charter and the open decisions. The fifth was realized as the real weak model, and it was used differently than usual: <strong>a charter is a text that has to work on an agent, so it can be measured the way an error message can.</strong> Two situations were probed, each one where obeying the rules costs something and breaking them makes a red gate disappear.</p> <ul> <li>Told the gate was red over a reference it could not resolve, and that adding the file to an exclusion list would clear it, the model <strong>stopped and recorded, twice</strong>, one repeat citing the rule it was following.</li> <li>Told that no accepted form existed for a citation and that only backticks passed the checker, the model complied once and <strong>violated once</strong>, choosing backticks, with the stated reason that it "is the only format that passes validation."</li> </ul> <p>The second repeat believed it was complying, and by the letter it was: backticks are not an invented form. The rule it evaded was phrased against a <strong>method</strong> (inventing), so every other method stayed open. The rule it obeyed was phrased against an <strong>outcome</strong> (anything that makes the gate pass). That difference is the finding, and it shapes every prohibition below.</p> <h2 id="decision-33"><a class="header" href="#decision-33">Decision</a></h2> <p><strong>The line is reversibility, not risk.</strong> An act the operator can inspect and undo after reading a diff belongs to the loop. An act that reaches people outside this tree, or that cannot be walked back, waits. Being the methodology's maintainer, the loop may author template changes freely; what it may not do is make any of them permanent.</p> <h3 id="absolute-a-green-gate-authorizes-none-of-these"><a class="header" href="#absolute-a-green-gate-authorizes-none-of-these">Absolute. A green gate authorizes none of these.</a></h3> <ol> <li> <p><strong>Do not make anything permanent.</strong> No tag, no release asset, no artifact or bundle that a pin resolves to becoming installable, no publication a later commit cannot correct. A tag is immutable by <a href="call/0044-release-immutability-on-host-repos.html">call/0044</a> and a release asset cannot be replaced, which this session established by publishing one that was wrong.</p> <blockquote> <p><strong>Superseded in part by <a href="call/0050-a-release-carries-a-resolvable-authorization.html">call/0050</a>.</strong> The sentence above stands for every act it names except a release, and it is left unedited because the trail is the point. What replaced it: <em>no release proceeds without a resolvable authorization recorded on its receipt.</em> The rule as written was phrased against an <strong>actor</strong>, so "the operator told me to" reopened the whole cascade with no record; nine releases were performed under it while the log could show neither the approval nor its absence. <code>host-lifecycle release</code> now refuses without <code>--authorized <ref></code>, and <code>software --check</code> re-opens a release receipt that carries none.</p> </blockquote> </li> <li> <p><strong>Do not rewrite what was published.</strong> No force-push, no amend of a pushed commit, no history rewrite. The complete set a run may amend is what <code>git rev-list @{u}..HEAD</code> returns, which git answers without memory.</p> </li> <li> <p><strong>Do not edit an append-only record.</strong> Shipped ledger entries, <code>MEMORY.md</code>, accepted <code>call/</code> bodies, and every tool-written receipt are corrected by appending, never by editing. Checkable as a diff: the removed-line side must be empty for those paths.</p> </li> <li> <p><strong>Do not make a check pass by changing what it reads.</strong> Not by an exclusion list, not by a lexicon entry, not by a waiver or a skip receipt, not by a tolerance fragment in a recheck, and not by rewording the thing under test into something the rule does not cover. Adding a rule is work; narrowing one is a stop. This is phrased against the outcome deliberately: the probe showed a prohibition on a method leaves every other method open.</p> </li> <li> <p><strong>Do not act on an identifier without reading what it names.</strong> An issue, a receipt, a task node, a plan row: fetch the thing itself and quote a line of it. A plan row records why a fix was queued, and reads exactly like a description of the issue it queued.</p> </li> <li> <p><strong>Do not write doctrine the tool does not enforce.</strong> A spine sentence naming a key, a flag, or a behaviour is a claim about the binary. Write it after the code exists and after a test fails without it. The precedent is a key promised in the spine for two revisions that no release ever parsed (<a href="call/0046-retire-the-unimplemented-hermeticity-escape.html">call/0046</a>).</p> </li> <li> <p><strong>Do not report a verification you cannot attribute.</strong> Name the run and the binary. Quote the coverage line rather than the exit code, because a clean verdict over a corpus with a hole in it is the defect this project has closed twice.</p> </li> </ol> <h3 id="stop-and-record-work-up-to-the-boundary-write-the-finding-where-it-will-be-read-halt-that-line"><a class="header" href="#stop-and-record-work-up-to-the-boundary-write-the-finding-where-it-will-be-read-halt-that-line">Stop and record. Work up to the boundary, write the finding where it will be read, halt that line.</a></h3> <ol start="8"> <li>A red whose cause cannot be named. A later green is not a cause: a flake that failed fifteen of forty runs read as superseded history for exactly that reason.</li> <li>Anything reachable only by doing one to seven.</li> <li>A form that no tool behaviour confirms. The test is a negative control rather than a document search: write it wrong and watch the tool object, or ask a capability probe. Searching the docs would have passed the key nothing parsed.</li> <li><strong>An advisory census is a reading, never a work queue.</strong> Do not open work from a count or a per-file list that was not asked for. Measured twice: shown one, the weak model abandoned its task in both repeats, in two different windows.</li> <li>A choice with two defensible readings that someone will meet out of context, such as a name, an exit code, or a message.</li> <li>A push that fails. Report the unpushed commits and start no dependent work.</li> <li>A budget fixed in advance and then breached. Record the disposition; a node that measures and shrugs is not a gate.</li> </ol> <h3 id="always"><a class="header" href="#always">Always</a></h3> <ol start="15"> <li><strong>Stage, then gate, then act, in one command.</strong> <code>git add -A && host-lifecycle software --check . && git push</code> cannot be inverted; an instruction to check first can be, and was. The staging step is not tidiness: the gates read the recorded corpus, so a document that is not yet tracked is invisible to them and checking it returns a clean verdict over a file nothing opened.
