The recorded revision is what a case-(c) upgrade diffs from.</li> <li><strong>Mechanical work is token-free.</strong> <code>host-lifecycle</code> does the classify / scaffold / stamp; <code>host-lint --all</code>/<code>--log</code> does the audit. Model effort is spent only on the case-(b) merge, case-(a) elicitation, and audit triage.</li> </ul> <h2 id="consequences-47"><a class="header" href="#consequences-47">Consequences</a></h2> <ul> <li>Good: adoption and upgrade are repeatable and auditable; a fresh session can read <code>MIGRATION.md</code> and the stamp and continue.</li> <li>Good: the dangerous operation (history rewrite) is gated behind an explicit mode with an archive-first rule, not reached by default.</li> <li>Cost: the protocol adds two new artifacts to maintain (the <code>MIGRATION.md</code> payload and the <code>host-lifecycle</code> verbs) and a stamp file per repo.</li> <li>Validated by dogfood: the host migrates itself (case c) under this decision; external repos follow as their own milestones.</li> </ul> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><blockquote> <p><strong>Superseded.</strong> Retained as immutable history, not current guidance.</p> </blockquote> <h1 id="host-lint-exempts-sanctioned-vocabulary-via-a-repo-root-allow-file"><a class="header" href="#host-lint-exempts-sanctioned-vocabulary-via-a-repo-root-allow-file">host-lint exempts sanctioned vocabulary via a repo-root allow file</a></h1> <ul> <li>Status: superseded by the methodology spine (host-template @ 94a1ac7)</li> <li>Date: 2026-06-14</li> </ul> <h2 id="context-and-problem-statement-29"><a class="header" href="#context-and-problem-statement-29">Context and Problem Statement</a></h2> <p>The migration protocol (<code>call/0005</code>) says history is immutable by default and legacy tells are <em>acknowledged, not rewritten</em>. But the audit engine had no way to <em>express</em> an acknowledgement: <code>host-lint</code> knew only "is this a tell?", with repo policy hardcoded in a shell wrapper. So a token that is legitimate vocabulary in a given repo, a version string (<code>NT 3.1</code>, <code>DOS 6.22</code>), a release identity, a cross-repo filename one is forbidden to rename, flagged with no sanctioned way to clear it short of editing the file.</p> <p>This bit hard on the first external dogfood. The Agentic-MCP-Win32s migration (PR #1) chased "zero tells" the only way the tool allowed: by rewriting protected content (append-only <code>MEMORY.md</code> and closed, immutable milestone bodies) which violated two standing rules and dissolved precise historical identifiers (review codes, work-item codes) into vague prose. The missing capability, not the agent's judgement alone, forced the over-reach.</p> <h2 id="considered-options-18"><a class="header" href="#considered-options-18">Considered Options</a></h2> <ol> <li><strong>An acknowledged baseline</strong>: record the existing flagged <em>occurrences</em> (by file + text), exempt exactly those, keep flagging anything new. Solves "acknowledge this historical body" precisely; carries a baseline file that must be regenerated as files move.</li> <li><strong>A sanctioned-token allow-list</strong>: list <em>phrases</em> that are legitimate vocabulary anywhere in the repo; never flag those tokens. Location-independent; simple; does not by itself protect an arbitrary historical line that happens to contain a real tell.</li> <li><strong>Both.</strong></li> </ol> <h2 id="decision-outcome-8"><a class="header" href="#decision-outcome-8">Decision Outcome</a></h2> <p>Chosen option 2: <strong>a sanctioned-token allow-list, and only that, for now.</strong> A repo-root <code>.host-lint-allow</code> file lists one phrase per line (<code>#</code> comments, blank lines ignored). Each phrase is masked out of every line before classification (case-insensitively, at word boundaries) so the occurrence never flags in any mode (<code>--stdin</code>, files, <code>--all</code>, <code>--log</code>); a missing file means no allow-list, so the feature is opt-in and behaviour is unchanged.</p> <p>The word-boundary rule keeps an entry honest: an entry masks only its exact phrase, not a longer tell that merely shares its prefix, and a <em>different</em> tell on the same line still flags (the concrete demonstration lives in host-lint's README). Masking reuses the existing classifier untouched rather than adding a parallel suppress path.</p> <p>Baseline (option 1) was <strong>deliberately deferred</strong>, not rejected on the merits. The Win32s lesson is that the right migration move is to <em>rename</em> ordinal milestone docs to content names, not to baseline their old bodies, so the acute need is exempting genuine vocabulary, which the token list covers. A per-site baseline is the correct tool for "this real tell is acknowledged legacy we will not touch" (the pgs-release history class); add it when a target concretely needs it, against a real case, rather than speculatively.</p> <p>This does <strong>not</strong> relax the methodology: the allow-list is for tokens that are not slop. The standing preference is still to name work after its content (<code>host-lint</code>'s <code>VOCABULARY.md</code>); the allow file is the escape hatch for genuine vocabulary, sized so it cannot quietly silence a real tell.</p> <h2 id="consequences-48"><a class="header" href="#consequences-48">Consequences</a></h2> <ul> <li>Good: a migration can acknowledge legitimate numbered vocabulary instead of rewriting protected, append-only, or immutable content, the failure mode that produced Win32s PR #1.</li> <li>Good: the rule is small and predictable (literal phrase, word-boundaried, location-independent) and adds no dependency to a deliberately dependency-free binary.</li> <li>Cost: an allow file can be abused to hide real tells; mitigated by the boundary rule, by keeping it opt-in, and by the documented "not for silencing slop" guidance. It remains a trust surface, reviewed like any config.</li> <li>Deferred: the per-site acknowledged baseline (option 1) remains unbuilt; the pgs-release dogfood is the likely forcing case.</li> </ul> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><blockquote> <p><strong>Superseded.</strong> Retained as immutable history, not current guidance.</p> </blockquote> <h1 id="adoption-is-a-clean-break-to-a-pristine-state-upgrade-is-a-shallow-delta"><a class="header" href="#adoption-is-a-clean-break-to-a-pristine-state-upgrade-is-a-shallow-delta">Adoption is a clean break to a pristine state; upgrade is a Shallow delta</a></h1> <ul> <li>Status: superseded by the methodology spine (host-template @ 94a1ac7)</li> <li>Date: 2026-06-14</li> <li>Refines: <code>call/0005</code> (does not supersede it: the cased/moded protocol stands; this corrects how mode is chosen and fixes a factual error in a target audit).</li> </ul> <h2 id="context-and-problem-statement-30"><a class="header" href="#context-and-problem-statement-30">Context and Problem Statement</a></h2> <p><code>call/0005</code> made <strong>Shallow the universal default</strong> and treated history as immutable-by-default, gating any rewrite behind a provenance prohibition. Two problems surfaced while applying it.</p> <ol> <li><strong>The token ledger.</strong> A clean break costs <em>more</em> at migration time but <em>less</em> per future session: one naming system, <code>host-lint --all</code> exiting 0 outright, no dictionary to consult, no "clean-modulo-acknowledged-legacy" subtraction to re-derive each session. For an <em>active</em> repo the recurring saving dominates. Shallow's real home is the small, frequent case (a stamped repo bumping the template revision), exactly like <code>copier update</code>. Treating Shallow as the universal default mis-priced first-time adoption.</li> <li><strong>A wrong audit premise.</strong> <code>call/0005</code> and the pgs-release brief recorded that pgs-release carries <em>external</em> FFmpeg patch-series provenance forbidding a rewrite. Examination (2026-06-14) showed otherwise: pgs-release is <strong>not a fork</strong> (567 KB, no parent): it is planning docs (<code>PHASE1–14</code> + variants) plus four vendor submodules; the FFmpeg fork (<code>connollydavid/FFmpeg</code>) and its patch series are <strong>ours</strong>; the host repo's own history is ~199 commits, <strong>100% authored by us</strong>, with tells in only a minority of <code>docs:</code> subjects. The prohibition rested on a misattribution.</li> </ol> <h2 id="decision-outcome-9"><a class="header" href="#decision-outcome-9">Decision Outcome</a></h2> <p><strong>Correlate mode with intent, and define a clean break as three risk tiers.</strong></p> <ul> <li><strong>Adoption</strong> (first-time: case (a)/(b), or a first-stamping case (c)): a <em>transformation</em> of what the repo is, so a <strong>clean break to a pristine live state.</strong></li> <li><strong>Upgrade</strong> (a stamped case (c) bumping template revision X to Y): a <em>delta</em>, so <strong>Shallow.</strong> Small, frequent, non-disruptive.</li> </ul> <p>A <strong>clean break</strong> is unbundled by risk, because the tiers are not equally safe:</p> <ol> <li><strong>Live files</strong> (structure, governance, plan docs, skills): rewrite freely to content names. No ceremony. This is where most of the recurring saving lives.</li> <li><strong>Owned append-only record</strong> (<code>MEMORY.md</code>, closed milestone bodies): may be rewritten at adoption <strong>only archive-first + map-only + recorded</strong>, the document analog of a Deep history rewrite, governed by <code>CLAUDE.md</code> §6. Original archived verbatim; only mapped rename tokens substituted; unmapped identifiers (review codes, version strings, work-item codes) left byte-for-byte; the diff shows nothing but substitutions. Never free-form, never self-authorized.</li> <li><strong>Git commit history</strong>: <strong>acknowledged, not rewritten, by default</strong>, even in a clean break. Re-shaing every commit (re-pointing tags, diverging branches, stale refs) rarely beats the value of de-numbering old subjects. Reserve Deep for the exceptional case where history coherence genuinely matters <em>and</em> the history is ours.</li> </ol> <p><strong>Provenance test, corrected.</strong> The bar is "history whose shas external consumers depend on," <strong>not</strong> "touches a patch series." A patch series we author (e.g. <code>connollydavid/FFmpeg</code>) is ours and rewrite-tolerant: rebasing is its native lifecycle, and a local rewrite produces a normal v2/v3; it cannot corrupt an already-submitted series. So no target is categorically Deep-forbidden merely for having patches; the decision is cost + ownership, per <code>call/0005</code>'s selection rule.</p> <h2 id="consequences-49"><a class="header" href="#consequences-49">Consequences</a></h2> <ul> <li>Good: the model matches how scaffolding tools actually work (clean <em>generate</em>, incremental <em>update</em>) and stops mis-pricing adoption as a minimal diff.</li> <li>Good: corrects the pgs-release provenance error before it hardened into doctrine.</li> <li>Good: the one dangerous operation (rewriting the owned record) is gated by an explicit, verifiable discipline (archive-first, map-only, recorded) rather than forbidden outright or (as in Agentic-MCP-Win32s PR #1) done free-form under a self-invented authorization.</li> <li>Cost: "adoption = clean break" raises the one-time spend and the tier-2 fabrication risk; mitigated by the map-only discipline and by preferring the deferred <code>host-lint</code> baseline (<code>call/0006</code>) to carry <code>--all</code>-cleanliness when a record rewrite costs more than it is worth.</li> </ul> <h3 id="per-target-consequences-correcting-the-call0005-audit"><a class="header" href="#per-target-consequences-correcting-the-call0005-audit">Per-target consequences (correcting the <code>call/0005</code> audit)</a></h3> <ul> <li><strong>Agentic-MCP-Win32s</strong> (adoption): clean break. Live PHASE docs to content homes freely; <code>MEMORY.md</code> + closed bodies rewritten <strong>map-only, original archived</strong>; host git history acknowledged; record the authorization in a <code>call/</code>.</li> <li><strong>pgs-release</strong> (adoption): <strong>Staged-Shallow for the host migration, by cost, not prohibition.</strong> ~199 owned commits, 11 release tags (<code>n*-pgsN.N</code>) and two branches make a host-history Deep rewrite not worth it. Clean-break the live PHASE docs into content homes (tier 1); acknowledge host git history (tier 3); keep the release tags as identities; submodules untouched. Cleaning the ffmpeg patch subjects for upstream is a separate, <strong>permitted</strong> rebase in our fork, out of scope for the host migration.</li> </ul> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><blockquote> <p><strong>Superseded.</strong> Retained as immutable history, not current guidance.</p> </blockquote> <h1 id="adoption-remap-is-enforced-by-a-dictionary-applied-deterministically-then-removed"><a class="header" href="#adoption-remap-is-enforced-by-a-dictionary-applied-deterministically-then-removed">Adoption remap is enforced by a dictionary applied deterministically, then removed</a></h1> <ul> <li>Status: superseded by the methodology spine (host-template @ 94a1ac7)</li> <li>Date: 2026-06-14</li> <li>Relates to: <code>call/0007</code> (clean-break tier 2 is "map-only"), <code>call/0006</code> (the allow-list), <code>call/0003</code> (tools composed as submodules), <code>CLAUDE.md</code> §6 (the append-only escape valve this enforces).</li> </ul> <h2 id="context-and-problem-statement-31"><a class="header" href="#context-and-problem-statement-31">Context and Problem Statement</a></h2> <p><code>call/0007</code> says the owned record may be rewritten at adoption only "map-only": substitute the documented rename tokens, invent nothing. As <strong>prose discipline</strong> this failed in Agentic-MCP-Win32s PR #1: parallel sub-agents denumbered the record independently and <strong>drifted</strong>: the same concept surfaced under names that were in no map ("the network-and-transport milestone" was invented). Two needs follow: the map-only rule must be <strong>mechanically enforced</strong>, not promised; and the migration must not leave the old vocabulary behind as a permanent artifact.</p> <h2 id="decision-outcome-10"><a class="header" href="#decision-outcome-10">Decision Outcome</a></h2> <p><strong>An enforced mapping dictionary, applied token-free, used as removable scaffold.</strong></p> <ul> <li><strong>One declared dictionary</strong>: <code>old-concept to canonical-new-name</code>, human-approved. It covers milestone names and any sub-codes the human chooses to denumber; the <strong>new name is always supplied by the human</strong>; the tool never coins one.</li> <li><strong>Deterministic applier</strong> (in <code>host-lifecycle</code>, the token-free migrator): applies <em>only</em> declared substitutions, word-bounded, archives originals first, and <strong>refuses to touch any unmapped token</strong>. No LLM in the substitution loop, so fabrication and spatial drift (inconsistent names across files/agents) are <em>structurally impossible</em>, not merely discouraged.</li> <li><strong>Completeness check</strong>: enumerates every token <code>host-lint</code> flags; each must be dispositioned as <strong>map</strong> (rename it), <strong>allow</strong> (<code>.host-lint-allow</code> vocabulary), or <strong>acknowledge</strong> (legacy residue). It fails while any flagged token is undispositioned, so there is no silent residue and no guessed mapping.</li> <li><strong>No ongoing gate; fault, policy-free.</strong> Preventing <em>future</em> drift is already <code>host-lint</code>'s job; a new numbered concept is a tell the detector catches regardless of the dictionary. An ongoing gate that resolved every reference against the dictionary would also <strong>cost tokens on every commit, forever</strong>, for drift already prevented for free. So <code>host-lint</code> stays a <strong>pure detector that faults on any tell and never consults the dictionary</strong>; all dictionary logic is confined to the one-time <code>host-lifecycle</code> applier; the engine never learns policy. After a clean remap there are no tells, so a policy-free fault is exactly right: anything that faults later is a genuine new tell to fix, not something to resolve.</li> <li><strong>Removable scaffold, applied then cleaned.</strong> Applying the map runs with the dictionary committed (so the diff reviews as <em>only</em> mapped substitutions, beside the archive). A follow-up deletes the dictionary file: the repo must not permanently carry an artifact whose content is the old ordinal names. The durable copy lives in the migration <code>call/</code> decision (documenting old-to-new is appropriate <em>there</em>) and in the apply commit, recoverable via <code>git</code>; the Rosetta stone sits in the same stratum (history/decision) as the old names it decodes; the live tree stays clean.</li> <li><strong>Coupling.</strong> Removable-scaffold requires the <strong>full</strong> clean break: the live <em>record</em> is remapped too (archived), so nothing live still references an old name. The alternative, keep+dictionary (record left verbatim), makes the dictionary load-bearing and permanent; that is the non-clean-break mode and accepts the elephant by design.</li> </ul> <h2 id="consequences-50"><a class="header" href="#consequences-50">Consequences</a></h2> <ul> <li>Good: "map-only" is a mechanical guarantee, not a promise; PR #1's spatial drift and fabrication cannot recur under the applier.</li> <li>Good: the completeness check makes the residual explicit and human-dispositioned (the irreducible non-mappable codes, review codes, bare version-like numbers, are surfaced and consciously allow-listed or acknowledged, never silently left or invented away).</li> <li>Good: no permanent old-vocabulary artifact and no redundant ongoing gate.</li> <li>Cost: more human input up front: a canonical name for every flagged concept. That input <em>is</em> the anti-fabrication guarantee, not overhead to optimise away.</li> <li>Builds on the trio: <code>host-lint</code> enumerates the flags (and gates new tells forever), <code>.host-lint-allow</code> dispositions vocabulary, the dictionary dispositions renames.</li> </ul> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><blockquote> <p><strong>Superseded.</strong> Retained as immutable history, not current guidance.</p> </blockquote> <h1 id="a-migrated-project-excludes-its-append-only-record-from-the-audit"><a class="header" href="#a-migrated-project-excludes-its-append-only-record-from-the-audit">A migrated project excludes its append-only record from the audit</a></h1> <ul> <li>Status: superseded by the methodology spine (host-template @ 94a1ac7)</li> <li>Date: 2026-06-14</li> <li>Refines: <code>call/0007</code> (the record tier). Builds on <code>host-lint</code> <code>.host-lintignore</code>.</li> <li>Superseded in part by <code>call/0019</code>: the <code>plan/*/README.md</code> blanket exclusion in the Decision Outcome below is <strong>retired</strong>. Editable plan docs stay linted; an irreducible literal citation is boxed in a <code>host-lint:ignore</code> fence (the per-block mechanism), not path-excluded. Only the append-only record (<code>MEMORY.md</code>) remains path-excluded. The blanket exclusion existed only because path-exclusion was the sole mechanism in 2026-06.</li> </ul> <h2 id="context-and-problem-statement-32"><a class="header" href="#context-and-problem-statement-32">Context and Problem Statement</a></h2> <p><code>call/0007</code> left the record (append-only <code>MEMORY.md</code>, closed milestone bodies) either rewritten (governed, map-only) or kept. Applying it to a real target (Agentic-MCP-Win32s) showed rewriting the record is the wrong trade: the record is a dense lab-notebook where token-substitution produces awkward prose (<code>"the bridge core bridge first-green"</code>) and ~25 review/tracking codes (<code>weed #1</code>, <code>R1</code>/<code>F1</code>/<code>G1</code>, and the like) resist content-naming. So a "full clean break" of the record is expensive and degrades it.</p> <p>The decisive fact, <strong>verified on the target</strong>: nothing re-scans the historical tree. The commit hooks lint only the commit subject and the <em>staged diff</em>; CI runs no linter (<code>mdbook</code> only). <code>host-lint --all</code> is a manual one-shot for migration events. So old names sitting in the record cost <strong>zero</strong> on an ongoing basis; they are read by no automated gate, ever.</p> <h2 id="decision-outcome-11"><a class="header" href="#decision-outcome-11">Decision Outcome</a></h2> <p><strong>A migrated project excludes its append-only record from the <code>--all</code> audit via a <code>.host-lintignore</code>, rather than rewriting it or acknowledging-modulo.</strong> The migration writes, e.g.:</p> <pre><code>MEMORY.md plan/*/README.md </code></pre> <ul> <li>The <strong>live layer</strong> (indexes, governance, skills, cross-refs) is clean-broken to content names (via the <code>remap</code> dictionary, <code>call/0008</code>) and stays in audit scope.</li> <li>The <strong>record</strong> is left verbatim and excluded, so <code>--all</code> is genuinely <code>0</code> without a rewrite and without abusing the token allow-list. Old milestone names survive only where history lives; the renamed <code>plan/<NNNN-slug>/</code> folders are the implicit old-to-new map (a reader hitting an old ordinal name in the record finds <code>plan/0004-command-execution/</code>).</li> <li><code>host-lint</code> stays general/policy-free; it honours an ignore file the way <code>git</code>/<code>ripgrep</code> do; the <em>methodology</em> supplies the policy by writing the file.</li> </ul> <p><strong>Token rationale (the deciding lens):</strong> rewriting the record is one-time cost with <strong>no</strong> recurring payback (nothing re-scans it), and risks negative value (degraded prose costs future readers). Excluding it is near-zero one-time and zero recurring. So exclusion is the token-optimal record handling. The live-layer clean break keeps its recurring payback and stays.</p> <h2 id="consequences-51"><a class="header" href="#consequences-51">Consequences</a></h2> <ul> <li>Good: <code>--all</code> means "no live tells," cleanly, with no record rewrite, no lossy prose, no allow-list abuse.</li> <li>Good: this is the concrete resolution of the deferred baseline question (<code>call/0006</code>) for the record class, a path exclusion, not a per-finding baseline.</li> <li>Cost: a reader auditing <em>history</em> must run <code>host-lint</code> against the excluded paths deliberately; that is the rare, correct time to look. The exclusion is explicit and reviewable in <code>.host-lintignore</code>.</li> </ul> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><blockquote> <p><strong>Superseded.</strong> Retained as immutable history, not current guidance.</p> </blockquote> <h1 id="embed-the-software-as-a-bare-store-with-named-worktrees"><a class="header" href="#embed-the-software-as-a-bare-store-with-named-worktrees">Embed the software as a bare store with named worktrees</a></h1> <ul> <li>Status: superseded by the methodology spine (host-template @ 94a1ac7)</li> <li>Date: 2026-06-14</li> <li>Relates: <code>call/0003</code> (compose tools as referenced submodules; the software embedding is the counterpart question for the "Where" room).</li> </ul> <h2 id="context-and-problem-statement-33"><a class="header" href="#context-and-problem-statement-33">Context and Problem Statement</a></h2> <p>The "Where" room (the software under test) has been a single git <strong>submodule</strong>: one gitlink, one pinned SHA, one working tree. That gives audit/reproducibility but only one live checkout, which serializes work. Two realistic needs break that: <strong>parallel agents</strong> on one codebase (the prevailing idiom is a bare repo + worktrees), and <strong>multiple production release branches live simultaneously</strong> (a maintained project servicing several shipped versions cannot have its single tree flip between them). The established "many live branches, one object store" idiom is a <strong>bare clone + worktrees</strong>; but that is not a gitlink, so adopting it means deciding what the host pins and how audit survives.</p> <h2 id="decision-45"><a class="header" href="#decision-45">Decision</a></h2> <p>Embed each software component as a <strong>bare object store plus named worktrees</strong>, with the pin recorded in host config rather than as a gitlink:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Layout.</strong> <code><name>.git/</code> is the bare clone (shared object store, no working tree). <code><name>/</code> is the <strong>canonical worktree</strong>, the audited state, where CI and the verification lanes run. Parallel lines are sibling worktrees <code><name>.<line>/</code>, one per agent or release branch; worktrees are never nested inside another worktree (it breaks <code>.git</code> resolution). A host may embed <strong>several</strong> software components; each <code><name></code> is its own bare store plus worktrees.</li> <li><strong>Recipe, not trees.</strong> The bare store and all worktrees are local artifacts (gitignored). The host commits a recipe (<code>.host-software</code>): <strong>one <code>[software "<name>"]</code> stanza per component</strong>, mirroring <code>.gitmodules</code>, each recording <code>url</code>, the <strong>pinned canonical SHA</strong>, and the worktree set, that a setup step materializes: <code>clone --bare</code>, set the <code>+refs/heads/*:refs/remotes/origin/*</code> fetch refspec, <code>fetch</code>, <code>worktree add <name></code> at the pinned SHA, init nested submodules per worktree, then add the parallel worktrees.</li> <li><strong>Audit moves to our tooling.</strong> With no gitlink, <code>host-lifecycle</code> owns the "is <code><name>/</code> at its recorded SHA?" check; the recipe's pinned SHA is the reproducibility anchor the gitlink used to be.</li> <li><strong>Nested submodules stay native.</strong> If the software has submodules, each worktree initializes them with <code>git submodule update --init --recursive</code> (worktrees share superproject objects, not submodule checkouts).</li> </ul> <h3 id="migration-an-existing-submodule-to-a-bare-store"><a class="header" href="#migration-an-existing-submodule-to-a-bare-store">Migration (an existing submodule to a bare store)</a></h3> <p>A project already embedding its software as a gitlink converts mechanically, <strong>preserving the software exactly</strong>, with no software commit created, rewritten, or moved:</p> <ol> <li><strong>Preserve the pin.</strong> Record the current gitlink SHA as the recipe's pinned canonical SHA; the bare+worktree state begins at precisely the commit the submodule pinned.</li> <li><strong>De-register the gitlink.</strong> <code>git rm --cached <name></code>, delete the <code>[submodule "<name>"]</code> stanza from <code>.gitmodules</code>, remove <code>.git/modules/<name></code>. The path <code><name>/</code> is freed.</li> <li><strong>Write <code>.host-software</code></strong> with <code>url</code>, <code>pin</code> (the preserved SHA), and the worktree set (at minimum the canonical <code><name></code>).</li> <li><strong>Gitignore the layout:</strong> <code>/<name>/</code>, <code>/<name>.git/</code>, <code>/<name>.*/</code>, all rebuilt from the recipe.</li> <li><strong>Path continuity is the win.</strong> The canonical worktree keeps the path <code><name>/</code>. Only the embedding mechanism changed, so every reference that pointed at <code><name>/…</code> (build commands, routing tables, hook paths) still resolves. Audit references for the few that named the submodule <em>qua</em> submodule.</li> <li><strong>Pointer-bump becomes pin-update.</strong> "Merge in the software repo, then bump the submodule pointer in the host as a separate commit" becomes "…then update the recipe <code>pin</code> as a separate commit." Same audit trail (a tracked one-line commit recording the software's new SHA), different mechanism; update <code>CLAUDE.md</code> and the completion step accordingly.</li> </ol> <h2 id="consequences-52"><a class="header" href="#consequences-52">Consequences</a></h2> <ul> <li>Good: parallel agents and multiple live release branches coexist on one object store; the canonical worktree stays the single audited, CI-run state.</li> <li>Good: symmetric, idiomatic layout; the bare store is visibly infrastructure; the canonical worktree keeps the conventional path, so migration is reference-preserving.</li> <li>Neutral: audit shifts off native <code>git submodule status</code> onto a <code>host-lifecycle</code> check against the recorded SHA; a fresh host clone no longer auto-fetches the software; the setup step (recipe, then materialize) replaces <code>submodule update --init</code> and must be documented/scripted.</li> <li>Bad / accepted: worktrees share git objects while keeping separate environments; each carries its own build output and submodule checkouts; heavy-vendor repos pay real disk per live line. This cost is <strong>required</strong>, not incidental: it is the price of holding several production releases (or several agents' branches) materialized at once, which a single tree cannot do.</li> </ul> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><blockquote> <p><strong>Superseded.</strong> Retained as immutable history, not current guidance.</p> </blockquote> <h1 id="references-to-the-software-worktree-must-survive-its-absence"><a class="header" href="#references-to-the-software-worktree-must-survive-its-absence">References to the software worktree must survive its absence</a></h1> <ul> <li>Status: superseded by the methodology spine (host-template @ 94a1ac7)</li> <li>Date: 2026-06-15</li> <li>Refines: <code>call/0010</code> (the bare-store-with-worktrees embedding).</li> </ul> <h2 id="context-and-problem-statement-34"><a class="header" href="#context-and-problem-statement-34">Context and Problem Statement</a></h2> <p><code>call/0010</code> moved the software off a gitlink submodule onto a bare store with worktrees. A submodule gave the software <strong>auto-presence</strong>: <code>git checkout</code> always left at least an empty directory, so symlinks into it resolved and tree-scans did not choke. The bare-store model <strong>removes that</strong>: the worktree is genuinely absent in any fresh clone or CI job until <code>host-lifecycle software --materialize</code> runs.</p> <p>This bit immediately: the self-migration turned the host's mdBook <strong>Site CI red</strong>. <code>.claude/skills/host-lint -> ../../host-lint</code> is a tracked symlink into the worktree; with <code>book.toml src = "."</code>, mdBook scanned the dangling link (the worktree is not materialized in CI) and failed. <code>call/0010</code>'s "path continuity" (references resolve to the same <em>path</em>) was not enough; it assumed the path was <em>populated</em>. The missing guarantee is about <strong>presence</strong>, not path. And: a feature was declared "complete" while this sibling CI was red. <strong>Complete must mean the whole suite is green</strong>, not one artifact built.</p> <h2 id="decision-46"><a class="header" href="#decision-46">Decision</a></h2> <p>Treat every host reference into a software worktree as valid only where the worktree is materialized, and harden against the gap three ways:</p> <ol> <li><strong>Prevention (don't track the hazard).</strong> Do not git-track an artifact that depends on the worktree existing. The skill symlink <code>.claude/skills/host-lint</code> is now <strong>gitignored and local</strong> (recreated after <code>software --materialize</code>) so a fresh clone has no dangling worktree symlink at all.</li> <li><strong>Detection (mechanical, bounded).</strong> <code>host-lifecycle software --check</code> flags a <strong><code>HAZARD</code></strong> for any host-tracked symlink whose target resolves into a worktree path; it would dangle wherever the software is not materialized. Bounded to symlinks deliberately: a path-<em>string</em> reference in a script or config cannot be told from prose statically, so widening the scan would only reproduce the <code>host-lint --all</code> noise. Those stay on the rule + an un-materialized CI job.</li> <li><strong>The un-materialized context must be exercised, and gate "done."</strong> CI's docs build <em>is</em> a fresh-clone-without-materialize context; it already catches this class; the failure was not looking at it. So: an un-materialized CI job must exist for each runtime-critical artifact, and "done" is gated on the <strong>whole</strong> CI sweep being green, not on the feature alone.</li> </ol> <p><strong>Docs-vs-skills semantics (resolved):</strong> the published site does <strong>not</strong> include the tool skills (they were never in <code>SUMMARY.md</code>). The Site build prunes dangling symlinks; with the skill symlink now untracked, there is nothing to prune for it.</p> <h2 id="consequences-53"><a class="header" href="#consequences-53">Consequences</a></h2> <ul> <li>Good: the exact break is now caught mechanically (<code>--check</code> reports the hazard, exit 1) and prevented (the symlink is untracked), and the CI is green again.</li> <li>Good: the rule generalises to the upcoming migrations (Win32s, pgs, greenfield), which all carry skill symlinks, hooks, and CI that assume the old auto-presence.</li> <li>Neutral: a fresh clone must run <code>software --materialize</code> and recreate the local skill symlink before host-lint's skill is discoverable; the honest cost of the software being absent until materialized.</li> <li>Limit: detection covers the symlink class only; path-string references (a hook's binary path, a build <code>--manifest-path</code>) remain a rule-and-CI concern, not a tool gate.</li> </ul> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><blockquote> <p><strong>Superseded.</strong> Retained as immutable history, not current guidance.</p> </blockquote> <h1 id="a-single-file-named-host-is-the-front-door-that-owns-the-adoption-and-upgrade-process"><a class="header" href="#a-single-file-named-host-is-the-front-door-that-owns-the-adoption-and-upgrade-process">A single file named <code>host</code> is the front door that owns the adoption-and-upgrade process</a></h1> <ul> <li>Status: superseded by the methodology spine (host-template @ 94a1ac7)</li> <li>Date: 2026-06-16</li> </ul> <h2 id="context-and-problem-statement-35"><a class="header" href="#context-and-problem-statement-35">Context and Problem Statement</a></h2> <p><code>call/0005</code> defined the migration protocol and shipped it <em>as the template's <code>MIGRATION.md</code></em>, driven by <code>host-lifecycle</code>. But adoption has no front door: there is no single thing an agent (or a patient human) can be pointed at to turn a repo into a host and keep it current. The protocol prose also sits inside the template, which overloads it: the template is pulled toward serving a capability rather than being the versioned source of the techniques (<code>call/0004</code>).</p> <p>We want: point an agent or a human at <strong>one URL</strong>, and out comes an agentic project with all the techniques present and <strong>upgradable</strong>. The open question was <em>what owns what</em>, because a self-contained instruction file and a revision-keyed upgrade ledger cannot both be canonical without forking the spine.</p> <h2 id="considered-options-19"><a class="header" href="#considered-options-19">Considered Options</a></h2> <ol> <li><strong>Template doubles as a plugin marketplace.</strong> One URL, but inverts the template's role, making a <em>source of techniques</em> into a <em>server of capabilities</em>, the overload <code>call/0004</code> exists to avoid.</li> <li><strong>Standalone repo, multi-file plugin/skill.</strong> Cleaner separation, but more to maintain and it buries the front door inside an engine.</li> <li><strong>Standalone repo, a single instruction file named <code>host</code> that owns the <em>process</em>; the template keeps the <em>techniques</em> and the <em>ledger</em>.</strong> One file, one URL, no overload.</li> </ol> <h2 id="decision-outcome-12"><a class="header" href="#decision-outcome-12">Decision Outcome</a></h2> <p>Chosen option 3.</p> <ul> <li><strong><code>host</code> is a single instruction file</strong> in its own repo (<code>https://github.com/connollydavid/host</code>). It is the front door: an agent or a human follows it to <strong>adopt</strong>, <strong>migrate</strong>, or <strong>upgrade</strong>, and ends with an agentic project carrying the methodology's techniques.</li> <li><strong><code>host</code> is developed here as software, not as a tool submodule of this repo.</strong> It gets a <code>[software "host"]</code> stanza in <code>.host-software</code>: a bare store with a worktree, pinned by SHA, gitignored, exactly like <code>host-lint</code> (<code>call/0010</code>). It is <em>consumed</em> downstream as a submodule; it is <em>developed</em> here as a worktree.</li> <li><strong><code>host</code> owns the process; the template owns the techniques and the ledger.</strong> This is the split that keeps "upgradable" true with no fork: <ul> <li><strong><code>host</code></strong> = the adopt/migrate/upgrade <strong>procedure</strong> (what <code>MIGRATION.md</code>'s steps were). Stable; rarely edited.</li> <li><strong>template</strong> = the <strong>techniques</strong> (the <code>CLAUDE.md</code> spine, the room scaffold, the tool pins) <em>and</em> the revision-keyed <strong>upgrade ledger</strong> (<code>UPGRADING.md</code>, one <code>[upgrade "<revision>"]</code> stanza per structural migration). The ledger is data the template's own changes generate, so it lives with them.</li> </ul> </li> <li><strong>Upgradability is automatic and lockstep-free.</strong> A produced folder records its adopted template revision in <code>.host</code>. To upgrade, <code>host</code> tells the operator to run <code>host-lifecycle upgrade <dir></code>, which prints every template ledger entry newer than the stamp; apply them; re-stamp. The procedure (<code>host</code>) does not change when the template adds a ledger entry; only the template does.</li> <li><strong>Copy-at-version, not embed.</strong> A produced folder copies the spine in at the adopted revision and stamps it (<code>call/0004</code>); it does not submodule the template. (This forge embeds the template as a submodule for development convenience only; it is adopter-zero, not a produced folder.)</li> </ul> <p>This <strong>amends <code>call/0005</code></strong>: the protocol is no longer shipped <em>as the template's <code>MIGRATION.md</code></em>. Its procedural content moves to <code>host</code>; the template's <code>MIGRATION.md</code> is reduced to a pointer at <code>host</code>. <code>UPGRADING.md</code> stays in the template. The cased/moded protocol itself (<code>call/0005</code>) and the clean-break / delta distinction (<code>call/0007</code>) are unchanged; only their home moves.</p> <h2 id="consequences-54"><a class="header" href="#consequences-54">Consequences</a></h2> <ul> <li>Good: one URL, one file, dual-audience (agent or human). The template stops drifting toward being a capability server; <code>call/0004</code> holds.</li> <li>Good: <code>host</code> stays a stable single file because the per-revision ledger (the part that churns) remains in the template with the techniques that cause it. No lockstep between <code>host</code> and template revisions.</li> <li>Cost: the procedure and the ledger now live in two repos, so a reader must follow one reference (<code>host</code> to the template's ledger) instead of reading one document. The single-file ideal is "self-contained <em>procedure</em>", not "everything inline".</li> <li>Cost: a new repo to maintain and a new <code>.host-software</code> stanza in this forge.</li> <li>Migration of this decision itself: move <code>MIGRATION.md</code>'s steps into <code>host</code>, leave <code>UPGRADING.md</code> in the template, and replace the template <code>MIGRATION.md</code> with a pointer, tracked as follow-on work, not done by accepting this record.</li> </ul> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><blockquote> <p><strong>Superseded.</strong> Retained as immutable history, not current guidance.</p> </blockquote> <h1 id="the-canonical-doc-site-publisher-is-host-lifecycle-book"><a class="header" href="#the-canonical-doc-site-publisher-is-host-lifecycle-book">The canonical doc-site publisher is <code>host-lifecycle book</code></a></h1> <ul> <li>Status: superseded by the methodology spine (host-template @ 94a1ac7)</li> <li>Date: 2026-06-17</li> <li>Refines: <code>call/0011</code> (worktree-absence coherence; the <code>src = "."</code> hazard).</li> </ul> <h2 id="context-and-problem-statement-36"><a class="header" href="#context-and-problem-statement-36">Context and Problem Statement</a></h2> <p>The methodology mandates five rooms (Who/What/When/Where/Why/How) and two spec formats, but shipped <strong>no canonical way to publish them</strong>. <code>host-template</code> carried only a one-line note ("scope <code>src</code> to <code>docs/</code>"); every adopter therefore hand-rolled an mdBook generator, and each got the same things wrong. A complete case-(b) adoption reported it (the <code>agentic-host</code> repo issue on doc-site gaps), and four of its findings reproduce on <strong>this repository's own published site</strong>:</p> <ul> <li>The Software/Where room (the action the project exists to produce) has no page, though <code>.host-software</code> carries the data to render a stub.</li> <li>Spec bodies (<code>.allium</code>/<code>.tla</code>) are never published.</li> <li>The sidebar is in source-call order, not the five-rooms lifecycle order (Cast, the Who, sits near the bottom).</li> <li>Nothing asserts a page per room, so a half-room site ships green.</li> </ul> <p>The root cause is singular: a missing, maintained publisher. Worse, this repository's own <code>book.toml</code> set <code>src = "."</code> (the exact hazard <code>call/0011</code> warned against) and survived only because CI prunes dangling symlinks and the worktrees are absent in checkout.</p> <h2 id="decision-47"><a class="header" href="#decision-47">Decision</a></h2> <p>Ship one canonical publisher, <strong><code>host-lifecycle book</code></strong>, and route every adopter (this repository included) through it instead of a hand-rolled generator.</p> <ol> <li><strong><code>src = "docs"</code>, never <code>"."</code>.</strong> <code>book</code> writes <code>book.toml</code> scoped to a generated <code>docs/</code>, encapsulating the <code>call/0011</code> rule once, centrally, so no adopter re-derives it wrong.</li> <li><strong>Lifecycle order.</strong> <code>SUMMARY.md</code> is emitted Cast (Who), then Plan + specs (What/When), then Software/Where, then Call (Why), then Reference/CLAUDE (How), then Memory.</li> <li><strong>The Where stub is read from <code>.host-software</code>.</strong> Component, url, pin, worktrees, and the materialize command, from the committed recipe only, so it is safe in an un-materialized checkout (the worktrees themselves are never walked; <code>call/0011</code>).</li> <li><strong>Specs render.</strong> Each spec becomes a fenced code page, navigable from its milestone; the What contract is published, not listed as bare filenames.</li> <li><strong>A coverage gate.</strong> <code>host-lifecycle book --check</code> fails the build naming any room that has source material but renders no page with content; a room with no source (a fresh <code>call/</code>, a project with no software yet) is legitimately empty and skipped.</li> </ol> <p><code>book.toml</code> and <code>docs/</code> are generated output (gitignored), regenerated in CI before <code>mdbook build</code>. The publisher lives in <code>host-lifecycle</code> (the token-free generator), the reference Site workflow and the canonical-order documentation live in <code>host-template</code>, and the upgrade is recorded in the template's <code>UPGRADING.md</code> ledger (requires <code>host-lifecycle v0.6.1</code>).</p> <h2 id="consequences-55"><a class="header" href="#consequences-55">Consequences</a></h2> <ul> <li>Good: the four findings stop reproducing on this repository's site, and every future adopter inherits one maintained, tested artifact instead of a footgun.</li> <li>Good: the <code>src = "."</code> contradiction with the template's own guidance is resolved; this repository now obeys the rule it published.</li> <li>Neutral: the doc site is now a build-time generation step (run the publisher, then mdBook) rather than a hand-maintained <code>SUMMARY.md</code>.</li> <li>Limit: prose pulled in by copy keeps its own relative links; cross-room links resolve because <code>docs/</code> mirrors the room layout, but a generator change that moves a room would need the links revisited. The coverage gate guards room presence, not link correctness.</li> </ul> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><blockquote> <p><strong>Superseded.</strong> Retained as immutable history, not current guidance.</p> </blockquote> <h1 id="rung-discharge-requires-a-signed-verifier-pass-attestation-not-name-presence"><a class="header" href="#rung-discharge-requires-a-signed-verifier-pass-attestation-not-name-presence">Rung discharge requires a signed verifier-pass attestation, not name-presence</a></h1> <ul> <li> <p>Status: superseded by <code>call/0018</code>. The CI-signed ed25519 token requires per-adopter key management (a deal-breaker: operator burden + a fragile, human-rooted trust anchor) and complicates the bare-store/parallel-worktree model (per-project secrets + <code>.att</code> files in every worktree). <code>call/0018</code> keeps this decision's principle (<code>AVAILABLE ≠ DISCHARGED</code>, discharge needs a real PASS) but replaces the mechanism with <strong>re-derivation in a pinned toolchain</strong> (no keys, no CI overfit). The body below is the historical record of the rejected approach.</p> </li> <li> <p>Date: 2026-06-20</p> </li> <li> <p>Scope: host-prove, host-lifecycle, host-lint (the verification toolchain)</p> </li> <li> <p>Relates: <code>call/0002</code> (verification lanes by property type, the rungs extend it); <code>plan/0023</code> (the verification ladder this hardens); <code>plan/0024</code> (the milestone that implements this); connollydavid/host #8 (discharge is name-presence), #9 (bound dropped), #10-#12, #13 (LEXICON provenance). Generalizes the reproducible-build attestation already shipping in <code>.host-software</code> (<code>artifact = … <sha256></code> + <code>toolchain = …@sha256</code>, recomputed offline by <code>software --verify-build</code>).</p> </li> </ul> <h2 id="context-and-problem-statement-37"><a class="header" href="#context-and-problem-statement-37">Context and Problem Statement</a></h2> <p><code>plan/0023</code> added deep-verification rungs (Apalache, TLAPS, Kani) discharging obligations dispositioned <code>apalache:</code>/<code>tlaps:</code>/<code>kani:</code>. The tool validated a disposition with <code>obligation_gaps</code> calling <code>src.contains(name)</code>: it checked the proof was <strong>present by name</strong>, never that it <strong>passed</strong>. So a stub, a failing check, or a vacuous <code>THEOREM X == TRUE</code> satisfied <code>obligations</code> and <code>software --check</code>; the rung sold as "stronger than a test" became weaker than one (#8). Compounding it, the soundness <strong>bound</strong> of the bounded tools (Apalache <code>--length=N</code>, Kani <code>--unwind=K</code>) was unrepresentable, dropped from <code>verdict.py</code>, and a bounded check was presented as a complete proof (#9).</p> <p><code>AVAILABLE ≠ DISCHARGED</code>: availability of a proof is not discharge of an obligation. The audience includes a weak (4B) agent who will forge or shortcut anything not mechanically enforced, and the hook path must stay network-free and fast. A committed plaintext attestation is forgeable (the 4B hand-types <code>{PASS, bound, sha}</code>); running the verifier in the hook breaks network-free.</p> <h2 id="decision-48"><a class="header" href="#decision-48">Decision</a></h2> <p><strong>An obligation discharges only against a CI-signed attestation token that binds the verifier's PASS verdict, its bound, and the digests of the proven inputs, verified offline at check time.</strong></p> <ul> <li><strong>Token:</strong> one <code>.att</code> per obligation / per cited reference, co-located with the spec in the software repo (<code>call/0010</code>, plan/0012). Fields: <code>claim</code> (the disposition verbatim), <code>verdict</code> (<code>verdict.py</code>'s exact PASS line), <code>bound</code> (required for bounded tools; <code>unbounded</code> only for TLAPS; absent ⇒ HAZARD), <code>inputs</code> (<code>git hash-object</code> of each consumed source; for LEXICON, <code>content-sha</code> of the fetched URL body), <code>tool</code> (from <code>tools.lock</code>), <code>sig</code> (ed25519 over the canonical concatenation).</li> <li><strong>Minter:</strong> the CI verification lane (the one <code>call/0002</code>/plan/0023 already require) signs with an ed25519 private key held only in CI secrets, after the verifier exits 0. The agent commits the <code>.att</code>; CI fails if it does not match a fresh run (no write-back).</li> <li><strong>Consumer:</strong> <code>host-lifecycle obligations</code>/<code>software --check</code> verify the signature against a public key shipped in the binary, recompute the input digests (mismatch ⇒ stale ⇒ HAZARD), and require <code>verdict</code> be a PASS word and <code>bound</code> ≥ the declared bound. This replaces <code>src.contains</code>.</li> </ul> <p>The same token grounds LEXICON (#13) reference provenance: a network-having lane binds and signs the cited URL's <code>content-sha</code>, which the offline gate verifies; the weak agent cannot fabricate a URL whose CI-fetched body-hash matches a token it never obtained.</p> <h2 id="consequences-56"><a class="header" href="#consequences-56">Consequences</a></h2> <ul> <li><strong>Weak agents are hard-gated; strong agents keep authoring latitude.</strong> No shortcut mints a token without a real CI pass; a strong agent authors the proof/bound freely, but the output is verified, not trusted, and a later silent weakening re-stales the token via the input digest.</li> <li><strong>Bound becomes first-class:</strong> <code>verdict.py</code> must emit it from the real invocation before it can be signed (the #9 fix is a prerequisite, not an add-on).</li> <li><strong>Property triviality is explicitly NOT closed.</strong> The token attests that the verifier ran and passed at bound N, not that the property is meaningful; a vacuous proof still passes. Whether a proof proves the <em>right</em> thing stays a human/strong-agent review concern; it is not mechanizable, and this decision does not claim to gate it.</li> <li><strong>Key management is now soundness-critical</strong> (a leaked CI key forges tokens); key rotation is a future <code>call/</code> decision. A new crypto dependency (ed25519 verify) enters host-lifecycle.</li> </ul> <h2 id="alternatives-considered-3"><a class="header" href="#alternatives-considered-3">Alternatives considered</a></h2> <ul> <li><strong>Plaintext committed attestation:</strong> forgeable by a 4B (hand-typed); relocates #8, does not fix it.</li> <li><strong>Run the verifier in the hook / on <code>--check</code>:</strong> sound but breaks the network-free, fast hook constraint (Kani/Apalache/TLAPS are heavy); CI-only, it is just "the lanes already run it."</li> <li><strong>Query live CI status:</strong> network + platform coupling, unavailable offline / fresh-clone / non-GitHub, carries no bound, forgeable via workflow YAML.</li> </ul> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><blockquote> <p><strong>Superseded.</strong> Retained as immutable history, not current guidance.</p> </blockquote> <h1 id="every-lifecycle-phase-discharges-to-a-tool-written-receipt-release-is-a-strict-tool-carried-phase"><a class="header" href="#every-lifecycle-phase-discharges-to-a-tool-written-receipt-release-is-a-strict-tool-carried-phase">Every lifecycle phase discharges to a tool-written receipt; release is a strict, tool-carried phase</a></h1> <ul> <li>Status: superseded by the methodology spine (host-template @ 617e420, where the lifecycle manifest makes every phase emit a receipt)</li> <li>Date: 2026-06-20</li> <li>Scope: host-lifecycle, host-template (the lifecycle tool and the spine it reads)</li> <li>Relates: <code>call/0016</code> (the attestation primitive, same idea, here applied to phases not proofs); <code>plan/0022</code> (the <code>.host</code> applied-set this generalizes from upgrades to all phases); <code>plan/0005</code> / <code>call/0010</code> (<code>repro-exempt</code>, the migrated-software escape pattern reused for release); <code>plan/0024</code> (the attestation infra the strict release consumes); connollydavid/host #14 (verify-build in the pinned toolchain, a strict-release prerequisite). Implemented by <code>plan/0025</code>.</li> </ul> <h2 id="context-and-problem-statement-38"><a class="header" href="#context-and-problem-statement-38">Context and Problem Statement</a></h2> <p>The lifecycle (classify / adopt / embed / remap / verify / publish / upgrade) is realised as scattered skills + <code>host-lifecycle</code> subcommands. The phase <strong>order</strong> lives only in spine prose, re-typed in three places (CLAUDE.md, STRUCTURE.md, UPGRADING.md); there is no tool-readable manifest, and no <code>release</code> phase at all, so every software release is hand-orchestrated with raw git/cargo/docker.</p> <p>This session demonstrated the failure mode directly. A <strong>strong</strong> agent (the author of this decision), with the rules in hand, skipped the <code>verify</code> gate and hand-rolled a release, nearly mis-recording the artifact hash (the byte-identity assumption). A <strong>weak</strong> agent (Fen, the real 4B) skips structurally; it cannot assemble multi-step orchestration. Instructions are advisory; they fail for <strong>both</strong> classes, for different reasons. The methodology already has nine receipt-like mechanisms (obligation <code>waived:</code>, the <code>.host</code> applied-set, <code>upgrade --unverified call/NNNN</code>, <code>repro-exempt = call/NNNN</code>, the <code>software --verify-build</code> artifact re-derivation, <code>.host-lintignore</code>, <code>call/</code> <code>Status:</code>, <code>.host-software</code> artifact hashes, append-only MEMORY/PLAN descopes), and most already record skips. But no single format binds them, so a skip recorded in one mechanism is invisible to the gate of another.</p> <h2 id="decision-49"><a class="header" href="#decision-49">Decision</a></h2> <ol> <li> <p><strong>Universal receipts.</strong> Every lifecycle phase, on every project, discharges to an append-only, <strong>tool-written</strong> receipt: <code>done</code> (with machine-checkable evidence) or <code>skip</code>/<code>n-a</code> (with a recorded reason: free text for the trivial, a <code>call/NNNN</code> citation for the substantive). A phase named in the manifest with <strong>no</strong> receipt is the <em>sole</em> defect <code>software --check</code> gates. Silent skipping becomes mechanically impossible, equally for weak and strong agents: a weak agent cannot forge <code>done</code> evidence, a strong agent cannot omit the receipt. The receipt unifies the nine existing mechanisms under one format and one gate.</p> </li> <li> <p><strong>A tool-readable lifecycle manifest</strong> in the spine (host-template), single-source, replaces the three prose copies. Each phase carries its <strong>modality</strong>: <code>once</code> (classify/adopt/remap), <code>continuous</code> (verify/publish), <code>per-revision</code> (upgrade), <code>conditional-on-Where</code> + <code>recurring-per-component</code> (embed, release), plus its command/skill and the shape of its evidence. <strong>release</strong> joins as a first-class phase.</p> </li> <li> <p><strong>Strict, tool-carried release.</strong> <code>host-lifecycle release</code> orchestrates the release as single commands (<code>--next</code> / <code>--record</code>): run <code>verify</code> (refuse on red), then build <strong>in the recorded toolchain</strong> (host#14), then require a CI attestation (plan/0024) so <strong>BUILT ≠ RELEASED</strong>, then re-pin <code>.host-software</code>, then tag, then write the release receipt; <code>software --check</code> re-verifies every receipt. Strict means <em>maximum mechanical enforcement, minimum agent steps</em>; the tool carries it so Fen can execute it (the resolution of the Fen ↔ Orin/Bly tension the persona review surfaced: soundness is non-negotiable for Orin/Bly, un-orchestratable by Fen; the tool, not the agent, holds the sequence).</p> </li> <li> <p><strong>Migrated escape.</strong> A case-(b) component may discharge <code>release</code> as <code>skip: call/NNNN</code>, which mirrors <code>repro-exempt</code> (it keeps its own foreign release process). The escape is itself a receipt: recorded, not silent.</p> </li> </ol> <h2 id="consequences-57"><a class="header" href="#consequences-57">Consequences</a></h2> <ul> <li>The spine's "all lifecycle phases are <strong>unconditional</strong>, no opt-out" rule is <strong>revised</strong>: the invariant becomes "every phase emits a <strong>receipt</strong>," not "every phase <strong>runs</strong>." Conditionality and recurrence are expressed as receipt <em>types</em>, never as silent absence. This is a real spine semantics change, delivered through an UPGRADING entry (honest, not free).</li> <li>The strict release <strong>depends on</strong> host#14 and plan/0024; a shallow interim is explicitly rejected (the operator's "build the strictest possible"). Build order is software-first: host#14, then attestation, then host-lifecycle (manifest parse + receipts + release), then spine manifest, then dogfood.</li> <li>The receipts ledger is <strong>copy-at-version sensitive</strong>: a project behind on upgrades carries an older manifest, so enforcement is only as current as its last upgrade. Mitigation: the manifest ships via UPGRADING; <code>software --check</code> degrades (warns) on a missing/old manifest rather than crashing. This is in tension with plan/0022's honest-partial-upgrades and is recorded, not resolved here.</li> <li>Attestation key-management risk is inherited from <code>call/0016</code>.</li> </ul> <h2 id="alternatives-considered-4"><a class="header" href="#alternatives-considered-4">Alternatives considered</a></h2> <ul> <li><strong>Spec-only modality typing, no receipts:</strong> encodes conditionality yet still permits the <em>silent</em> skip of a phase that does apply; it does not gate the strong-agent failure this session exhibited.</li> <li><strong>Shallow release orchestration</strong>: rejected by the operator ("strictest possible") and by Orin/Bly: a shallow release lets a stale or unattested artifact ship, and a later cold read cannot catch it.</li> <li><strong>A new orchestrator tool</strong>: rejected: it fragments lifecycle ownership across two binaries; host-lifecycle already owns every phase. (The operator's earlier skepticism, "are you correct in suggesting a new one?", was right.)</li> </ul> <h2 id="review-hardening-post-adversarial-review"><a class="header" href="#review-hardening-post-adversarial-review">Review hardening (post-adversarial-review)</a></h2> <p>An adversarial review of the implementing milestone (<code>plan/0025/design-review.md</code>, 39 findings, proceed-with-changes) confirmed the decision but forced the mechanism to be strictly mechanical; the first cut's receipts were too self-asserted. The decision holds as written, refined by:</p> <ul> <li><strong>A receipt is never a plaintext self-assertion.</strong> <code>done</code> requires a re-runnable <code>recheck =</code> post-condition or signed/digest evidence; a phase whose evidence cannot be re-derived offline may not be <code>done</code>. (Inherits, not weakens, <code>call/0016</code>'s anti-forgery standard.)</li> <li><strong><code>n-a</code> is tool-computed from project state</strong>, not agent-asserted; a protected core (<code>verify</code>) is un-skippable; phase modality constrains the legal dispositions, gate-enforced.</li> <li><strong>The skip escape is content-validated</strong>: the cited decision is parsed (accepted Status, a Scope/<code>authorizes-skip:</code> header naming this phase+component, content-hashed), allowed only for recipe-proven migrated components, never greenfield. Mere file-existence is insufficient.</li> <li><strong>The manifest is read at the adopted revision; a missing one HAZARDs</strong> (never a silent pass).</li> <li><strong>Release has no degraded mode</strong>: plan/0024 is a hard prerequisite; absent it, an artifact-bearing release blocks. The tool computes the version and the hash; irreversible mutations (tag, re-pin) run last and resumably, after attestation.</li> </ul> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><blockquote> <p><strong>Superseded.</strong> Retained as immutable history, not current guidance.</p> </blockquote> <h1 id="releasing-a-tool-updates-the-templates-pins-of-that-tool"><a class="header" href="#releasing-a-tool-updates-the-templates-pins-of-that-tool">Releasing a tool updates the template's pins of that tool</a></h1> <ul> <li>Status: superseded by the spine</li> <li>Date: 2026-07-04</li> <li>Scope: the release process for any <code>host-*</code> tool that <code>host-template</code> carries. The template pins each such tool in more than one place, and a release is complete only when every one of those pins equals the released commit. Surfaced as connollydavid/host-lifecycle#9 and folded into <code>plan/0056</code>. This binds how a release propagates, next to the existing propagate rule.</li> <li>Relates: <code>plan/0056</code> (the robustness superset that surfaced it); <code>call/0021</code> and <code>plan/0032</code> (re-vendor and propagate to consumers on a tool release); <code>call/0010</code> (software as a bare store pinned in <code>.host-software</code>); the dual-release-authority rule (the producer tag is the release, and <code>.host-software</code> pins it).</li> </ul> <h2 id="supersession"><a class="header" href="#supersession">Supersession</a></h2> <p>The anti-ouroboros validate gate (<code>host-template/CLAUDE.md</code>) retires an <code>accepted</code> <code>call/</code> decision whose <code>Scope:</code> names <code>host-template</code>: such a rule is spine-resident, owned by the methodology. The cast deliberated whether to author the rule into the spine or keep it agentic-host-specific, and the operator ruled to author it. The rule now lives in the host-template spine as the release-side complement of the reference-don't-vendor rule, that a release reconciles every carried-template pin, phrased so a generic adopter reads the first clause and skips it, and validated Fen-safe by probing the real weak agent before it was authored. This record is kept for its history, and the rule stays enforced by <code>software --check</code>'s template-pin gate.</p> <h2 id="context-and-problem-statement-39"><a class="header" href="#context-and-problem-statement-39">Context and Problem Statement</a></h2> <p><code>host-template</code> is the scaffold for new agentic projects and the source of the methodology spine. It carries the <code>host-*</code> tools it depends on and pins each in more than one place:</p> <ul> <li>host-lifecycle: the <code>prose.yml</code> CI install (<code>cargo install … --rev <sha></code>) and the <code>tools/host-lifecycle</code> submodule gitlink, which <code>reproducible-build.yml</code> and <code>site.yml</code> build.</li> <li>host-lint: the <code>tools/host-lint</code> submodule gitlink.</li> </ul> <p>Each of these drifted while <code>.host-software</code> moved forward. At discovery the <code>tools/host-lifecycle</code> submodule sat at v0.15.1, <code>prose.yml</code> at v0.30.1, and <code>tools/host-lint</code> at v0.2.0, against a host gating on host-lifecycle v0.35.1 and host-lint v0.12.1. So the template handed new adopters tools twenty releases old, and the pin comment's claim to track "the same host-lifecycle the host gates on" was false. The <code>prose.yml</code> pin is the visible one; the two submodule gitlinks are easy to overlook, and they were the most stale.</p> <p>The release sequence re-pins <code>.host-software</code> and propagates to the consumer components (<code>call/0021</code>), but the template sits outside that consumer set, so its pins drift on every release with nothing to catch them.</p> <h2 id="decision-50"><a class="header" href="#decision-50">Decision</a></h2> <p>Every release of a <code>host-*</code> tool bumps every host-template pin of that tool to the released commit:</p> <ul> <li>host-lifecycle: the <code>prose.yml</code> <code>--rev</code> and the <code>tools/host-lifecycle</code> submodule gitlink.</li> <li>host-lint: the <code>tools/host-lint</code> submodule gitlink.</li> </ul> <p><code>host-lifecycle release</code> prints these as explicit outward steps next to the <code>.host-software</code> re-pin. <code>software --check</code> gates the invariant: <code>template_pin_problems</code> reads each template pin site and HAZARDs any that does not match the recorded <code>.host-software</code> pin of that tool, so a release that leaves a pin behind fails the whole-suite check. The invariant: every host-template pin of a tool equals the commit <code>.host-software</code> records for it.</p> <h2 id="consequences-58"><a class="header" href="#consequences-58">Consequences</a></h2> <ul> <li>New projects scaffold with current tools, and the template's own CI matches what it publishes.</li> <li>The template joins the surfaces a release reconciles, next to <code>.host-software</code> and the vendored-dependency bundle, and the gate covers every pin site.</li> <li>Each drifted pin is one HAZARD line that carries the site and both commits.</li> </ul> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><blockquote> <p><strong>Superseded.</strong> Retained as immutable history, not current guidance.</p> </blockquote> <h1 id="call0048-the-gate-runs-the-reference-sweep-over-the-record-rather-than-the-working-tree"><a class="header" href="#call0048-the-gate-runs-the-reference-sweep-over-the-record-rather-than-the-working-tree">call/0048: the gate runs the reference sweep, over the record rather than the working tree</a></h1> <ul> <li>Status: superseded by the spine (the rule lives in the template manual's reference discipline)</li> <li>Scope: the <code>verify</code> phase's recheck in <code>host-template/lifecycle.manifest</code>, host-lint's document walk, host-lifecycle's embedded engine, the upgrade ledger's verify convention</li> <li>Date: 2026-07-27</li> </ul> <h2 id="context-and-problem-19"><a class="header" href="#context-and-problem-19">Context and problem</a></h2> <p><a href="call/../plan/0077-reference-resolver/README.html">plan/0077</a> shipped a reference resolver and a sweep that nothing invokes. Its adversarial round named that the largest remaining gap: the capability is correct and surfaces nowhere. No lane runs it, no skill calls it, and the verify gate does not know it exists.</p> <p>The first proposal was to append it to the <code>verify</code> phase's recheck in <code>lifecycle.manifest</code>, which the tool reads live from the host-template submodule, so a pointer bump delivers it to every adopter with no per-project file to migrate. Because the recheck is an <code>&&</code> chain in which any non-zero result breaks the chain, and because the sweep exits 3 over this tree's several hundred advisory references, the proposal carried a shell fragment to tolerate that one code:</p> <pre><code>&& (host-lifecycle refs --check . || [ $? -eq 3 ]) </code></pre> <p>That fragment is correct POSIX and it was refused. What follows is why, and what replaced it.</p> <h2 id="how-this-was-decided-2"><a class="header" href="#how-this-was-decided-2">How this was decided</a></h2> <p>Two review rounds with the five personas, the fifth realized as the real weak model rather than simulated, then a question round in which the operator ruled. Every persona returned wire-with-changes in both rounds; none defended the fragment; none argued for leaving the sweep uninvoked.</p> <p>The weak-agent probes settled two things and failed at a third, which is recorded because the failure is the useful part.</p> <ul> <li><strong>The census captures the agent.</strong> Shown a <em>green</em> gate whose tail carried this tree's advisory block, the model abandoned the task it was on and went to remediate references, in both repeats. The words "Advisory: nothing is blocked" were in front of it both times. This reproduces plan/0077's recorded finding: shown a report of hundreds of items, the model acts on them whatever the text says.</li> <li><strong>The blocking half is legible.</strong> Shown a dead pointer, both repeats ran the exact command the output named.</li> <li><strong>The naming probe failed on position, and the failure exposed a second defect.</strong> Four candidate spellings presented as a list, rotated: the model chose the first-listed candidate in one rotation and the second-listed in the other. That is position bias rather than a preference for a word, so the probe settled nothing against <a href="call/0047-the-reproducibility-waiver-is-named-for-its-record.html">call/0047</a>'s standard. Worse, the candidate it chose from the second rotation named a quality rather than a thing, which the naming rule forbids, so an unscreened list let the probe hand back a name the rule rejects. Redesigned as a comprehension probe, one spelling per prompt with nothing to compare against, both rule-legal spellings were read correctly in every repeat, and neither invented a third exit code.</li> </ul> <h2 id="what-the-rounds-found"><a class="header" href="#what-the-rounds-found">What the rounds found</a></h2> <p>Four findings changed the design, and each was verified in the tree rather than taken on report.</p> <ol> <li><strong>The proposed verify condition was tautological.</strong> It grepped the fetched template, and <code>upgrade</code> refuses to run unless that template is checked out at the target revision, so the condition is a post-condition of the command's own precondition. It can never refuse a false record, and it can never detect a revert. The class is not confined to the new entry: of 49 ledger entries, 30 carry a <code>verify</code> and 26 of those grep a file under <code>host-template/</code>.</li> <li><strong>The gate corpus included the working tree.</strong> The sweep walks tracked and untracked markdown alike, so an uncommitted scratch note naming a record that does not exist turns the sweep red, which re-opens the verify receipt, which stops a component release at its first step.</li> <li><strong>The recheck's other clauses fail open.</strong> host-lint's document walk reads each file with <code>if let Ok(content)</code> and no else branch, so a document it cannot read is silently dropped and the run still reports clean. Reproduced: a tracked document carrying a real tell, made unreadable, yields <code>prose: clean</code> at exit 0. host-lifecycle's own walk carries the same shape, and two of its call sites turn a failed walk into an empty document set. This is the coverage class plan/0077 spent a milestone closing for one checker, alive in the clauses that actually run.</li> <li><strong>The ledger's version floor is printed and never enforced.</strong> It is parsed and stored, and nothing ever compares it to the running tool. An adopter who moves the template pointer while pinned to an older tool gets a usage failure that reads as a defect in their documents.</li> </ol> <h2 id="decision-51"><a class="header" href="#decision-51">Decision</a></h2> <ol> <li><strong>The gate calls a mode of the tool, never a shell fragment.</strong> The manifest line stays one verb per clause. The exit partition belongs where the tool's own tests can bite on it rather than in an unlinted string in a config file, and positional exit arithmetic is a trap for whoever extends the chain next, because the next clause appended binds to the wrong command.</li> <li><strong>The asymmetry is stated with its reason wherever it is read.</strong> A prose warning gates and a reference advisory does not, and the two sit in the same chain. Left unexplained it reads as an inconsistency, and the obvious repair is to tolerate the prose warning too, which would disarm a gate that an entire ledger entry exists to install. The reason is that a prose trope is the author's own text and always rewordable, while only the author knows which tracker a bare number meant.</li> <li><strong>The gate judges the record; the hook scans the working tree.</strong> A gate that reddens over an uncommitted note asserts something about a record that does not contain the note, which no one can re-derive from any clone. The hook keeps the wider corpus, because catching a document before it is staged is its job.</li> <li><strong>A walk that cannot read a document says so.</strong> Failing closed is right and blaming the file is not. This applies to every walk in the chain rather than the one that was fixed.</li> <li><strong>A verify condition that the command's own preconditions make true is not a verify.</strong> The new entry tests a capability of the adopter's own binary, in one command with no shell operators so it survives a non-POSIX shell, and it accepts a tree that the gate would redden, because requiring a clean tree would wedge an adopter whose one dead pointer sits in a record they must not rewrite.</li> <li><strong>The census keeps a home, away from the gate.</strong> The blocking half reports in the gate; the per-file enumeration answers a question someone asked, so the debt stays visible without ambushing a session that asked something else.</li> </ol> <h2 id="consequences-59"><a class="header" href="#consequences-59">Consequences</a></h2> <ul> <li>The reference sweep runs in the <code>verify</code> recheck, so a reference naming a record that does not exist re-opens the verify receipt and stops a release at its first step, over tracked documents only.</li> <li>host-lint gains a corpus selector and a walk that reports what it could not read; host-lifecycle's embedded engine moves to that release, which closes a divergence in which two engines gave two verdicts over one file while neither named which had spoken.</li> <li>The upgrade ledger gains its first entry whose verify tests something the adopter did. The other 26 are a finding of their own and are not swept here; they need a documented map and their own milestone, on the same discipline the append-only exception requires.</li> <li>The reference discipline lands in this repository's own operating manual before the entry that ships it is recorded, because an entry whose author never applied it is the defect the upstream seat is worst at seeing.</li> <li>Nothing in this decision retires the shell fragment as a technique elsewhere. It is refused for the recheck, where the manifest is the one spine file whose contents are executed and no test has ever executed one.</li> </ul> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><blockquote> <p><strong>Superseded.</strong> Retained as immutable history, not current guidance.</p> </blockquote> <h1 id="call0060-a-teaching-layer-change-re-baselines-in-place-and-the-record-keeps-the-trail"><a class="header" href="#call0060-a-teaching-layer-change-re-baselines-in-place-and-the-record-keeps-the-trail">call/0060: a teaching-layer change re-baselines in place, and the record keeps the trail</a></h1> <ul> <li>Status: superseded by the spine</li> <li>Scope: agentic-host, and the host-template spine it carries</li> <li>Date: 2026-10-17</li> <li>Relates: plan/0100, plan/0090, plan/0091, call/0059, the append-only rule in the root manual</li> </ul> <h2 id="context-and-problem-20"><a class="header" href="#context-and-problem-20">Context and problem</a></h2> <p>The operator asked for a "good forgetting" modality: a paradigm change whose teaching surfaces carry no hint that the change was ever a change, beginning with the address possessive (<code>lemu</code> = you, <code>lemr</code> = your). Taken whole, the ask collides with three load-bearing rules: MEMORY.md is append-only with one narrow map-only exception, the certification of plan/0091 measured a named list of forms and must not silently cover a different one, and the <code>UPGRADING.md</code> ledger is the spine's memory, without which adopters cannot date their own manuals. Taken as a statement about the teaching layer, the ask is already house practice: the zh partials left the manuals wholesale with the doctrine kept whole, and the <code>lself</code> ruling corrected the manual in place while the adjudication went to memory.</p> <h2 id="decision-52"><a class="header" href="#decision-52">Decision</a></h2> <p>The modality is adopted in bounded form, named honestly as re-baselining with an audit trail.</p> <ul> <li>The teaching layer (manuals, skills, vocabulary, classifier tables, the manual's exemplar exchanges) states the paradigm in present tense. No "newly added" markers, no transition notes, no deprecation text.</li> <li>The enforcement instruments carry no transition state: no warning tier for a retired form, no sunset schedule, no scheduled escalation. A paradigm rule enforces at full strength from the moment its entry lands.</li> <li>The record layer stays append-only exactly as the standing rules require: memory entries, decisions, closed plans, and receipts are never struck.</li> <li>A measurement names the form list it measured; a paradigm change either re-measures or scopes the standing chart by name, never silently.</li> <li>The ledger entry carries the version truth: a cold reader dates any manual by reconciling it against the ledger, which is why the teaching layer may forget safely.</li> </ul> <p>First test case: the address possessive of plan/0100.</p> <h2 id="consequences-60"><a class="header" href="#consequences-60">Consequences</a></h2> <ul> <li>A future paradigm change on this host follows the same shape: rule it (cast, then a blind bench where the question admits one), re-baseline the teaching layer, append the record, scope the measurement, ledger the entry.</li> <li>An unrecorded forgetting is indistinguishable from an error; the decision authorizing forgetting is itself permanent record and is never struck by the modality it authorizes.</li> <li>The bench's named cost of the no-transition axiom (old and new prose can coexist without a marker) is answered by the ledger, not by the instruments.</li> </ul> <div style="break-before: page;
